units.title: How key presses are written
units.summary: The press types TE's guide draws (single, combo, sequence, hold, turn, click, hold and turn, keyboard, chords) and the text notation this manual uses for them, such as `shift + M1` or `record + play → play`.

facts.text: TE's diagrams show a few press types: single, combo (hold one key, press another), sequence (one after the other), hold, turn or click an encoder, hold a key while turning, keyboard notes and chords.
When a diagram highlights all four encoders, any of them will do.
A diagram that shows the whole keyboard is there for orientation, not as a request to play it.
The guide's legend labels its hold-and-turn picture as a second sequence press and swaps two captions (all encoders, keyboard).
This manual writes a combo with a plus sign (`shift + M1` = hold shift, press `M1`) and a sequence with an arrow (`record + play → play` = release, then press play again).
`hold com` is a long press, `turn E2` and `click E4` move an encoder, and `Tn`, `step n` or `key` stand for any track, step or keyboard key.

units.body:
TE's guide draws its shortcuts as highlighted keys; this manual writes the same gestures as text,
which the agent can say and the replica can animate.

units.title: Main modes
units.summary: Four mode keys switch the whole unit between making sounds (instrument), the utility tracks (auxiliary), building the song (arrange) and balancing it (mix).

facts.text: Each main mode has its own key, and TE frames them as stages of a track's life — compose in `instrument`, transpose and process in `auxiliary`, assemble in `arrange`, balance in `mix`.
In instrument mode `T1`…`T8` select and edit the eight instrument tracks, each running a synth engine or a sampler.
In auxiliary mode the same keys reach the eight auxiliary tracks, which transpose other tracks, play punch-in FX, handle external inputs and outputs and hold the send effects.
Arrange groups the tracks' patterns into scenes and chains scenes into songs.
Mix sets each track's level and pan and holds the master EQ and compressor.
In arrange, pressing `arrange` again swaps the track keys between instrument and auxiliary tracks.
In mix, pressing `mix` again swaps the track keys between instrument and auxiliary tracks.
`shift + instrument` opens the preset settings of the selected instrument track.
In arrange, `shift + arrange` opens song mode.

units.body:
The track keys, module keys and encoders keep their jobs in every mode — pick a track, open a page,
turn a knob — but what they address changes with the mode.

units.title: Module pages (M1–M4)
units.summary: In instrument, auxiliary and mix mode the keys `M1…M4` under the screen open four pages (modules), and the encoders edit what the open page shows. Arrange has no modules.

facts.text: Every main mode except arrange splits its controls into four modules, opened with the keys printed 1 to 4 under the screen (`M1`…`M4`).
On a module page, `E1`…`E4` edit the parameters shown for the selected track.
Pages with more than four parameters show the rest while `shift` is held.

On instrument tracks the pages are engine (`M1`), envelopes (`M2`), filter (`M3`) and LFO (`M4`); `shift + M3` and `shift + M4` choose the filter type and LFO type, and `shift + M1` brings up the preset browser, where OS 1.1.33 changes the engine.
Auxiliary tracks use the pages their own way; on the brain track, `M1` sets key and scale and `M2` routes tracks into it.
In mix mode, `M1` holds levels, pans and sends per track, `M2` the master EQ, `M3` the master saturator and `M4` the master section.
On screen, each parameter carries a small dot or cap in its encoder's shade — dark for `E1`, mid grey for `E2`, light grey for `E3`, white for `E4` — so a glance tells which knob moves what.
Brief popups, such as the octave card or the mixer's send display, sit over the page and fade away on their own after a second or two.
On some auxiliary tracks the next page slides in sideways — the brain's routing page from its `M1`, and the external MIDI track's CC pages from `M1` to `M2` to `M3`.

procedures.goal: Edit a page's shift-layer parameters

units.body:
The mode decides what the pages are about and the track keys which track they edit. Any module-page
parameter of an instrument or auxiliary track can be parameter-locked per step.

units.title: Track keys and the active track
units.summary: The eight track keys select which track you play, sequence and edit — instrument tracks or auxiliary tracks, depending on the mode. The lit key marks the active track.

facts.text: The OP-XY has sixteen sequencer tracks in two sets of eight, instrument and auxiliary; `T1`…`T8` address the set the current mode shows.
In auxiliary mode the keys stand for brain (`T1`), punch-in FX (`T2`), external MIDI (`T3`), external CV (`T4`), external audio (`T5`), tape (`T6`), FX I (`T7`) and FX II (`T8`).
Notes you play, steps you enter and pages you edit all belong to the active track; pressing another track key makes that track active.
The active track's key lights white for an instrument track and red for an auxiliary track.
`shift + Tn` opens the preset browser for that track; on instrument tracks it also picks a synth engine or sample pack.
Over MIDI, CC102 on channel 1 selects a track counting from zero; value 2 selected track 3.

procedures.goal: Load a preset onto a track

steps.note: opens the preset browser for that track

units.body:
The mode sets whether the track keys mean instrument or auxiliary tracks; holding one track key
while pressing others links tracks instead of switching.

units.title: Linking tracks
units.summary: Hold one track key and press up to three others to link them; whatever you play on the held (primary) track then drives every linked track, which is how you layer sounds.

facts.text: To link tracks, keep one track key held and press the keys of the tracks to join it; four tracks at most can be linked.
The track whose key you held becomes the primary track, and playing or sequencing it controls all linked tracks.
A linked track still plays on its own when you select it directly rather than the primary track.
Pitchbend from the primary track reaches the linked tracks.
Arpeggiator notes are not passed on to linked tracks.
OS 1.1.15 reworked how octave offsets behave on linked tracks; the changelog gives no details.
The guide does not describe how to undo a link.
Linking tracks is unrelated to sound link in arrange, which keeps one sound across a track's patterns.

procedures.goal: Link tracks so that one track plays several

steps.note: keep the first key held and press up to three more track keys

procedures.result: The held track is the primary; playing it also plays the linked tracks.

units.body:
Linking is the layering tool: `hold T3` and press `T4`, and a bass line played on track 3 also
sounds through track 4's synth, each track keeping its own sound and settings.

units.title: Patterns, scenes, songs and projects
units.summary: A project holds everything; each track has up to 16 patterns, a scene says which pattern every track plays, and a song is an ordered list of scenes. The guide's workflow chapter still gives older limits.

facts.text: A pattern is one track's sequence of notes or sounds and holds at most 120 notes.
Each track holds up to 16 patterns (OS 1.1.15 raised it from nine, the number older TE texts still give).
A pattern has up to four bars; with track scale it can last up to 64 bars.
Each pattern can carry its own sound unless sound link (arrange) holds one sound for the track.
A pattern added since OS 1.1.25 starts with the player type the track is using.
A scene records which pattern each track plays, plus the track volumes and mutes, and lasts as long as its longest pattern; a project has 99 scenes.
A song plays up to 96 scenes in order; a project holds up to 14 songs, one per white key (older TE texts say nine).
A project contains the tracks with their patterns, scenes and songs; the unit stores thousands of projects.

units.body:
Nested boxes: patterns per track, scenes that freeze a combination of patterns and mutes, songs
that play scenes in order, all inside one project.

units.title: From first notes to a song
units.summary: The usual path on the OP-XY — sequence one track at a time, make pattern variations in arrange, capture them as scenes, then order the scenes into a song and mix it.

facts.text: The OP-XY is built around sequencing one track at a time and stacking tracks into the layers of a song.
TE's workflow chapter offers one suggested way of working, not the only one.
A song starts with sequencing the tracks in instrument mode.
In arrange you then add new patterns, or copy existing ones and change them, to get the variations for different parts.
Moving between scenes and giving each its own pattern combination builds the sections of the song.
Once a few scenes work, song mode puts them in playing order.

procedures.goal: Put a first note into a track's sequence

steps.note: play a note on the keyboard, then press the step where it should go

procedures.result: The note plays on that step every time the pattern comes round.

procedures.goal: Order finished scenes into a song

steps.note: type the scene numbers in playing order

units.body:
The suggested path mirrors the modes — write in instrument, vary and combine in arrange, balance in
mix — but nothing forces that order.

units.title: Firmware versions and this manual
units.summary: TE's guide describes OS 1.1.15, while this manual targets OS 1.1.33; facts that changed later carry the release that changed them. How to see which OS your unit runs.

facts.text: TE's online guide is labelled v1.1.15 and describes OS 1.1.15.
The newest release is OS 1.1.33 (2 September 2026); the releases after the guide are 1.1.17, 1.1.18, 1.1.21, 1.1.25, 1.1.32 and 1.1.33.
This manual was checked on a unit running OS 1.1.33, hardware revision 2.
The installed OS version appears on screen, with the logo, every time the unit starts.
Over USB MIDI the unit reports its OS version when asked with TE's own SysEx greeting; the standard MIDI identity request leaves the version blank.

units.body:
OS 1.1.17 to 1.1.33 added features and fixes that TE's guide does not mention yet. When an answer
depends on the version, check the boot screen first; this manual assumes 1.1.33.

units.title: Panel layout
units.summary: A map of the top panel — mode keys, module keys, track and step keys, transport, keyboard, function keys, encoders, screen and sockets — and the names this manual uses for each.

facts.text: Seen from above, the controls sit on a grid of 17 columns and 6 rows. The top two rows hold the speaker, the volume knob, the screen and the four encoders; keys fill the four rows below.

Row three runs mode keys, `M1`…`M4`, then `T1`…`T8`; row four is `step 1`…`step 16`; the bottom two rows put `record`, `play`, `stop` above `[-]`, `[+]`, `shift` on the left, with the keyboard to their right.
The rightmost column holds `sample`, `com`, `player` and `bar`, top to bottom; `project` and `tempo` sit just below the volume knob.

Four keys pick the main mode: `instrument` for the eight sound tracks, `auxiliary` for the eight utility tracks (brain, punch-in FX, external gear, tape, send effects), `arrange` for patterns, scenes and songs, and `mix` for levels, pans, EQ and the master compressor.
The keys printed 1 to 4 directly under the screen are the module keys, written `M1`…`M4`. Each opens one page of the current mode, and the four encoders then edit what that page shows.
Arrange is the only main mode without module pages.
Some pages keep a second set of parameters on a shift layer, reached by holding `shift`.
The eight track keys under the encoders choose which track you edit — an instrument track in instrument mode, an auxiliary track in auxiliary mode.
The sixteen step keys across the middle form the step sequencer, the grid you program notes and sounds into.
`record` arms recording of notes and knob moves, `play` starts playback and `stop` halts it.
Pressing `play` again during playback jumps back to the start of the pattern.
A second press of `stop` cuts off every note and sound that is still ringing.
`[-]` and `[+]` move the keyboard one octave down or up; several pages give them other jobs.

On an instrument page, `[-]` and `[+]` bring up a small white card low in the middle of the screen, with a mini keyboard and the octave offset in thin digits (+0, +1, −1, −3 …); it fades after a second or two. On the external CV page the offset appears inside the meter card instead.
`shift` does nothing alone: held with another key it opens that key's secondary function or page.
The two-octave keyboard of 24 keys lies right of the transport keys, below the step keys.
Every white key carries the icon of one step component; counted from the left they are `natural 1`…`natural 14`.
The ten black keys double as number keys, marked 1–9 and 0 from the left; this manual calls them `accidental 1`…`accidental 0`.
`sample` (top right corner) starts sampling from any screen.
`project` opens the list of projects, where you create, open and manage them.
`tempo` sets the song speed, the swing and the metronome.
`com` is the hub for system settings, wired and wireless connections and output routing.
`player` turns the notes of a track into arpeggios, chords and other note effects.
`bar` lengthens the sequence and holds sequence-wide settings such as quantisation.
The volume knob is at the top left, next to the speaker.
The four encoders shade from dark to light: dark gray, mid gray, light gray and white. This manual calls them `E1`, `E2`, `E3` and `E4` in that order.
The pitchbend strip on the lower left edge responds to pressure — push its left end to bend down, its right end to bend up.
The right side carries the power switch, the USB-C port and four 3.5 mm jacks — audio out, multi-out, MIDI in and audio in.
A small built-in microphone and a vertical LED level meter sit in the top right margin.
Holding `com` turns the level meter into a rough battery gauge.

units.body:
The OP-XY packs everything into one flat grid of square keys, so a few landmarks make it easy to
find your way. The left block is about _where you are_: the four mode keys (`instrument`,
`auxiliary`, `arrange`, `mix`) and, below them, the transport. The middle is about _what you edit_:
the module keys `M1`…`M4` under the screen choose a page, the track keys under the encoders choose a
track, and the step keys below them are the sequencer. The right-hand column holds the utility keys
(`sample`, `com`, `player`, `bar`).

Most editing follows one pattern: pick a mode, pick a track, pick a page, then `turn E1`…`E4`.
`shift` reaches a second layer of almost every key and page, and the keyboard's white and black keys
double as step-component and number keys when a page asks for them.

units.title: Power, battery and charging
units.summary: The power switch on the right side turns the unit on (up) and off (down); work is kept automatically. The battery charges over USB-C from 5 V USB power.

facts.text: The power switch sits on the right side; push it up to switch on and down to switch off.
At start-up the screen shows the logo and the OS version, then the last selected track.
Switching off loses nothing; the unit stores your work automatically and comes back exactly as you left it.
The system settings offer an instant or a delayed power-off; delayed guards against accidental switch-offs.
The battery charges over USB-C from a computer or USB charger; the level meter shows when it is full.
Charge only from 5 V USB power; TE's warranty excludes damage caused by any other charging method.
Charge the battery at least every six months; a battery left unused for a long time may no longer charge.
The battery page of the system settings shows the charge level and the input current limit.

procedures.goal: Switch the OP-XY on or off

steps.note: up is on, down is off

procedures.goal: Check the battery level

steps.note: read the level meter at the top right

units.body: There is no need to save before switching off; the OP-XY writes your work as you go.

units.title: Connectors and jacks
units.summary: The right edge carries four 3.5 mm jacks — audio out, multi-out, MIDI in, audio in — plus the USB-C port and the power switch. What each one is for.

facts.text: Along the right edge, starting at the back, sit audio out, multi-out, MIDI in and audio in, then the USB-C port, the charge LED and the power switch near the front.
The 3.5 mm stereo audio out feeds headphones or speakers.
The audio out also supports headsets with a built-in microphone.
The 3.5 mm stereo audio in records line-level sources directly into the OP-XY.
The 3.5 mm MIDI in lets other MIDI gear play and control the OP-XY.
The multi-out jack works in one of six modes at a time — audio, MIDI, CV and gate, or sync pulses at sync8, sync16 or sync24.
The USB-C port charges the battery and carries audio and MIDI in both directions.

units.body:
None of the jacks is a dedicated MIDI out: wired MIDI and sync leave through the multi-out, in the
mode picked on the com page, or over USB. Levels for each jack are listed under the specifications.

units.title: Technical specifications
units.summary: Size, build, screen, storage, battery, processing and the electrical figures of the audio, CV and sync connections.

facts.text: The body is black anodised aluminium, the low-profile keyboard is backlit, and the custom colour LCD sits directly on the keyboard.
It measures 288 × 102 × 29 mm and weighs 900 g.
There are 68 mechanical keys (the keyboard included), four encoders and a pressure-sensitive pitchbend strip.
The guide lists a 480 × 220 pixel IPS TFT screen.
TE's product page gives the screen as 480 × 222 pixels.
There are 8 GB of user storage.
Over MTP a unit shows an 8.59 GB volume.
The rechargeable battery is rated for 16 hours.
Bluetooth LE MIDI is built in.
Inside are two Blackfin processor cores, a three-core DSP co-processor and a 6-axis motion sensor.
Polyphony is 24 voices, shared by all tracks.
The model number is TE033AS001; a unit checked on OS 1.1.33 reports hardware revision 2.
Audio out: 8 dBu (2 Vrms) level, 124 dBA signal-to-noise ratio.
Audio in: 8 dBu (2 Vrms) level, 98 dBA signal-to-noise ratio, 13 kΩ impedance, 0–31 dB of analogue gain.
Multi-out: audio at 2 dBu (1 Vrms), CV within ±5 V, sync and gate pulses at 5.2 V.

units.body: Where TE's pages disagree (the screen height), both figures are given.

units.title: TE boot (bootloader menu)
units.summary: The bootloader menu, reached by holding `com` while switching on. `T1` installs firmware, `T7` factory-resets and `T8` opens the system menu with the key test; switching off and on leaves.

facts.text: TE boot is the OP-XY's bootloader, the program that loads and starts its firmware.
Firmware updates, factory resets and hardware tests all run from TE boot rather than from the normal OS.
To reach it, switch the unit off, then keep `com` held while switching it back on.
The TE boot screen offers three numbered choices, each picked with the track key of its number: firmware upload (1), factory reset (7) and the system menu (8).
Switching the unit off and on again leaves TE boot without changing anything.

procedures.goal: Start the OP-XY in TE boot

steps.note: hold com while switching back on

procedures.result: The TE boot menu lists its three options.

procedures.goal: Leave TE boot

units.body:
TE boot sits underneath the normal OS, so it is reachable even when the OS itself misbehaves.
Updating (`T1`) and resetting (`T7`) have their own units, and the system menu (`T8`) is for
checking faulty keys or recalibrating the volume knob.

Nothing in TE boot happens by accident: every action needs a track key, and a power cycle leaves.
This app never switches the unit into TE boot; you do it on the device.

units.title: Updating the OS
units.summary: TE offers two ways to install a new OS — its web updater over USB, or copying the firmware file onto the unit while it sits in TE boot. Back up first and never install 1.0.29.

facts.text: The screen shows the installed OS version while the unit starts up.

TE's OP-XY downloads page (teenage.engineering/downloads/op-xy) lists every release with its notes and, except for the withdrawn 1.0.29, a firmware file; the newest is OS 1.1.33, the version this manual describes.
The easy route is TE's MIDI updater, a web page on that downloads page that updates the connected unit straight from the browser.
The manual route goes through TE boot, where `T1` makes the OP-XY show up on a computer as a removable disk.
Copy the firmware file onto that disk and eject it; the update then runs by itself — let it finish and follow the screen.
Never install OS 1.0.29, which TE withdrew because it could corrupt files over 64 KB copied off the unit over MTP.
Copy your projects, samples and presets to a computer before updating.

preconditions: the firmware file from TE's downloads page is on the computer

steps.note: hold com while switching on — TE boot appears
connect the USB-C cable; the unit mounts as a disk

procedures.result: Copy the file, eject the disk, and the update runs.

units.body:
Updating is always your action, done with TE's tools; this app shows which OS the unit runs but
never installs firmware or starts TE boot. Features tagged "since 1.1.x" in this manual need that
version or newer.

units.title: Factory reset
units.summary: `T7` in TE boot erases every user setting and all user content and rebuilds the original file structure. There is no undo: copy everything you want to keep to a computer first.

facts.text: A factory reset wipes all user settings and user content, recreates the original folder structure and returns the unit to its factory state.
Anything not copied off the unit beforehand — projects, your own samples, saved presets — cannot be recovered after a reset.
TE advises backing up first and points to its project backup recipe.
The reset starts from TE boot with `T7`; the screen then guides you through it.

procedures.goal: Return the OP-XY to its factory state
preconditions: everything you want to keep is copied to a computer

steps.note: hold com while switching on to reach TE boot
factory reset; follow the on-screen instructions

procedures.result: User settings and content are gone and the factory file structure is back.

units.body:
Treat a reset as a last resort, for instance before passing the unit on. Copy the whole drive over
MTP first: the reset also removes the samples and presets you added. This app never triggers a
reset.

units.title: Function test and pot calibration (system menu)
units.summary: TE boot's option 8 opens the system menu, with a function test for the keys and a reset of the volume pot calibration.

facts.text: `T8` in TE boot opens the system menu, which starts with the function test.
In the function test, a key that still shows red after you have pressed it points to a fault; contact TE support.
In the system menu, `M2` or `T2` selects reset volume pot calibration; afterwards the unit returns to TE boot.
OS 1.0.9 improved the response curve of the volume pot.

procedures.goal: Run the key function test
Reset the volume pot calibration
procedures.result: The calibration is reset and TE boot is shown again.

units.body:
Both tools are for hardware doubts: the function test checks the keys, and the calibration reset is
for a volume control whose range seems wrong.

units.title: Safety, care and warranty
units.summary: TE's safety notes for connecting, charging, temperature, cleaning and the battery, and what the 12-month warranty covers.

facts.text: Switch every device off before cabling them together; when you have to plug in while running, plug the lead into the OP-XY before the other device.
Never run a cable from the OP-XY's jacks into a microphone input with phantom power switched on; it can damage the unit.
Charge only from 5 V USB power, such as a computer's USB port or a USB charger.
Use the unit between 10 and 35 °C (50–95 °F) and store it between 0 and 35 °C (32–86 °F).
Wipe the shell with a slightly damp cloth and let it dry before use.
Do not charge or use a unit whose battery looks damaged; replacement batteries must come from TE and be fitted by qualified staff, and heat, fire or crushing can make a battery explode or leak.
Avoid long listening sessions at high volume to protect your hearing.
The unit is factory tested and has a 12-month warranty from the purchase date; it does not cover misuse (drops, crushing, wrong voltages on the connectors, faulty modifications) or shipping costs.

units.body:
The two that catch people out: phantom power on a mixer or interface channel the OP-XY is plugged
into, and charging from anything but plain 5 V USB.

units.title: Box contents and the factory-sound licence
units.summary: The box holds the unit, a quick start guide, a USB-C cable and velcro fasteners. You may use the built-in sounds in your own music, but not redistribute them as sounds.

facts.text: The box contains the OP-XY, a quick start guide, a USB-C cable and a pair of velcro fasteners for the underside.
The velcro rings on the underside hold the unit on a surface, in a case or on a stand.
The samples, sounds and other built-in material may be used to create, perform, record and release your own music.
Sharing, selling or publishing that material itself, as is or edited, is not allowed unless it has been turned into a substantially new original work.
Samples you bring in yourself remain your responsibility with respect to other people's copyrights.

units.body:
In short: making and releasing tracks with the factory sounds is fine; passing the sounds themselves
on (as a sample pack, for example) is not. This is a summary of TE's notice, not legal advice.

units.title: Step sequencer overview
units.summary: The 16 step keys program the selected track's pattern — up to four bars and 120 notes — by pressing steps, recording live or step recording; the bar menu, parameter locks and step components refine it.

facts.text: The row of 16 step keys is the step sequencer, the grid that stores the notes and sounds of every track.
The step keys light up with the pattern of the selected track.
Auxiliary tracks such as punch-in FX are sequenced with the same techniques as instrument tracks.
A pattern can grow to four bars of 16 steps, 64 steps in all.
A pattern holds at most 120 notes.
Notes get in three ways: pressing steps after choosing a note, recording live while the pattern plays, or step recording with playback stopped.
Step components attach rules to single steps — repeats, ratchets, random notes, skips — without re-recording anything.
OS 1.1.32 fixed occasional sequencer stalls while browsing presets and samples.

procedures.goal: Show a track's pattern on the step keys

units.body:
Every track keeps its own patterns. Choose the input that suits the part: press steps for drums and
exact lines, record live to keep your feel, or step record a melody without the sequencer running.
Then the bar menu sets length and timing for the whole pattern, parameter locks change the sound on
single steps, and step components change how single steps behave on each pass.

units.title: Entering notes on steps
units.summary: Play a note on the keyboard, then press steps to place it; hold a step to see and change its notes, or hold several keys while pressing a step for a chord.

facts.text: The OP-XY remembers the last note or sound you played on the keyboard, and pressing a step stores that note on it; the step then lights.
Holding a step lights the keyboard keys of every note stored on it.
To store a chord, keep its notes held and press the step, or hold the step and play the notes.
With a step held, pressing a key adds that note to the step, or takes it off if the step already has it.
On a drum track each of the 24 keys is a different sound, so step entry places sounds rather than pitches.
Since OS 1.1.25 a chord entered by holding keys and pressing a step can contain one note in two octaves.
Pressing or holding a step shows its number in a small box on the screen.

steps.note: further steps get the same note

Add or remove a note on a step

units.body:
Step entry works like a pen that holds the last note you played: tap a key, then tap the steps where
it should sound. To add one drum sound to steps that already carry others, use the one-sound view.

units.title: Step recording
units.summary: With the sequencer stopped, keep `record` held and play; each note lands on the next step, `record + [+]` leaves a rest and `record + [-]` goes back one step.

facts.text: Holding `record` while playback is stopped starts step recording; the step 1 key turns red to mark where the next note goes.
Each note played while `record` stays held fills the step under the red cursor, which then moves on; filled steps light white.
`record + [+]` moves the red cursor forward without writing anything.
`record + [-]` moves the cursor back one step; a sound already there plays and its key lights, ready to change.
Tapping a step you have recorded deletes it from the recording.

procedures.goal: Enter a line note by note

steps.note: each note takes the next step

procedures.goal: Delete a step entered by mistake

steps.note: TE only says to tap the step; keeping record held is our assumption

units.body:
The quickest way to type in a line with a simple rhythm: notes fill consecutive steps in the order you
play them, with no need to keep time. Shape longer notes afterwards by extending them.

units.title: Live recording
units.summary: `record + play` arms recording, which begins with your first note; during playback, hold `record` to overdub or press `record + play` to latch recording. Holding `record` and pressing `play` twice (`record + play → + play`) adds a count-in.

facts.text: `record + play` arms live recording: the step 1 key flashes red while the sequencer waits.
The first note you play starts playback and recording together.
Steps that receive notes turn red while recording and show white after `stop`.
While a pattern plays, holding `record` records into it until you let go.
Pressing `record + play` during playback latches recording on without holding `record`.
Encoder moves made while recording are stored per step, like parameter locks; `bar + turn E4` smooths them.
Holding `record`, pressing `play`, then `play` again (`record + play → + play`) plays a count-in before recording starts; `record` stays down throughout.
A take longer than the pattern wraps round and plays over itself, so lengthen the pattern first.
Notes arriving over MIDI while recording is armed land in the pattern too, according to community test tools.

procedures.goal: Record a part live

steps.note: recording starts with the first note

procedures.goal: Add notes to a playing pattern
Record with a count-in

steps.note: keep record down while you press play the second time

units.body:
Arming means nothing runs until your first note, so a take starts exactly on the downbeat. Once a
pattern loops, holding `record` layers new notes on each pass. Live takes are pulled onto the grid by
the track's quantisation in the bar menu.

units.title: Extended notes and note length
units.summary: Hold a step and press a later step to stretch its notes up to there; pressing the later step again switches between "full step" and "overlap". Other step-entered notes take the bar menu's note length.

facts.text: Holding a step and pressing a later step stretches the step's note or chord until the later step; this is how chords and pads span several steps.
Pressing that end step a second time switches the note between two endings, "full step" and "overlap".
TE does not define them; presumably "full step" stops at the step boundary and "overlap" runs into the next step, which matters for legato and glides.
Notes placed by pressing steps take their length from `bar + turn E2`; live-recorded and extended notes keep their own.
In a new project that setting reads 50, about half a step, according to decoded project files.

procedures.goal: Make a note last several steps

steps.note: press the step where the note should end; press it again to switch the ending

units.body:
The bar menu's length suits drums and plucked lines; anything that has to sustain is better stretched
note by note. Pulse hold is related but also pauses the track.

units.title: Nudging steps off the grid
units.summary: Hold a step and press `[-]` or `[+]` to move its notes slightly earlier or later; this needs the track's quantisation below 100.

facts.text: Holding a step and pressing `[-]` or `[+]` moves the step's notes earlier or later, off the step grid.
Each press is a fine adjustment; keeping `[-]` or `[+]` held moves faster.
Nudging only works while the track's quantisation (`bar + turn E1`) is below 100.

Since a nudged note keeps its offset under quantisation below 100, quantisation most likely acts as notes play rather than when they are recorded, so lowering it after a take lets the take's own timing back in. Not checked on a unit.
Decoded project files show quantisation at 100 in a new project, so turn it down before nudging.

procedures.goal: Move a step's notes slightly off the grid

units.body:
If `[-]` and `[+]` seem to do nothing while a step is held, quantisation is at 100. For the feel of a
whole track rather than single steps, use groove instead.

units.title: Sequencing one sound at a time
units.summary: Hold a keyboard key and tap `record` to see only the steps that play that note or drum sound; with the key still held, press steps to sequence just that sound.

facts.text: Holding a key and tapping `record` makes the step keys show only the steps where that note or sound is recorded.
While the key stays held, pressing steps sequences that one sound, even on steps that already carry other sounds.
Holding a key and pressing a step enters the same view directly, recording the note on that step.
Letting go of the key appears to end the view; TE's drum walkthrough just says to let go when done.

procedures.goal: Program one drum sound without seeing the others

units.body:
Made for drum tracks, where all 24 sounds share the same 16 steps: hold the hi-hat, set its steps,
let go, hold the snare, and so on. On melodic tracks it shows where one pitch is used.

units.title: Shifting a sequence (rotate)
units.summary: Hold a track key and press `[-]` or `[+]` to slide that track's whole sequence by one step, wrapping at the ends. Added in OS 1.1.15; since 1.1.21 step components and parameter locks move too.

facts.text: Holding a track key and pressing `[-]` or `[+]` moves that track's whole sequence by one step, the two keys choosing the direction.
Notes pushed past the end of the sequence come back in at its start.
Rotating arrived with OS 1.1.15.
Since OS 1.1.21 step components and parameter locks travel with their notes; the guide mentions only notes.
The rotation covers the whole pattern length, not only the bar on screen, according to decoded project files.

procedures.goal: Slide a track's sequence by one step

units.body:
A quick way to hear a part in a new place, such as moving a hi-hat figure from on-beat to off-beat.
On 1.1.15–1.1.18 locks and components stayed behind on their old steps.

units.title: Copying and pasting steps
units.summary: Hold a step to copy its notes, step components and parameter locks, let go, then press an empty step to paste.

facts.text: Holding a step copies everything on it — notes, step components and parameter locks.
After you let go, pressing an empty step pastes the copy onto it.
Copying by holding a step arrived in OS 1.0.13.
When a held step is copied, its number box on the screen adds the word copied.
The copy is taken while you are still holding the step, about half a second in, which is when copied appears; the word stays for a second or two after you let go.

procedures.goal: Copy one step to another

units.body:
Repeats a finished hit — say a snare with a ratchet and a filter lock — without rebuilding it. For
larger chunks, duplicate a bar or copy the pattern in arrange mode.

units.title: Transposing a track's sequence
units.summary: `shift + [-]` or `shift + [+]` moves every note of the current sequence down or up — an octave on synth and sampler tracks, a semitone on drum-sampler tracks.

facts.text: Holding `shift` and pressing `[-]` or `[+]` moves the current sequence an octave down or up on synth and sampler tracks.
On drum-sampler tracks the same keys move the sequenced notes by one semitone instead.
Without `shift`, `[-]` and `[+]` only change the keyboard's octave and leave recorded notes alone.

procedures.goal: Move a track's recorded notes down or up

units.body:
Handy when a bass line sits too high. In a drum kit each semitone is another sound, so on drums it
tries the same rhythm on the neighbouring hits.

units.title: Parameter locks
units.summary: Store a module-page value on individual steps; whenever such a step plays, the parameter jumps to the stored value.

facts.text: To lock a value, keep a step held and turn an encoder; the step remembers the value you dial in.
Each time the sequencer reaches a locked step, the parameter takes that step's stored value.
Any parameter on the four module pages can carry locks; the settings of players cannot.
By default the value jumps at each locked step. The shape control in the bar menu (`bar + turn E4`) smooths the movement between locks.
Knob moves recorded live while holding `record` are also stored step by step, so they play back stepped until you add smoothing.
Copying a step to an empty step brings its locks along with its notes and step components.
`bar + M2` removes every lock in the pattern and leaves the notes in place.
Clearing the whole track with `record + hold stop` removes its locks too.
The skip parameter lock step component (`natural 12`) lets a step's locks play only on every Nth pass, for automation that appears once every few repeats.
Tracks using the drum or synth sampler accept locks as well.
Duplicating a bar with `bar + shift + [+]` copies its locks and step components too.
Shifting a track's sequence with `Tn + [-]/[+]` moves the locks together with the notes.
A lock can sit on a step that has no note; before OS 1.1.33 a bug prevented adding one there.
While you record a lock, the held step's number box on the screen turns orange.
Holding a locked step shows its locked values in the page's top bar instead of the track's own — shape 00 and detune 06, say, on a track set to 15 and 05.

procedures.goal: Lock a parameter value on one step
preconditions: the module page with the parameter is on screen

steps.note: keep holding the step while turning; any page parameter works

procedures.result: The step plays back with the new value from now on.

procedures.goal: Record knob movements into the pattern while it plays
procedures.result: The movement is stored per step, like locks.

procedures.goal: Glide between locked values instead of jumping
Remove all locks from the pattern but keep its notes
Copy a step, locks included, to another step

steps.note: let go of the first step, then press the target step, which must be empty

units.body:
A parameter lock pins one value of one parameter to one step. Hold a hi-hat step and open the
filter a little, hold the next one and close it, and the pattern gains movement without any
recording pass. Locks work on everything the module pages show — engine, envelopes, filter, LFO —
but not on player settings.

Locks and live-recorded knob moves share their storage and their smoothing: both change the value
in steps unless the bar menu's shape control (`bar + turn E4`) blends between them. To thin locks
out over time, pair them with the skip parameter lock step component.

Firmware history matters here: sampler tracks gained locks in 1.1.0, rotating a sequence has
carried its locks along since 1.1.21, and locks on empty steps work reliably from 1.1.33.

units.title: Clearing a sequence and undo
units.summary: `record + hold stop` wipes the current track; `bar + M1` clears only notes, `bar + M2` only parameter locks, `bar + M4` both; `shift + record` undoes the last change.

facts.text: Holding `record` and `stop` until the step LEDs fill red clears everything recorded on the current track.
That clear takes the parameter locks as well; OS 1.0.15 fixed it leaving them behind.
The same gesture clears the track during step recording.
In the bar menu, `M1` deletes the pattern's notes but keeps its parameter locks, `M2` deletes the locks but keeps the notes, and `M4` deletes both.
`shift + record` undoes the last change; there is one undo level and not every action can be undone.

procedures.goal: Wipe the current track

steps.note: until the whole step row is red

procedures.goal: Clear only the notes, only the locks, or both
Undo the last change

units.body:
`bar + M1` keeps a filter movement while you record a new melody over it; `bar + M2` keeps the notes
but drops the automation. Save a project version before a big clear.

units.title: Step components
units.summary: Per-step modifiers — repeats, ratchets, fixed velocity, pitch ramps, randomness, glides, bends, transposition, jumps and skip rules — added by holding `shift`, choosing a white key for the component and a black key for its value.

facts.text: A step component changes how a step plays — repeating it, splitting it into rapid retriggers, bending, randomising or skipping it — while the recorded notes stay as they are.
There are 14 components, one per white key; the icon printed on each natural names its component.

From the left, the naturals are: 1 pulse, 2 pulse hold, 3 multiply, 4 velocity, 5 ramp up, 6 ramp down, 7 random, 8 portamento, 9 bend, 10 tonality, 11 jump, 12 skip parameter lock, 13 skip step component, 14 skip trigger.
The black keys then pick the component's value. Each component reads the ten digits its own way, and the screen spells out what the chosen digit does.
For ten of the 14 components, `accidental 0` (the last black key) picks a random amount, count or shape; ramp up, ramp down, random and tonality use it for their strongest setting instead.
While `shift` is down, steps that hold notes turn dim to show they carry no component yet, and steps you select blink.
A single step can carry any combination of the 14 components at the same time.
To take a component off, select the same steps with `shift` held and press that component's white key again.
Pulse and pulse hold stretch time — the step repeats or holds for extra steps before the sequence moves on — whereas multiply fits several triggers inside the one step, the classic ratchet.
Duplicating a bar copies its notes together with their step components and locks.
Shifting a track's sequence with `Tn + [-]/[+]` carries the step components along with the notes.
Holding a step and changing its note no longer wipes the step's components; OS 1.1.32 fixed that.

procedures.goal: Add a step component to one or more steps
preconditions: the track already has notes in its sequence

steps.note: keep shift down throughout — select the steps, choose the component, then its value

procedures.result: Once `shift` is released, the chosen steps play with the component.

procedures.goal: Remove a step component

steps.note: select the same steps, then press the white key of the component to take off

units.body:
Step components are the OP-XY's answer to trig conditions and ratchets: small rules attached to a
step that change how it plays every time the pattern comes round. The keyboard becomes their control
surface while `shift` is held — the 14 white keys choose _which_ component, the 10 black keys choose
_how much_.

The components fall into a few families. Timing: pulse, pulse hold and multiply. Level: velocity.
Pitch: ramp up, ramp down, random, portamento, bend and tonality. Flow: jump moves the playhead to
another step. The three skip components thin things out, letting locks, components or the whole
trigger through only on some passes, which keeps long loops from sounding repetitive.

Because one step can stack several components, simple patterns grow into evolving ones quickly. The
value each digit selects is listed per component in the step-component reference.

units.title: Step component values
units.summary: What each black key (1–9, then 0) selects for each of the 14 step components, in white-key order.

facts.text: Pulse (`natural 1`): 1–9 repeats; 0 a random number.
Pulse hold (`natural 2`): held for 1–9 steps; 0 a random number.
Multiply (`natural 3`): 1–8 hits inside the step; 0 a random number; for 9 see the multiply unit.
Velocity (`natural 4`): 1–8 give 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 100, 112, 127; 9 gives 0; 0 a random velocity.
Ramp up (`natural 5`), ramp down (`natural 6`) and random (`natural 7`): 1–5 mean 2–6 steps within one octave; 6–9 and 0 mean 2–6 steps over three octaves.
Portamento (`natural 8`): 1–9 give 10–90%; 0 a random amount.
Bend (`natural 9`): 1 down-up, 2 up-down, 3 bump down, 4 bump up, 5 spring out, 6 spring in, 7 fade down, 8 fade up, 9 random 1, 0 random 2.
Tonality (`natural 10`): 1 ignore chord progression, 2 transpose only, 3 octave up, 4 fifth up, 5 third up, 6 chromatic up, 7 chromatic down, 8/9/0 quantize 33/66/100%.
Jump (`natural 11`): 1–4 go to step 1, 5, 9 or 13; 5 one forward; 6 one back; 7 forward or back; 8 stay; 9 align the track position; 0 a random step.
Skip parameter lock (`natural 12`), skip step component (`natural 13`) and skip trigger (`natural 14`): 1 every pass, 2–9 every 2nd to 9th pass, 0 at random.
Added without a digit, a component keeps a default value; decoded device files show 4 for most, 2 for multiply and the skips, 5 for velocity and 1 for bend.
The ramps and random stay in the current scale, presumably the song scale set on the brain track.

Key icons from `natural 1` to `natural 14`: four dots, open hand, ÷, rising wedge, stairs up, stairs down, "rnd", glide sign, twin fins, four-petal fan, arrow to a dot, spoked wheel, ring of wedges, sun.

units.body:
A pass is one time the playhead reaches the step. For most components 0 means chance; the ramps,
random and tonality use it for their strongest setting instead. The screen names the chosen value
while `shift` is held; each component has its own unit with an example.

units.title: Pulse (step component)
units.summary: Step component on `natural 1` that repeats a step before the track moves on.

facts.text: Pulse replays a step a chosen number of times while the track stays on it; then the sequence continues.
The black keys 1–9 give 1–9 repeats; 0 a random number.
Because the track waits during the repeats, the steps after a pulsed step play later than written.

procedures.goal: Make a step play three extra times

units.body:
Use pulse for rolls and stumbles built from one hit. To fit extra hits inside the step without
delaying anything, use multiply.

units.title: Pulse hold (step component)
units.summary: Step component on `natural 2` that holds a step for extra steps while the sequence waits.

facts.text: Pulse hold keeps the track on a step for a chosen number of steps before the sequence moves on.
The black keys 1–9 hold the step for 1–9 steps; 0 for a random number.
Since OS 1.0.29 the length of the held note is set from the track scale.
Since OS 1.0.29 pulse hold leaves the length of arpeggio notes alone.

procedures.goal: Hold a step for two steps

units.body:
Where pulse re-triggers the step, pulse hold lets its note ring while the rest of the pattern waits.
For a long note that delays nothing, extend the note instead.

units.title: Multiply (step component)
units.summary: Step component on `natural 3` that splits a step into several quick hits inside its own length, a ratchet.

facts.text: Multiply divides a step into several shorter hits that fit inside the step, the ratchet effect common on hi-hats.
The black keys 1–8 split the step into 1–8 hits (1 leaves it unchanged); 0 picks a random number.
`accidental 9` most likely gives 9 hits; TE's table prints 3 for it, apparently a slip. Not checked on a unit.

Three hits in a step are triplets of that step's length, so multiply 3 on a sixteenth step gives a thirty-second-note triplet roll, and on a step of an eighth (track scale 2) sixteenth-note triplets; the track scales alone have no triplet value.

procedures.goal: Turn a hi-hat step into a three-hit ratchet

units.body:
Unlike pulse, multiply does not delay the next step. Pair it with skip step component so the burst
fires only every few passes.

units.title: Velocity (step component)
units.summary: Step component on `natural 4` that plays a step at a fixed or random velocity.

facts.text: The velocity component makes a step play at a set velocity, whatever velocity was recorded.
The black keys 1–8 set 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 100, 112 or 127; 9 sets 0; 0 picks a random velocity.
How much velocity changes the sound depends on the preset's velocity sensitivity, set in its preset settings.

procedures.goal: Accent a step at full velocity

units.body:
Use it for accents and ghost notes — 127 on the backbeat, 16 or 32 on the hi-hats between — or the
random setting for a looser feel.

units.title: Ramp up (step component)
units.summary: Step component on `natural 5` whose note climbs one stage of an in-scale ramp each time the step plays.

facts.text: Each time the step plays, ramp up moves its note one stage higher along a ramp that stays inside the current scale.
The black keys 1–5 give a ramp of 2–6 steps within one octave; 6–9 and 0 give 2–6 steps over three octaves, so 0 is the widest ramp rather than random.

procedures.goal: Make a step climb in four stages through an octave

units.body:
One repeated note becomes a figure that rises from pass to pass, such as a bass note climbing each
time the loop comes round.

units.title: Ramp down (step component)
units.summary: Step component on `natural 6` whose note drops one stage of an in-scale ramp each time the step plays.

facts.text: Each time the step plays, ramp down moves its note one stage lower along a ramp that stays inside the current scale.
The black keys 1–5 give a ramp of 2–6 steps within one octave; 6–9 and 0 give 2–6 steps over three octaves, so 0 is the widest ramp rather than random.

procedures.goal: Make a step fall in two large stages

units.body: The mirror of ramp up, for falling bass lines and cascades built from a single step.

units.title: Random (step component)
units.summary: Step component on `natural 7` that gives a step a random note from the current scale.

facts.text: Random replaces the step's note with one picked at random inside the current scale.
The digit sets the range: 1–5 give 2–6 steps within one octave, 6–9 and 0 give 2–6 steps over three octaves, so 0 is the widest range rather than random.

procedures.goal: Let a step wander between nearby notes

units.body:
A narrow range keeps a melody recognisable while it shifts; a wide one scatters notes. Add skip
step component so the randomness strikes only on some passes.

units.title: Portamento (step component)
units.summary: Step component on `natural 8` that glides the pitch into and out of a step.

facts.text: The portamento component makes the pitch glide into the step and out of it again.
The black keys 1–9 set the amount from 10% to 90%; 0 picks a random amount.
It acts on single steps, whereas the portamento setting on the `M2` shift page glides every note of the track.

procedures.goal: Slide into one step

units.body: It puts a slide exactly where you want it, such as the one bass note that should swoop.

units.title: Bend (step component)
units.summary: Step component on `natural 9` that runs one of ten pitch-bend curves over a step.

facts.text: Bend runs a pitch-bend curve over the step; the black key chooses the shape.
1 down-up, 2 up-down, 3 bump down, 4 bump up, 5 spring out, 6 spring in, 7 fade down, 8 fade up, 9 random 1, 0 random 2.
The depth may follow the track's bend range (`M2` shift page), in which case bend range off would silence the effect. Not confirmed.

procedures.goal: Give a step a dip-and-return bend

units.body: A small pitch envelope for one step: dips, falling kicks, chirps on percussion.

units.title: Tonality (step component)
units.summary: Step component on `natural 10` that transposes a step by a fixed interval or changes how it follows the brain's key.

facts.text: Tonality transposes the step by a set interval.
1 ignore chord progression, 2 transpose only, 3 octave up, 4 fifth up, 5 third up, 6 chromatic up, 7 chromatic down, 8 quantize 33%, 9 quantize 66%, 0 quantize 100%.
Options 1, 2 and 8–0 appear to set how the step follows the brain track's transposition and scale; TE does not explain them.

procedures.goal: Lift a step by a fifth

units.body:
Intervals add harmony to single steps, such as an octave jump on every fourth bass note. Tonality
has no random setting.

units.title: Jump (step component)
units.summary: Step component on `natural 11` that sends the playhead from a step to another one.

facts.text: Jump overrides the order of steps, sending the playhead from this step to a chosen one instead of the next in line.
1–4 go to step 1, 5, 9 or 13; 5 one step forward; 6 one step back; 7 forward or back; 8 stay on the step; 9 align the track position; 0 a random step.
Align presumably returns the track to where it would be without jumps, in line with the other tracks.
Jumps land in the bar that is playing; OS 1.0.50 fixed them landing in the bar shown for editing.

procedures.goal: Send the playhead back to step 1 from chosen steps

units.body:
Jumping back to step 1 halfway through shortens one track's loop; a random target makes a part
reshuffle itself as it plays.

units.title: Skip parameter lock (step component)
units.summary: Step component on `natural 12` that lets a step's parameter locks apply only on some passes.

facts.text: The step's parameter locks take effect only on some passes of the pattern; on the others the step plays with the track's normal settings.
1 applies the locks every time, 2–9 only on every 2nd to 9th pass, and 0 at random.

procedures.goal: Let a step's locks play only every fourth pass

units.body:
For automation that turns up now and then, such as a filter opening on one pass in four. The notes
play on every pass.

units.title: Skip step component (step component)
units.summary: Step component on `natural 13` that lets a step's other components apply only on some passes.

facts.text: The step's other components act only on some passes of the pattern; on the rest the step plays without them.
1 applies them every time, 2–9 only on every 2nd to 9th pass, and 0 at random.

procedures.goal: Ratchet a step only every second pass

units.body:
A ratchet, bend or random note that appears only every few passes sounds like a deliberate variation
rather than a loop.

units.title: Skip trigger (step component)
units.summary: Step component on `natural 14` that lets a step's notes play only on some passes.

facts.text: Skip trigger lets the step's notes sound only on some passes of the pattern.
1 plays the step every time, 2–9 only on every 2nd to 9th pass, and 0 at random.

procedures.goal: Play a step only every second pass

units.body:
A one-in-N trig condition: a crash on a step with value 4 lands once every four passes, turning a
one-bar loop into a four-bar phrase. Value 0 leaves each pass to chance.

units.title: Bar menu
units.summary: Holding `bar` shows the selected track's pattern settings; the encoders set quantisation, note length, groove and lock smoothing, and other keys handle bars, track scale, length and clearing.

facts.text: The bar page stays on screen only while `bar` is held; `shift + bar` pins it until you press `bar` again.
In a new project the card reads quant 100, length 50 and track scale 1, with groove shown as a dash and shape as a small step symbol.
Since OS 1.1.25, tracks with an odd track scale (3, 5, 6 or 7) quantise to a grid made for that scale.
The groove type (shuffle, bombora and the rest) is picked on the tempo page; the bar menu sets only this track's amount.
Decoded project files store length, track scale, quantisation, groove and smoothing in each pattern, so a track's patterns can differ.

Holding `bar` lays a white card over the dimmed page — bar numbers 1 to 4 along the top with the current one inverted, the track scale beside them, then rows for quant, length, groove and shape, each marked with its encoder's dot. The card fades when `bar` is let go.
A faint mini piano roll on the right of the card shows a dash for each note in the shown bar, as long as the note.
With the card up, `bar + [+]` or `bar + [-]` adds or removes a bar box at once; the shown bar's box is filled and the other bars are outlined.
The card's footer names the clearing keys — clr notes on `M1`, clr params on `M2`, clr all on `M4`.

procedures.goal: Change a pattern-wide setting

parameters.name: quantisation
parameters.note: pulls live-recorded notes onto the steps; at 100 nothing can be nudged

parameters.name: quantisation on/off
parameters.note: 1.1.15 added a click that toggles quantisation; that it is this encoder is assumed

parameters.name: note length
parameters.note: for notes entered by pressing steps

parameters.name: groove
parameters.note: this track's amount; replaces the tempo page's swing

parameters.name: shape
parameters.note: smooths between parameter locks and recorded automation

units.body:
Everything here acts on the whole pattern, whereas step edits and locks act on single steps. The
keys handle structure — `[+]` and `[-]` add and remove bars, black keys set the track scale, step
keys set the length, `M1`, `M2` and `M4` clear — while the encoders handle feel.

units.title: Track scale
units.summary: `bar + accidental` sets how long one step of the selected track lasts: at 1 a sixteenth note, at 4 a quarter note, at 1/2 a thirty-second. Each track has its own scale.

facts.text: Holding `bar` and pressing a black key sets the track scale, the time one step takes; every track keeps its own.
The scale multiplies the length of every step; at 4 a step lasts four normal steps, so four steps fill a 4/4 bar.
`bar + accidental 4`, the black key marked 4, sets scale 4; the step lights then move four times slower.

Scale 1/2 halves every step, so a pattern plays at double time beside tracks at 1; scale 2 doubles every step, half time. A pattern at 1/2 lasts half as long, so it plays twice in a scene of its length at 1.
Raising the scale is how a pattern outgrows four bars; 64 steps at scale 16 last 64 bars.
TE's guide lists the scales 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 16 and 1/2.
The changelog also names 1/5 and 1/7, repaired in OS 1.0.15.
OS 1.1.25 gave the odd scales 3, 5, 6 and 7 their own quantisation grid, so 5 and 7 exist too.

procedures.goal: Change how long each step of the track lasts

units.body:
Tracks at different scales share a scene: a slow pad at 4 next to hi-hats at 1/2. TE ties only the
key marked 4 to a value; which keys give 16 and the fractions is not documented.

units.title: Bars and pattern length
units.summary: `bar + [+]` adds a 16-step bar (four at most), `bar + [-]` removes one, `bar + shift + [+]` duplicates, tapping `bar` switches bars, and `bar + step n` sets how many steps the last bar plays.

facts.text: `bar + [+]` adds a bar of 16 steps and `bar + [-]` removes one; a pattern holds at most four bars.
`bar + shift + [+]` duplicates the current bar; in a two-bar pattern it doubles the phrase, copying bar 1 to bar 3 and bar 2 to bar 4.
Since OS 1.1.3, duplicated bars keep their step components and parameter locks.
Tapping `bar` changes which bar the step keys show; a bar picked during playback or recording stays on the keys instead of following the playhead.
Holding `bar` and pressing a step key sets how many steps the pattern plays; with several bars it trims the final bar only.
Bars and length together allow any pattern length from 1 to 64 steps.

units.body:
Duplicate the first bar, then change a detail in the copy. Length makes odd patterns easy: 12 steps
for a bar of 3/4. The OS changelog calls bars "pages".

units.title: Players
units.summary: A player reworks the notes a track plays — into arpeggios, transposed chords (maestro) or latched notes (hold) — and is switched on per track with the player key.

facts.text: A player takes the notes a track receives, from the keyboard or its sequence, and turns them into a variation such as an arpeggio or a chord hit; the recorded notes stay as they are.
Every instrument track and every auxiliary track can run a player of its own.
The first press of `player` shows the selected track's player page, dimmed under an off box; a second press switches the player on.
`shift + player` opens the player list, headed with the track number and the word player: arpeggio, hold and maestro, the current type boxed.

With the list up and shift still held, turning `E1` moves the box between arpeggio, hold and maestro; pressing `player` again only switches the player on or off. Letting go of shift opens the chosen player's page.
Player settings cannot be parameter-locked; only module-page parameters can.
Since OS 1.1.25, a pattern you add to a track starts out with the player type that is selected at that moment.

units.body:
Players sit between what you play and what the track sounds: the arpeggio spells a chord out note
by note, maestro plays whole chords from one finger, and hold keeps notes ringing after you let go.
The sequence is untouched, so switching the player off brings the original notes back. Since new
patterns copy the current player type (1.1.25), the type seems to belong to the pattern.

units.title: Arpeggio player
units.summary: Plays held or sequenced notes one after another; the encoders set speed, note order, range and hold, and the shift layer adds note length, style, glide and stereo spread.

facts.text: The arpeggio player breaks the notes a track receives into a repeating run, playing them one at a time instead of together.
The guide says that both pattern (`E2`) and the shift-layer style change the order of the notes, without explaining how the two differ.
Notes made by the arpeggio are not passed on to linked tracks.
Since OS 1.1.0, held arpeggio notes still sound when their track is muted.
Since OS 1.1.17, a sustain pedal has no effect on arpeggiated notes.
Since OS 1.1.17, the brain transposes arpeggios along with the rest of the track.
Since OS 1.1.21, moving to another pattern stops any arpeggio notes that were being held.

The arpeggio page shows four boxes in the encoders' greys — a note value for speed, the pattern as a small staircase (or peak, arrow, scattered blocks), a ladder with the octave count for range, and a hand for hold, pale when off and black when on — then a small arrow meaning the page has a shift layer. Under the word arpeggio, fourteen pale blue bars picture the run, one per note, taller for higher notes; a range of 4 over a triad makes a twelve-step staircase.
Speed shows only a note symbol. It runs from a quarter note (slowest) to a 64th (fastest), with triplets among them; there is no number.

With `shift` held the boxes change to the shift controls — two tied notes whose tie fills white as the note length grows, the style (the first reads off, the others are small bar charts), a squiggle that darkens from the left as glide rises, and a ring that splits into two as stereo rises.

units.body:
The arpeggio steps through a chord, played live or sequenced, at the speed of `E1`, in the order of
`E2`, across the span of `E3`; hold (`E4`) keeps it going hands-free. The shift layer adds note
length, style, glide and stereo spread. Since the guide, arpeggios ignore the sustain pedal and
follow the brain (1.1.17), and a pattern change cuts held notes (1.1.21).

units.title: Maestro player
units.summary: Maestro remembers a chord you enter with shift held and then plays it from any single key, shifted up or down to that key; roll strums it, pattern sets the strum order and hold latches it.

facts.text: Maestro stores a chord; afterwards every key you press plays that chord, moved up or down so it follows the key.
To store the chord, keep `shift` held and play its notes on the keyboard.
The light gray encoder (`E3`) has no job on the maestro page; its box is crossed out.
Maestro's page shows roll as a wavy arpeggio sign with a number (0, 10, 12 …), pattern as up, down, up/down or random icons, and hold as a hand that fills in when on.

Under the word maestro two stacks of four pale blue slabs picture the stored chord. A slab stands up for each stored note, filling the left stack from the back and then the right one, and lies flat where there is none; while you enter a new chord they rise one by one, and they stand taller while the chord sounds.
With eight slabs on the page, maestro seems to keep at most eight notes per chord.

units.body:
Maestro turns the keyboard into a chord trigger. Enter a chord once with `shift` held — a minor
seventh, a stacked fifth, anything — and a single key then plays the whole shape wherever you press,
which makes progressions quick to play and record with one hand. The guide leaves open whether a new
chord fully replaces the old one.

units.title: Hold player
units.summary: The hold player keeps the notes you play sounding until you play the next ones; stop or switching the player off releases them.

facts.text: With the hold player on, notes keep sounding after you let go of the keys, until you play the next note or chord.
Hold suits bass notes and chords that should ring on while your hands are busy elsewhere.
Pressing `stop`, or switching the player off with `player`, releases every held note.
Since OS 1.1.3, pressing a key that is already held does not switch that note off, which makes held chords easier to play.
Since OS 1.1.25, stopping the hold player ends its notes with an ordinary note-off, so each note fades out through its release.
The hold page shows the word hold over a large infinity ribbon of concentric bands; its encoders have nothing to set.

units.body:
Hold is the simplest player: whatever you play stays on until the next thing you play replaces it —
a droning bass note under the pattern, or a chord that pads on while you tweak. Press `stop` or switch
the player off to clear it. Since 1.1.25 the held notes fade through their release when you stop.

units.title: Instrument mode
units.summary: Instrument mode holds the eight tracks that make sound. Each track runs one engine — a synth, a sampler or the midi engine — and is shaped on four pages: engine, envelopes, filter and LFO.

facts.text: Instrument mode holds eight instrument tracks, one per track key `T1`…`T8`; the eight auxiliary tracks have a mode of their own.
`M1` shows the engine, `M2` the amp and filter envelopes, `M3` the filter and `M4` the LFO.
On OS 1.1.33, `shift + M1` brings up the preset browser for the selected track, where loading one of an engine's presets changes the engine.
`shift + Tn` opens the preset browser for that track, where a preset, sample pack or engine can be loaded in one go.
`shift + instrument` opens the preset settings: tuning, velocity sensitivity, width and modulation routing of the track's sound.
With a track key held, the module keys act on that track's whole sound: `Tn + M1` scrambles it, `Tn + M2` copies it, `Tn + M3` pastes onto it and `Tn + M4` saves it as a preset.
A fresh project puts drums on tracks 1 and 2, a bass on 3, a pluck on 4, a lead on 5, a soft pluck on 6, strings on 7 and a pad on 8.
Community captures name the engines behind those sounds as the drum sampler on tracks 1 and 2, then prism, epiano, dissolve, hardsync, axis and multisampler on tracks 3 to 8.

procedures.goal: Open instrument mode and select a track

units.body:
Pick a track, then work through its pages: the engine creates the tone, the envelopes shape each
note, the filter colours it and the LFO adds movement; every value can be parameter-locked per step.
A track's complete sound travels as one preset, so a load from the browser (`shift + Tn`, or
`shift + M1` for the selected track) changes everything at once, the engine included. Brain, send
effects, external gear and tape live in auxiliary mode.

units.title: Engine page and changing engine (M1)
units.summary: `M1` is the engine page: its encoders edit the loaded engine's own parameters. On OS 1.1.33 `shift + M1` brings up the preset browser by engine, and loading one of an engine's presets changes the engine — along with the whole sound. Twelve engines: eight synths, three samplers and midi.

facts.text: On `M1` the four encoders edit the loaded engine's own parameters, so what each one does depends on the engine.
There are eight synth engines — axis, dissolve, epiano, hardsync, organ, prism, simple and wavetable — each with its own character.
Three sampler engines play recorded audio — the synth sampler, the drum sampler and the multisampler.
The midi engine makes no sound of its own; it turns the track into a MIDI sequencer for external gear and uses `M2` and `M3` for CC controls.
Twelve engines in all — the eight synths, the three samplers and midi.
Over MIDI, CC12–15 on the track's channel move the four `M1` parameters of every synth engine; the drum sampler, synth sampler and multisampler pages ignore them.

A synth engine page lists its four values in a top bar — coloured cells on prism, epiano and wavetable, plain text on simple and axis, none on organ — above a picture drawn from the four values; prism, dissolve and hardsync animate while notes sound, organ's drawbars glide to new values and wavetable's drift keeps its copies turning.

On OS 1.1.33 there is no separate engine list; `shift + M1` brings up the preset browser on the track's current preset — the track number over the word preset at the left, the engines in the middle with the track's engine boxed, and that engine's presets on the right.

On a unit running OS 1.1.33 it listed eleven engines, alphabetically (axis, dissolve, drum, epiano, hardsync, multisampler, organ, prism, sampler, simple, wavetable) and no midi engine; how OS 1.1.33 puts an instrument track on midi is still open, and this app's replica lists midi last.
Turning `E1` to an engine highlights its first preset; loading a preset changes the engine with the whole sound (all four pages) and returns to the track's `M1` page.
In the browser a click of `E1` swaps between by engine and by category (a popup says which) instead of confirming, as it did in the older engine list the guide describes.

units.body:
Synth engines build tones from oscillators, samplers play recorded audio, and the midi engine stays
silent and drives outside gear. Only `M1` belongs to the engine, but on OS 1.1.33 an engine arrives
with one of its presets, so a swap resets the envelopes, filter and LFO too: choose the engine first,
then shape the other pages. `shift + Tn` opens the same browser for any track.

units.title: Amp and filter envelopes (M2)
units.summary: `M2` holds two ADSR envelopes per track: the amp envelope shapes each note's level over time, the filter envelope moves the filter cutoff. Click any encoder to flip between them.

facts.text: Every instrument track has two envelopes, one for amplitude and one that drives the filter.
Clicking any encoder on `M2` flips the page between the amp and the filter envelope, on drum tracks as well as synth tracks.
How far the filter envelope moves the cutoff is set by envelope amount, `E3` on the filter page `M3`.
Over MIDI, CC20–23 set the amp envelope and CC24–27 the filter envelope, each in attack, decay, sustain, release order, whichever envelope the page shows.

The page draws both envelopes at once. The one the encoders edit is bright, with five square handles (start, peak, decay end, release start, end) and thin lines dropping from the inner three; the other is grey, without handles. Each is named, "amp" or "filter", just left of its release handle.

Each encoder slides one handle. Attack moves the peak right along the top, decay moves the decay end right of the peak, sustain raises the level, and release moves the release start right toward the end.

Release is set by where its handle sits, so turning `E4` clockwise (a higher value) gives a shorter release; fully clockwise the handle sits on the end and the note stops at once. Turn it counter-clockwise for a long fade.
There is no plateau after the attack; the decay starts at the peak. The attack rises steeply and bends into the peak, and decay and release fall steeply and level off.
The filter envelope is always drawn at full height; its real reach is set by envelope amount on `M3`.
The attack runs from instant at 0 to about 1.4 s at the middle and six minutes at the top, doubling every 6 or so steps; it rises like a charging capacitor, fastest at first, and stops at the peak.

Decay and release fall exponentially on one law, halving in about 5 ms at the short end, 0.28 s in the middle and 5 s at the long end (release runs the other way round); the law is gentle up to the middle and steepens past it.
A decay down to sustain 0 cuts to silence at about −41 dB, and a release ends at about −66 dB.
Sustain is linear in level: a quarter, half and three quarters of the way up give a quarter, half and three quarters of the peak.

units.body:
Envelopes give every note a shape in time: short and snappy amp settings for plucks and drums, slow
ones for pads. Read the graph as time running left to right: a peak far to the right is a slow
attack, a release handle far to the left is a long release (release turned down), one sitting on
the end is none (release turned all the way up). The filter envelope runs the same four stages but moves the cutoff instead, as far as
envelope amount on `M3` allows. The shift layer of `M2` holds the voice settings (play mode,
portamento, bend range, preset volume).

units.title: Play mode, portamento, bend range and preset volume (M2 + shift)
units.summary: Holding `shift` on `M2` reveals four voice settings — poly, mono or legato play mode, portamento (glide time), pitchbend range and a preset volume kept apart from the mixer level.

facts.text: Play mode (poly, mono or legato) sets both how notes are articulated and how many can sound at once.

Mono and legato both play one note at a time. Mono starts every note afresh, its envelopes from the top, and with portamento up every note glides from the last. Legato carries on from a note still sounding when the next starts, with no new attack, and glides there with portamento up; a note that starts just as the last ends starts afresh. This is how the replica plays them, from synth convention; it is not yet checked on a unit.
The curve of the portamento glide (portamento style) is set separately in the preset settings.
Turning bend range fully anti-clockwise switches pitch bending off, which is what you want when the pitchbend strip is routed to another target.
Over MIDI, CC28–31 reach these four settings; play mode reads the value as one of three steps.

Holding `shift` on `M2` brings up a white card of four rows over the dimmed page, each with its encoder's dot — play mode (poly, mono or legato), portamento (off, then numbers), bend range (semitones, up to an octave) and preset volume (a number).

units.body:
These settings decide how a sound responds to playing. Play mode separates chord parts (poly) from
single-note lines (mono, legato), portamento adds slides between notes, bend range sets the reach of
the pitchbend strip, and preset volume evens out loudness between presets without touching the
mixer. All four are saved with the preset.

units.title: Filter (M3)
units.summary: `M3` is the track's filter: cutoff, resonance, filter-envelope amount and key tracking. `shift + M3` picks one of four types — ladder, svf, z hipass or z lowpass — and then returns to `M1`.

facts.text: The filter takes away part of the frequency range and can emphasise the frequencies around its cutoff.
`shift + M3` opens the choice of filter types, each with its own character.
The type list, headed with the track number and the word filter, offers ladder, svf, z hipass and z lowpass, the current one boxed.
Picking a type takes you back to the engine page (`M1`); `M3` then shows the new type.
Presets also store whether the filter is switched on at all.
With the filter off, the page is dimmed under an off box; pressing `M3` again switches the filter on.

The page draws the filter's curve over tinted bands, with the type name at the top left, a frequency axis marked 50, 1k, 2k, 5k and 20kHz, and a small black box on the curve that shows the resonance, 00–99, rising as resonance goes up.

Cutoff slides the curve's slope along the axis, key tracking moves an arrow along the bottom from left to right, and any envelope amount above 0 adds a hatched ghost of the curve to its right; z hipass mirrors the drawing.
Envelope amount runs from none at 0 to full at 99; there is no negative setting that would sweep the cutoff down.
Over MIDI, CC32–35 on the track's channel move cutoff, resonance, envelope amount and key tracking, and the page redraws as they arrive.
No MIDI CC is known for the filter type.

Ladder and svf are 24 dB lowpasses modelled on analog circuits: the ladder four stages with feedback, the bass thinning as resonance rises; the svf two state-variable stages with a soft knee at resonance 0. z lowpass and z hipass are single two-pole digital filters, very gentle at resonance 0; the z lowpass rises to a whistling, nearly self-oscillating peak while the z hipass only reaches a mild one.
Cutoff spans from about 25 Hz to past 20 kHz; at the same setting the z hipass sits an octave below the z lowpass, and the svf a little above the ladder.
On the svf, raising resonance also lowers the peak by up to about half an octave and takes away up to 9 dB of level.
Key tracking pivots on C2: at 0 the cutoff ignores the note, at the middle it follows half an octave per octave, at the top an octave per octave.
At the envelope's peak, envelope amount opens the cutoff by about 0.85 of its own steps on the cutoff's scale, so a full amount from a closed filter opens it almost all the way.
