units.body:
The filter is a track's main tone control. Lower the cutoff to darken a sound, add resonance for a
sharper edge, and raise envelope amount so the filter envelope sweeps the cutoff on every note — the
classic plucky bass. The shift layer of this page holds the track's sends, not filter settings.

units.title: Track sends to aux out, tape, FX I and FX II (M3 + shift)
units.summary: Holding `shift` on `M3` turns the encoders into the track's four send levels — to the aux output, to the tape track and to the FX I and FX II send effects.

facts.text: Holding `shift` while `M3` is open brings up a white card of four send rows, worked by `E1`…`E4` from the top — aux out (a plug icon), tape (a reel icon), FX I and FX II; a row reads no send at zero.
Aux out feeds the external audio track (auxiliary `T5`), whose output leaves through the multi-out jack when that jack is set to audio.
The tape send makes the track's audio available to the tape track (auxiliary `T6`), which replays and mangles it.
In a new project every instrument track's tape send reads 99 (the other sends differ by sound); the tape is the normal path for a track's audio, so 99 there takes nothing away from the mix.
FX I and FX II are the two send-effect tracks (auxiliary `T7` and `T8`); what the send does depends on the effect loaded there.
Over MIDI, CC36–39 set the four sends in the same order.

procedures.goal: Send part of a track to the FX I effect

units.body:
Sends copy part of a track's audio to the auxiliary tracks and leave the dry sound as it is: FX I and
FX II for the shared send effects, tape for replaying tricks, aux out for the external audio track
and the multi-out jack. Sends are set per track and can be parameter-locked.

units.title: LFO page and LFO types (M4)
units.summary: `M4` holds one LFO per track in five types — duck, element, random, tremolo and value. `shift + M4` changes the type; most types share one layout: source or speed, amount, destination page, parameter.

facts.text: `shift + M4` switches the LFO type between duck, element, random, tremolo and value.
Duck arrived in OS 1.1.0; the guide's sentence listing the LFO types still counts four and leaves it out.
In element, random and value, `E1` sets the source or speed, `E2` the amount, `E3` the destination page and `E4` the parameter on that page; duck and tremolo use their own layouts.
The destination is one of the track's module pages and the parameter is one of that page's four encoders; `E4` can be turned or clicked to choose it.
Extra settings sit behind encoder clicks or `shift` plus a turn; on some types a click on `E1` changes the waveform shape.
Speed controls are tempo-synced over their anti-clockwise range; turned clockwise until a dial icon appears, they run at a free rate.

On screen a synced speed reads as a count beside a note value, 8 with a 32nd at the slow end, then 6 with a 16th, 4 with a quarter and 2 with a whole note as it turns; from the middle of its range a clock dial shows the free rate.

Synced, the speed doubles every eighth of the lane: in the middle of the synced range one cycle lasts a quarter note, anticlockwise an eighth, a 16th, a 32nd and a 64th, clockwise a half note and a bar.
Free, the LFO stands still at the dial's first position and speeds up ever faster, to about 21.5 cycles a second at the end.
Amount ladders are centred on zero (CC 64 over MIDI); either side of it sets the same depth with the modulation inverted.
Aimed at a filter's cutoff, value and random sweep its whole range at full amount; half the amount from a middle cutoff already reaches both ends.
The amount can go below zero to invert the modulation; OS 1.1.3 fixed how negative amounts are drawn.
On drum tracks the LFO restarts with every new note.
Over MIDI, CC40–43 on the track's channel drive the four `M4` encoders in order, in all five LFO types.
No MIDI CC is known for the LFO type.
With the LFO off, the page is dimmed under an off box; pressing `M4` again switches the LFO on.

procedures.goal: Change the LFO type of the selected track

units.body:
An LFO rides a knob for you. Choose what drives the movement — a repeating wave (value), random steps
(random), the unit's motion, microphone or envelope (element), another track's rhythm (duck) — then
aim it at an encoder on the track's pages. Tremolo skips the aiming: it is wired to pitch and volume.

units.title: Duck LFO (sidechain pumping)
units.summary: Since OS 1.1.0, the duck LFO dips a track's volume whenever another track or the metronome plays — the pumping sound of sidechain compression — triggered by audio or by notes.

facts.text: Duck lowers the track's own volume in response to a source, giving the pumping effect usually made with a sidechain compressor.
The duck LFO type was added in OS 1.1.0.
Any of the 16 tracks can be the source — instrument tracks 1–8 or auxiliary tracks 9–16 — and so can the metronome, for an even duck on every beat.
OS 1.1.3 fixed using a MIDI track as the duck source.
Duck shows its source as a track number (tr 1 and on), the last position a metronome icon, then amount, a live signal box and cards for hold and release.

At full amount the duck dips the track to silence in about 6 ms. Hold keeps it down from about 50 ms at 0 to 0.4 s at the top; release brings the level back within 0.64 s at 0 down to almost at once at the top, so a higher release is faster.
With a track as its source, the source card shows a MIDI plug when the track's notes trigger the duck, so even a silenced source track still ducks.

parameters.name: release
parameters.note: how long the level takes to recover

units.body:
Duck is the OP-XY's sidechain: choose the track that should push this one out of the way, and the
level drops every time the source plays. Note data reacts to each trigger, audio to the source's
sound. Hold and release shape the dip — short for tight pumping under a kick, longer for slow,
breathing swells.

units.title: Element LFO (gyroscope, microphone, envelope)
units.summary: The element LFO turns the unit's own sensors into a modulation source — tilt (gyroscope), the built-in microphone, the amp envelope, or all three summed.

facts.text: Element takes its modulation from the OP-XY itself rather than from an oscillator.
OS 1.0.50 raised the maximum depth of gyroscope modulation.
OS 1.1.0 fixed a bug that affected element when the amp envelope was its source.

Element shows its source as an icon — G for the gyroscope, a microphone, ^ for the envelope, or sum — then amount on a tick ladder, destination cards (synth wave, env, filter, amp) and a card naming the parameter, such as attack, cutoff, pitch or pan.

parameters.name: parameter
parameters.note: encoder on that page; clicking also selects

units.body:
Element makes the instrument physical. With the gyroscope, tilting the OP-XY sweeps whatever you aim
it at; with the microphone, sound in the room becomes modulation; the amp envelope source follows
the shape of each note. It suits live performance more than programmed patterns.

units.title: Random LFO
units.summary: The random LFO feeds random values to one parameter at a tempo-synced or free speed, with an envelope that fades the effect in or out.

facts.text: Random modulates its target with values from a random generator.
Every page appears twice as a destination, normal and free. On a normal one the modulation restarts with each key press; on a free one it keeps running.
Since OS 1.0.38, a random LFO on a free destination is not reset by new notes, and a reset snaps it to the correct value.
Random's page looks like the value LFO's, plus an animated random step wave under speed and an envelope-ramp card under the destination.

parameters.note: synced when turned anti-clockwise, free past the dial icon

parameters.name: envelope
parameters.note: fades the modulation in or out

units.body:
Random gives a part small changes that never repeat exactly: a wandering filter, drifting pitch,
jumping pans. Synced to the tempo it produces stepped, rhythmic changes; free-running it drifts. Pick
a free destination when the movement should carry on across notes instead of restarting on each one.

units.title: Tremolo LFO (vibrato and tremolo)
units.summary: The tremolo LFO is wired straight to pitch and volume — one depth for vibrato, one for tremolo — plus speed, a fade envelope and a waveform shape.

facts.text: Tremolo varies the track's pitch and volume directly, so it has no destination or parameter to choose.
`shift + turn E2` sets the tremolo's waveform shape. TE's caption for that control repeats the random LFO's envelope text; its title and diagram point to shape.
The tremolo page labels its fields rate, vib, vol and env, with a card labelled shape under env that shows the waveform (sine, square …); vib and vol are pointers on tick ladders.
While synced, rate shows a note-value icon with a multiplier (8, 6, 4, 2 …); turned further clockwise it becomes a clock dial whose hand turns, and the rate runs free.
Env is drawn as a line that rises at 0, lies flat at 64 and falls at 127.
The vol ladder dips the level to about a fifth at full; vib wobbles the pitch by about ±25 cents at a quarter, ±190 at half and more than an octave at full, growing ever faster.
Env at 64 keeps the tremolo steady; toward 0 it fades the tremolo in slowly, toward 127 it fades it out, at 127 at once.

parameters.name: speed
parameters.note: synced when turned anti-clockwise, free past the dial icon

parameters.name: envelope
parameters.note: fades the effect in or out

units.body:
Tremolo is the quickest way to make a sound move: no routing, just two depths. A little vibrato at a
moderate speed gives leads and strings a natural wobble, while the volume depth makes the classic
throbbing tremolo. Use the envelope so the effect grows in after the note starts instead of arriving
at once.

units.title: Value LFO
units.summary: The value LFO is a classic low-frequency oscillator, continuous or retriggered by notes, that sweeps any page parameter at a synced or free speed.

facts.text: Value drives its target with a low-frequency oscillator that either runs continuously or is triggered.
Every page appears twice as a destination, normal and free. On a normal one the modulation restarts with each key press; on a free one it keeps running.
The normal destinations give the triggered behaviour and the free ones the continuous behaviour.
Before OS 1.1.15, the slowest free-running speed stopped the value LFO altogether.
The value page shows speed, amount on a tick ladder, a scrolling column of destination cards and a large card naming the target parameter (attack, cutoff, res, key …) over an animated knob.
The destination column holds six cards, syn (the engine), env and filter, each followed by a twin labelled free with the same icon; there is no LFO destination.

procedures.goal: Sweep a track's filter cutoff in time with the tempo

steps.note: stay in the synced range and pick a rate

parameters.name: speed
parameters.note: synced when turned anti-clockwise, free past the dial icon

units.body:
Value is the general-purpose LFO: a repeating wave aimed at one parameter. Synced to the tempo it
makes rhythmic filter sweeps or pulsing levels; slow and free it gives gradual drift. With a normal
destination every note starts the wave from the same point, so repeated notes sound alike.

units.title: Axis synth engine
units.summary: An FM engine made for lush strings; its `M1` page sets tone, the ratio of one oscillator (detune or fifths), wave shape and a built-in tremolo.

facts.text: Axis is a frequency-modulation engine whose home ground is rich, full string sounds.
Ratio retunes one of the oscillators; values 0–50 detune it and 51–100 move it up in steps of a fifth.
Axis's picture is an isometric three-armed structure of cubes under a plain-text top bar; each encoder lengthens or reshapes one arm.

parameters.name: tremolo
parameters.note: speed and depth of a volume wobble, on one control

units.body:
In an FM engine one oscillator modulates another, and the ratio between them sets the timbre. Keep
axis's ratio in the detune half for chorused, ensemble-like strings; move into the fifths half for
stacked, interval-rich tones. Tone controls brightness, and the built-in tremolo adds movement
without using the LFO. Load it from the preset browser, `shift + M1`.

units.title: Dissolve synth engine
units.summary: A tonal-noise engine for airy ambient pads and bright, gritty leads; its `M1` page sets swarm (noise modulation), AM, FM and detune.

facts.text: Dissolve mixes noise into pitched oscillators, which suits ambient pads and bright, rough-edged leads.

Dissolve fills the screen with a mosaic of squares, re-dealt many times a second while notes sound and frozen when they stop; am raises the share of lit squares, fm lifts the brightest grey to white and swarm evens the greys.

parameters.name: fm
parameters.note: frequency modulation, for more tonal colour

parameters.name: detune
parameters.note: slight pitch offsets between oscillators, for a fuller sound

units.body:
Dissolve starts from oscillators and lets noise eat into them. Little swarm keeps a clear pitch with
a breath of air; a lot turns the tone into textured noise that still follows the keys. AM roughens,
FM adds harmonics, detune widens. Pair it with slow envelopes for pads or a short amp envelope for
noisy plucks. Load it from the preset browser, `shift + M1`.

units.title: Epiano synth engine
units.summary: An electric-piano model that also reaches plucks, strong leads and thick basses; its `M1` page sets tone, texture, tine and punch.

facts.text: Epiano imitates an electric piano and stretches to plucky keys, strong leads and heavy basses.
OS 1.1.25 corrected wrongly named parameters on the epiano screen, so older firmware may label its encoders differently.
On OS 1.1.33 the third encoder is tine and the fourth punch — the guide lists them the other way round.
Epiano's picture is an isometric stack of layers with tines, under a top bar of coloured cells labelled tone, texture, tine and punch.

parameters.name: tine
parameters.note: bright, metallic attack at the start of each note; the guide puts it on `E4`

parameters.name: punch
parameters.note: adds movement; the guide puts it on `E3`

units.body:
Epiano recreates the struck-tine electric piano. Tine sets how much bell-like attack each note has,
tone the overall brightness, texture adds dirt and punch adds movement. With the tine up and a medium
decay it sounds like classic keys; the guide also pitches it for leads and basses, so try it outside
piano parts. The guide (1.1.15) lists punch before tine; on 1.1.33, after the 1.1.25 fix to the
epiano's labels, tine sits on `E3` and punch on `E4`. Load it from the preset browser, `shift + M1`.

units.title: Hardsync synth engine
units.summary: A hard-sync engine for punchy stabs and firm basses; its `M1` page sets freq (a harmonic sweep), sub, noise and low cut.

facts.text: Hardsync is built for short stabs and firm, solid bass lines.

Hardsync's picture is a hair dryer whose blocks blow away while notes sound (fast at each note's start, slower as it holds), smaller as freq rises, with two dots for sub and an S-curve for the low cut that slides right as lowcut rises.

parameters.name: freq
parameters.note: shifts the harmonics, changing the tone

parameters.name: noise
parameters.note: adds noise to brighten the sound

units.body:
Hard sync restarts one oscillator from another, so sweeping freq produces the tearing, vocal sweep
sync sounds are known for — try a different freq lock on each step. Sub reinforces the bottom for
basses or thickens pads, noise brightens, and lowcut thins the sound so it sits above a bass line.
Load it from the preset browser, `shift + M1`.

units.title: Midi engine (called external in the guide)
units.summary: The midi engine makes an instrument track sequence outside gear — `M1` sets channel, bank and program, `M2` and `M3` hold eight CCs. TE's guide still calls it external, its name before OS 1.0.15.

facts.text: The midi engine makes no sound; the track's notes and settings go out as MIDI to an external instrument.
A midi-engine track sends on the channel chosen with `E1` on its `M1` page; the guide does not tie it to the project's MIDI channels.
OS 1.0.15 renamed the engine from external to midi; the guide (v1.1.15) and its MIDI how-to still use the old name.
`M2` and `M3` hold eight CC slots: turn an encoder to set a value, or hold `shift` and turn it to switch the slot on and choose its CC number.
Several instrument tracks can run the midi engine at once, one per device or channel, where the external MIDI track in auxiliary mode offers only one.
Since OS 1.0.45, presets saved from a midi-engine track keep their CC settings.
Since OS 1.0.50, switching a track to the midi engine and back keeps its synth settings.
Program changes can be parameter-locked per step; OS 1.1.15 fixed such locks not working.

On OS 1.1.33 the preset browser that `shift + M1` brings up listed no midi engine, so how that firmware puts an instrument track on midi is still open; the external MIDI track (auxiliary `T3`) always works, and this app's replica lists midi last in the browser.
OS 1.1.32 fixed the arpeggiator disturbing a midi-engine parameter.

procedures.goal: Sequence an external synth from an instrument track
preconditions: the synth is connected over USB or to the multi-out jack in MIDI mode

steps.note: the preset browser on OS 1.1.33 (the guide's engine list before)
choose midi, where it is listed
loads it (the old engine list took a click of `E1`)
switch a slot on and pick its CC number

procedures.result: Notes played or sequenced on the track now play the external synth.

parameters.name: channel
parameters.note: MIDI channel the track sends on

units.body:
Record or step-sequence on the track as usual and the notes play the connected synth; bank and
program pick its sound, and the CC slots send controller values that can be locked per step.

units.title: Organ synth engine
units.summary: An organ engine that spans transistor combos to church organs; its `M1` page sets organ type, bass, tremolo amount and tremolo speed.

facts.text: Organ covers a wide spread of organ sounds, from transistor instruments to church organs, chosen with the type control.
Organ's picture is four drawbars, each with a scale from 8 to 1 and an icon on its cap; each encoder slides one drawbar, and the bars glide into place.

units.body:
Organ is a quick route to a whole family of sounds: type swaps the organ model, bass adds weight, and
the built-in tremolo gives the familiar pulsing movement — slow for gentle swells, fast for a
shimmer. Because the tremolo lives on `M1`, the `M4` LFO stays free for something else. Load it from the preset browser,
`shift + M1`.

units.title: Prism synth engine
units.summary: A general-purpose synth engine for bass lines, leads and most other parts; its `M1` page covers waveform, oscillator ratio, detune and stereo width.

facts.text: Prism is one of the eight built-in synth engines. Each instrument track runs one engine, chosen per track.
Prism is the everyday workhorse among the engines, suited to bass lines, leads and most parts in between.
Only the `M1` page belongs to the engine. Envelopes (`M2`), filter (`M3`) and LFO (`M4`) work the same whichever synth engine a track uses.
Like every module-page parameter, prism's four `M1` settings can be parameter-locked per step.
Over MIDI, CC12, CC13, CC14 and CC15 on the track's channel move shape, ratio, detune and stereo.
Prism's picture is a row of four optics — a triangle, a convex lens, a concave lens and a wedge — with light rays passing through the lenses on every note.
Shape grows the triangle, ratio thickens the convex lens, detune slides the concave lens and stereo opens the wedge into an arrowhead.

Shape runs from a saw at 0 to a square at about 50, then narrows the two oscillators' pulses one after the other up to 99. Low is full and buzzy (every harmonic), the middle hollow (the even harmonics gone), the top thin and nasal.
Detune moves the second oscillator up to about 15 cents from the first, the same amount on every note, so the two beat slowly against each other, faster toward the top.

Ratio tunes the second oscillator against the first, an octave below at 2:1, in unison at 1:1, a fifth above at 2:3, an octave above at 1:2, and on up to four octaves above at 1:16, where it reads as a high overtone over the note more than a second note.

Stereo adds a copy of the sound through a slowly sweeping delay, a little sharp in one channel while flat in the other; up to the middle it fades the copy in, past it the sweep widens and quickens. The copy is high-passed, so the bass stays in the centre, and at 0 the sound is mono.

Ratio moves in ten equal steps of its 0–99 value and reads as the oscillators' frequency ratio, a step each ten — 00–09 2:1, 10–19 1:1, 20–29 2:3, 30–39 1:2, 40–49 1:3, 50–59 1:4, 60–69 1:6, 70–79 1:8, 80–89 1:12 and 90–99 1:16.

procedures.goal: Put the prism engine on the selected instrument track

steps.note: opens the preset browser by engine (OS 1.1.33)
scroll to prism; its first preset is highlighted
loads it, the whole sound with it

procedures.result: The track now plays through prism and `M1` shows its four parameters.

parameters.name: detune
parameters.note: small pitch offset between the oscillators, for a thicker sound

parameters.name: stereo
parameters.note: how far the oscillators spread across the stereo field

units.body:
Prism runs several oscillators and gives you four controls over how they relate: their waveform,
their tuning ratio, how far apart they drift in pitch and how wide they spread. Little detune and a
narrow image keep it tight for bass; more of both makes it broad enough for leads and pads.

Everything else about the sound — how notes start and fade (`M2`), the filter (`M3`) and modulation
(`M4`) — is shared by all engines, so a prism patch is shaped the same way as any other synth patch.
TE's guide gives no numeric ranges or defaults for prism's parameters; the screen shows them as you
turn, and the CC numbers are confirmed on OS 1.1.33.

units.title: Simple synth engine
units.summary: A basic engine for building leads and plucks quickly; its `M1` page sets waveform shape, pulse width, noise and stereo spread.

facts.text: Simple is meant for fast, basic patches, with leads and plucks as its strengths.
Simple's picture is an isometric glass jar on stacked slabs under a plain-text top bar; stereo splits the jar into two.

parameters.name: noise
parameters.note: noise level, from buzzy leads to soft pads

units.body:
Simple is the plain starting point: pick a waveform, narrow the pulse width for a hollow, nasal tone,
add noise for breath or buzz, and widen the stereo image. With the filter and envelopes doing most of
the shaping, it is the easiest engine to learn sound design on. Load it from the preset browser, `shift + M1`.

units.title: Wavetable synth engine
units.summary: An engine that morphs through a table of stored waveforms; its `M1` page picks one of nine tables and sets position, warp and drift.

facts.text: A wavetable is a row of waveforms stored one after another; moving through it morphs the oscillator smoothly from shape to shape.
The engine offers nine wavetables.
The first cell of the top bar names the current table; turning `E1` steps through basic, buzz, crush, drawbars, fibonacci, fractal, geometric, primes and zap.
The picture is the waveform itself, morphing and leaving trails as it changes; drift fans it out into moving ghost copies.

parameters.name: warp
parameters.note: bends the shape of the waveform

parameters.name: drift
parameters.note: lets the warp wander from the note's pitch, for inharmonic tones

units.body:
Wavetable suits evolving sounds: choose a table, then move the position to travel through its
waveforms. Position is the parameter to animate — lock it per step or aim the LFO at it — while warp
reshapes whatever waveform is current. Drift pulls the warping away from the played pitch for
metallic, unstable results. Load it from the preset browser, `shift + M1`.

units.title: Preset settings (tuning, velocity, width, mod routing)
units.summary: `shift + instrument` opens settings stored with the track's sound: tuning and transpose, a high-pass, velocity sensitivity, portamento style and width, plus a mod tab routing modwheel, aftertouch, pitchbend and velocity.

facts.text: `shift + instrument` opens the preset settings of the selected instrument track; `instrument` or any of `M1`…`M4` leads back to the pages.
The settings tab covers tuning (user tunings and transposition), a basic high-pass for trimming lows, velocity sensitivity, the portamento style and stereo width.
The preset high-pass is separate from the `M3` filter, so a track can use both.
The mod tab assigns the modwheel, aftertouch, pitchbend and velocity to parameters of the sound.
Each mod source has a target entry and an amount entry; a negative amount inverts the modulation.
Whether the built-in keys send velocity at all is a system setting (`com → M1`, keyboard section) with the choices off, soft and hard.
No MIDI CC is known for any preset setting.

procedures.goal: Route a mod source such as the pitchbend strip to a parameter

steps.note: the source's target entry, for example pitchbend target
choose the parameter, then set the matching amount entry the same way

units.body:
Preset settings are the parts of a sound you rarely touch while playing, and they travel with the
preset. The mod tab is how outside expression reaches the sound: aim a MIDI keyboard's modwheel or
aftertouch, or the pitchbend strip, at a parameter. To stop the strip also bending pitch, set bend
range (`M2`, shift layer) to off.

units.title: User tunings (microtonal)
units.summary: The preset settings hold 11 user tuning slots; in each, every note can be retuned in cents and finer micro-cent steps.

facts.text: There are 11 user tuning slots, found under settings → tuning in the preset settings.
`E3` picks a slot and `M4` opens it; in the editor, play a key to choose the note, then `turn E1` for cents and `E2` for micro-cents.
Presets store a user tuning as 12 offsets, one per pitch class, so the same pattern repeats in every octave.
OS 1.1.25 fixed user tunings not loading reliably into their user slots.

procedures.goal: Create a user tuning
procedures.result: The note plays at its new pitch wherever this tuning is selected.

units.body:
User tunings take the OP-XY outside twelve-tone equal temperament — just intervals, non-Western
scales or a gently detuned vintage feel. Each slot stores per-note offsets; select the slot as a
sound's tuning and the keyboard and sequencer play in it. Save the preset afterwards so the tuning
choice travels with the sound.

units.title: Preset browser (find and load sounds)
units.summary: `shift + Tn` in instrument mode opens that track's preset browser (on OS 1.1.33 `shift + M1` opens it for the selected track). Browse by engine or by category — a click of `E1` swaps them — and load a preset with a click of `E2`.

facts.text: In instrument mode, `shift + Tn` opens the preset browser for track n.
The unit ships with factory presets across the engines and the sound categories.
Loading a preset replaces the track's whole sound and copies it into the project, so later changes to the preset file leave existing tracks alone.
On OS 1.1.33 the category view lists bass, drum, keys, lead, organ, pad, pluck and strings, after any preset packs installed on the unit (an installed pack is listed first).
Top-level folders under presets on the unit's storage show up as categories.
Since OS 1.1.15, user preset folders can be nested more deeply.
The browser shows the track number over the word preset on the left, the engine list in the middle and that engine's presets on the right, the current preset highlighted.
A click of `E1` swaps between by engine and by category, and a popup names the view for a moment; the highlighted preset stays highlighted in the other view.

Presets sort by name, factory and user ones together; moving to another engine or category starts its list from the top with the first preset highlighted, and a list scrolls only as far as the highlight needs.
With one of your own presets highlighted the footer reads cut, paste, rename and delete over `M1`…`M4`; a factory preset shows none.
Loading leaves the browser for the track's `M1` page, showing the new sound's engine values.
On OS 1.1.33, `shift + M1` brings up this browser for the selected track, opening on its current preset in engine view; it is how that firmware changes engine.

procedures.goal: Load a preset on a track

steps.note: optional; swaps between engine and category view

procedures.result: The track plays the preset; all four pages and the preset settings change with it.

units.body:
The browser changes a track's whole sound in one step. Category view groups sounds by role; engine
view lists everything built on one engine, handy when you know the character you want. Your own
presets and folders sit beside the factory ones and are managed from the same screen.

units.title: Organise presets (cut, paste, rename, delete, folders)
units.summary: In the preset browser, `M1`–`M4` cut, paste, rename and delete user presets; `shift + M1`, `shift + M3` and `shift + M4` create, rename and delete folders. Folders and moving presets arrived in OS 1.1.15.

facts.text: The preset actions work on user presets; highlight one in the browser first.
`M1` cuts the highlighted preset and `M2` pastes it into the current folder, unless a preset of that name is already there — then nothing is overwritten.
`M3` renames the preset. `E1` moves between characters and the other encoders change the one selected; then `M1` confirms, `M2` goes to the next character, `M3` cancels and `M4` deletes.
`M4` deletes the highlighted user preset.
`shift + M1` creates a preset folder.
`shift + M3` renames a preset folder and `shift + M4` deletes it, which only works once the folder is empty.
Adding preset folders and moving presets between them came with OS 1.1.15.
OS 1.1.25 improved the behaviour when a user preset folder has the same name as factory presets.

procedures.goal: Move a user preset into another folder

steps.note: the category view, whose entries are the folders (on OS 1.1.33 the browser opens by engine)
go to the target folder; the guide does not say how nested folders are entered

procedures.goal: Create a preset folder

units.body:
User presets can be tidied without a computer: cut and paste move a preset between folders, rename
edits names with the encoders, and folders keep your own sounds apart from the factory library. The
actions apply to your own presets only.

units.title: Save, copy, paste and scramble a track's sound
units.summary: Hold a track key and press a module key — `Tn + M1` scrambles the sound, `Tn + M2` copies it, `Tn + M3` pastes onto that track and `Tn + M4` saves it as a new preset.

facts.text: `Tn + M1` scrambles the track's sound, a quick way to wreck a patch or audition random variations.
`Tn + M2` copies the sound of the held track and `Tn + M3` pastes it onto the held track.
`Tn + M4` saves the track's current sound as a preset.
Each save becomes a new dated preset in the snapshot folder, named like 2026-06-15 (1).
Saving copies the track's samples into the new preset, so it no longer depends on the original files.
A copied and pasted track takes its active octave along.
OS 1.1.32 fixed pasted tracks sometimes missing some of their settings.

procedures.goal: Save the selected track's sound as a new preset
Duplicate one track's sound onto another track

units.body:
These shortcuts act on a track's complete sound, preset settings included, without opening a menu.
Copy and paste duplicate a sound onto another track for layering or variations; scramble throws the
settings around for happy accidents, so save first if you may want the original back. A save never
overwrites: it adds a snapshot, unless you use the shift variant described in the related unit.

units.title: Save over the same preset snapshot
units.summary: Since OS 1.1.17, holding shift while saving a track's sound overwrites the snapshot it was loaded from instead of adding a new one. TE's guide does not mention it.

facts.text: The regular save, `Tn + M4` in instrument mode, stores the track's current sound as a preset.
A regular save creates a new snapshot instead of replacing the one the sound came from.
Keeping `shift` held while you save writes the sound back into the snapshot it came from.
Press the keys in the right order. `shift + Tn` on its own opens the preset browser, where `M4` deletes the selected user preset — so hold the track key first, then add `shift`.
On OS 1.1.17, saving into the same snapshot could lose the preset's samples; 1.1.18 fixed it, so use the feature on 1.1.18 or later.
Over MTP, the unit's storage shows a presets/snapshot folder next to the folders of user sound packs.

procedures.goal: Overwrite the loaded snapshot with the track's current sound
preconditions: the track's sound was loaded from a saved snapshot

steps.note: hold the track key as for a normal save, add shift, then press `M4` — the changelog only says to hold shift, so this order is not yet confirmed on a unit

procedures.result: The snapshot is updated in place; no new snapshot appears.

units.body:
Every regular save of a track's sound adds another snapshot, which is safe but fills the preset
folders with near-copies while you refine a patch. OS 1.1.17 added the alternative: hold `shift`
while saving and the snapshot you are working on is updated instead.

The guide (v1.1.15) predates the feature, so the exact gesture comes from the changelog alone.
Mind the order of the keys: starting with `shift` and then the track key opens the preset browser,
where `M4` means delete. Update to 1.1.18 or later before relying on it, because the first release
of the feature could drop the preset's samples.

units.title: Sustain pedal
units.summary: Since OS 1.1.15 a sustain pedal holds notes until it is let up, and since 1.1.17 it leaves arpeggiated notes alone. TE's guide never mentions it; with no pedal jack on the unit, the pedal arrives over MIDI.

facts.text: A sustain pedal keeps notes sounding until the pedal is released.
Since OS 1.1.17, the sustain pedal does not affect arpeggiated notes.
The OP-XY has no pedal socket, so a pedal has to reach it as MIDI — for example through a keyboard with a pedal input, connected over USB or MIDI in.
Over MIDI, sustain is controller 64 on the track's channel.

units.body:
The sustain pedal arrived with OS 1.1.15 and is absent from TE's guide, so what is known comes from
the changelog: held notes ring on until the pedal goes up, and arpeggios have ignored the pedal
since 1.1.17. Whether it works on every engine, and whether sustained notes are recorded, is not
documented.

units.title: Samplers at a glance
units.summary: Three instrument engines play samples — the synth sampler, the drum sampler and the multisampler; the sample key records into whichever one the selected track uses.

facts.text: The synth sampler (sampler among the browser's engines) plays one sample across the keyboard, with loop points for sustained sounds.
The drum sampler (drum among the browser's engines) gives each of the 24 keys its own one-shot sample.
The multisampler lays up to 24 samples of one instrument over zones of the keyboard.
On sampler tracks `M1` edits the sample; `M2…M4` work as on any instrument track.
In the mix, the drum sampler feeds the percussion group and the synth sampler the melodic group.
Drum sampler and synth sampler settings can be parameter-locked.
A blank project has drum samplers on tracks 1 and 2 and a multisampler on track 8.
Over MIDI, `M1`'s encoders answer CC12–15 — start, loop start, loop end, end on the synth sampler and multisampler; tune, start, end, play mode on the drum sampler.

procedures.goal: Put a sampler engine on the selected track

units.body:
Use the synth sampler to make one sound playable, the drum sampler for kits and one-shots (slicing
lives there too), and the multisampler when an instrument should sound natural across its range.

units.title: Sampling with the sample key
units.summary: `sample` opens a record page from any screen: set source, gain and threshold, then arm the recorder — `hold M1` on the library page, a key and then `hold M1` on the drum sampler and multisampler, a keyboard key on the synth sampler. The take starts once the input passes the threshold.

facts.text: On a sampler track, `sample` opens that engine's record page; on other tracks it records a stand-alone sample for the library.
A sample can be at most 20 seconds long, in every sampler.
On the library record page (a track without a sampler engine), holding `M1` arms the recorder.
Every record page has a threshold on `E4`, the level at which recording begins, so arming alone does not start the take; it starts when the input rises past that level.
On the drum sampler and multisampler record pages you first press the keyboard key the take should go to (it lights up), then `hold M1`.
The synth sampler's record page starts sampling from a keyboard key, which also becomes the sample's root note; the guide gives that page no `M1` gesture.
The guide does not say what ends a take before the 20-second limit, such as whether letting go of `M1` stops it; not yet checked on a unit.
The level meter previews the input while you set the gain, and TE's pictures draw the threshold as an orange line across it.
On the library record page, `M2` plays the take back and `M4` deletes it before it reaches the library.

A stand-alone take should land in the library's user folder (samples → user over MTP). The sample chapter says only that it goes to the library, but TE's load-samples how-to names user as the folder for samples recorded on the unit; not yet checked on a unit.
Pressing the lit track key closes the record page.
The sources TE documents for the sample page are the built-in mic, line in and USB; the guide names line in and USB as the ones with an input channel and draws the page with the mic selected.
Headset and main output belong to the external audio track's input list (`T5`); the guide never offers them on the sample page, and the page's full list has not been checked on a unit.
The built-in microphone can be the source, so sampling needs no cable.
Picking the input channel for line in and USB arrived in OS 1.0.29.
TE's audio-interface how-to picks the USB channel with `turn E2` instead; not yet checked on a unit.
