parameters.name: source
parameters.note: the documented sources; headset and main output are inputs of the external audio track, not of this page

parameters.name: threshold
parameters.note: the input level at which an armed recorder starts the take

units.body:
Every record page runs in the same order: choose the source, set the gain against the meter, put
the threshold just above the room noise, then arm. Arming only readies the recorder; the take
begins with the first sound that passes the threshold, so it starts on the note rather than on
silence. Each engine's unit has its own key handling.

units.title: Synth sampler
units.summary: Plays one sample across the keyboard. On its record page a keyboard key starts sampling and becomes the root note; `M1` sets start, loop and end points, and its shift layer direction, tune, loop crossfade, gain and loop type.

facts.text: On the synth sampler's record page you start sampling by pressing a keyboard key; the guide gives this page no `M1` gesture.
The key you press becomes the sample's root, the note the sampler tunes the recording to.
The page has the same source, gain and threshold controls as the other record pages (`E1`, `E3`, `E4`), so the key arms the recorder and the take begins once the input passes the threshold.
TE's picture of this record page reads "press key to sample" and labels none of `M1`…`M4`.
OS 1.0.45 corrected a latch text that the sample screen shows for the synth sampler; the changelog gives no wording, so the prompt on OS 1.1.33 may differ from TE's picture.
Not documented and not yet checked on a unit — whether `hold M1` also records here, whether the key has to stay held, and what ends a take before 20 seconds.
Pushing the encoder in while moving one of the four points gives finer steps.
Loop start at the very end of the sample means no loop.
Loop forever keeps cycling after release, loop until release stops cycling when you let go, loop off plays straight through.
After sampling on the unit, the loop runs from 20 % to 80 % of the sample, set to loop forever.
Tune works in cents; sample gain spans −30 to +20 dB.
Synth sampler settings accept parameter locks.
The page shows an overview strip of the sample on top (base layer only), the left and right waveforms, and start, loop and end markers.
With `shift` held it shows direction, tune as a note symbol and a value such as −12.00, crossfade as a percentage drawn as a dark wedge at the loop, and gain.
CC12–15 on the track's channel move nothing on this page.
Loop crossfade runs from 0 to 75 %, drawn as a dark wedge sloping down into the loop end over that share of the loop.

procedures.goal: Record a new sample into the synth sampler
preconditions: the track uses the synth sampler

steps.note: the source; `turn E3` sets the gain and `turn E4` the threshold
the note the sample should play at; this starts sampling

procedures.result: The sampler tunes the take to the key you pressed.

parameters.name: loop crossfade
parameters.note: smooths the loop, e.g. for pads

parameters.name: loop type
parameters.range: loop forever / loop until release / loop off

units.body:
TE's guide calls it the one shot synth sampler. To record, open `sample`, set source, gain and
threshold, then press the key whose pitch matches the sound you are about to play: the take is
tuned to that key, so the keyboard plays it in tune. Loop forever suits drones and pads, loop until
release leaves a natural tail when you let go, and loop off makes the sample a one-shot.

units.title: Drum sampler
units.summary: Gives each of the 24 keys its own one-shot sample; record straight onto a chosen key, step between filled keys, and copy, paste or multi-select keys on the `M1` page.

facts.text: Each key holds its own one-shot sample — built for kits, fine for any set of separate sounds.
On the record page, press the key the take should land on (it lights up), then `hold M1`; the recording itself starts once the input passes the threshold.
The guide ties no root note to a drum key — the key you choose is where the take goes, and tune on the `M1` page (`turn E1`) changes its pitch afterwards.
Over MIDI the 24 keys are notes 53–76 (F3–E5 with C4 = 60), left to right.
Every drum sampler recording is also saved to the samples folder named user.
On the record page, `M2` and `M3` jump to the previous or next key holding a sample; `M4` clears the current key but keeps its file.
On `M1`, `key + M2` copies that key's sample and `key + M3` pastes the last copy onto the held key.
Drum key copy and paste exists since OS 1.0.29.
`key + M4` selects several keys so one edit changes them all; the guide does not say how more keys join.
Long samples default to the key play mode (sound only while held) rather than oneshot.

TE's factory kits share one layout, left to right: kick, kick, snare, snare, rim, clap, tambourine, shaker, closed hat, closed hat, open hat, clave, low tom, ride, mid tom, crash, high tom, triangle, low conga, high conga, cowbell, guiro, metal, chi.

procedures.goal: Record a sample onto one key
preconditions: the track uses the drum sampler

steps.note: set source, gain and threshold here (`turn E1`, `turn E3`, `turn E4`)
the key lights up; choose it after `sample`, since a key held while pressing `sample` browses samples instead
the take starts once the input passes the threshold

units.body:
Treat the keyboard as 24 pads: on the record page press a key, `hold M1` and make the sound; the
recorder waits for the threshold, so the take starts on the hit. Takes also land in the library, so
clearing a key never loses a recording.

units.title: Drum sampler key settings
units.summary: The drum sampler's `M1` page shapes the selected key — tune, start, end and play mode, with direction, pan, fade and gain on the shift layer.

facts.text: The settings belong to the selected key, so every key keeps its own values.
Key plays only while held, oneshot always to the end, mute group is cut off by another mute-group key, loop repeats.
A kit has a single mute group, so all mute-group keys choke each other — handy for open and closed hats.
The mute group applies across live and sequenced notes alike.
Pan runs from −100 to +100, sample fade from 0 to 99, sample gain from −30 to +20 dB.
The screen draws the sample fade over the waveform.
The guide's texts for pan and sample fade describe tune and loop crossfade — copied from the synth sampler by mistake.

The page shows the selected key's waveform with the skipped parts tinted blue and start and end markers; tune reads as a note symbol and a signed value such as −16.10, moving in steps of 0.1, and play mode as one of four icons — an arrow to a bar, a plain arrow, an arrow with G, or a loop.
With `shift` held the page shows direction, pan as a bar from L to R, fade as a dark ramp that rises from the start marker over the wave, and gain, which scales the drawn wave.
Tune is always signed, so no transposition reads +0.00, and it reaches well past an octave (−16.10 was seen on a key).
CC12–15 on the track's channel move nothing on this page.
The sample fade is a fade-in from the start marker lasting a fixed time, about 0.25 s at 50 and 0.95 s at 99, so a short hit at a high fade never reaches full level.

units.body:
Trim each hit with start and end, retune it, and pick its behaviour: oneshot for drums, key for
held sounds, loop for textures, mute group for sounds that should cut each other off.

units.title: Slicing a sample across the keys
units.summary: On a drum sampler track, `key + M1` cuts that key's sample into slices spread over the keyboard — at its transients, into equal parts, or where you tap.

facts.text: Slice mode arrived in OS 1.1.0.
On a drum sampler track, `key + M1` opens the slicer for that key's sample.
`turn E1` chooses the mode: transient, even or tap.
The slices fill the keyboard on their own and choke each other, so one slice sounds at a time.
With one slice per key, a sample gives at most 24 slices.
Transient mode cuts at the loudest hits; `turn E4` sets how many slices, and after pressing a slice's key `turn E2` and `turn E3` move its start and end.
Even mode splits a section into equal parts; `turn E2` and `turn E3` set where the section starts and ends, `turn E4` the count.
In tap mode, tap `M1` to start the sample and again wherever a slice should begin; `M2` stops and lets the last slice run to the end.
In tap mode, press a slice's key and `turn E2` to move its start (the previous slice's end); `shift + key` deletes that slice.
The slicer screen offers cancel and done; which keys they sit on is not documented.

procedures.goal: Slice a drum loop at its hits
preconditions: the loop is on a key of a drum sampler track

steps.note: hold the key with the loop

units.body:
Slicing turns one recording into a playable kit. Transient suits drums with clear hits, even suits
loops cut to the grid, and tap marks musical phrases by ear while the sample plays.

units.title: Multisampler
units.summary: Up to 24 samples of one instrument, each on its own zone of the keyboard; a sample also plays the empty keys below it, and `M1` edits the selected zone like the synth sampler.

facts.text: Each range of notes plays from a recording made near its pitch, which sounds truer than stretching one sample.
While recording, select keys from left to right; every key that gets a sample becomes a zone.
Zones fill downwards — a sample also covers the empty keys below it, pitched down, as far as the next zone.
Up to 24 zones fit, about three samples per octave.

The record page works like the drum sampler's — press a key to choose the zone (it lights up), then `hold M1`; `M2` / `M3` step through filled keys, `M4` unassigns, and takes also go to the user folder.
As on every record page, the take starts only once the input passes the threshold set with `E4`.
The key you record on becomes the zone's top key and root (presets the unit writes set each zone's root to its top key), so play that key's note into the input.
The multisampler's `M1` page has the synth sampler's layout, loop type included (`shift + click E3`).
The guide titles `shift + turn E2` and `shift + turn E3` pan and sample fade but describes tune and loop crossfade; zones store tune and crossfade, not pan.
There are no velocity layers or round robins — one sample per zone.
OS 1.1.25 improved how multisamples follow global transpose.

The top strip is a full keyboard on which the zone of the sample being played lights up, jumping with the octave; each zone brings its own waveform and markers, and the shift layer matches the synth sampler's.
CC12–15 on the track's channel move nothing on this page.

procedures.goal: Multisample an instrument

steps.note: set source, gain and threshold here (`turn E1`, `turn E3`, `turn E4`)
start low and work to the right; the key lights up
play that key's note; the take starts once it passes the threshold. Repeat on the next key

units.body: Sample the instrument every few notes and let the zones fill the gaps below each one.

units.title: Sample library
units.summary: `shift + sample` opens the library of every sample on the unit: pick a folder, hear each sample as you land on it, and click an encoder to load it into the sampler.

facts.text: The library holds every sample on the unit and loads any of them into any of the three samplers.
In the library a sample plays as soon as it is selected; `stop` ends the preview.
Clicking any encoder opens a subfolder or loads the selected sample; subfolder names are in square brackets.
New folders are made on a computer, inside the samples folder, in MTP mode.
Samples you record on the unit are kept in the library's user folder, which a computer sees as samples → user in MTP mode.
For the drum sampler and multisampler, `M2` and `M3` step through filled keys and `M4` clears a key without deleting its file.
Holding a keyboard key and pressing `sample` browses samples for that key.
Samples used by your own presets are gathered in one group.
A system setting controls the sample preview; the changelog does not say where it is.

procedures.goal: Load a sample into the current sampler

units.body:
The library is the shared pool behind all three samplers: your recordings, factory sounds and files
copied from a computer. Browsing auditions as you turn.

units.title: Sample files, pitch and memory
units.summary: The samplers read WAV and AIFF files copied into the samples folder over MTP; pitch comes from the file's metadata or a note in its name, and a project can load up to 64 MB of samples.

facts.text: The OP-XY reads WAV and AIFF files.
To add samples, connect a computer, put the unit in MTP mode and copy the files into the sample library.
Over MTP the unit shows a samples folder containing user, next to presets and projects.
Deleting a sample for good needs MTP; clearing a key on the unit only removes the assignment.
Pitch is read from the WAV metadata; failing that, from a note name such as a3 in the file name.
The unit writes the root note into the metadata of the WAVs it records.
Current factory and device files name notes with C4 = 60, older device files with C3 = 60; metadata avoids the mix-up.
Recordings examined so far are 16-bit, 44.1 kHz mono WAV files.
File names should use only letters, digits, spaces, - and #.
Folders can nest more than one level deep.
A project can have up to 64 MB of samples loaded at once.

units.body:
Anything copied into the samples folder shows up in the library, sorted by folder. Give files a root
note in their metadata, or a note name in the file name, so the samplers play them in tune.

units.title: Auxiliary mode and its eight tracks
units.summary: `auxiliary` turns the track keys into eight fixed utility tracks — brain, punch-in FX, external MIDI, external CV, external audio, tape, FX I and FX II — sequenced like instrument tracks.

facts.text: Aux tracks vary the built-in sounds or control and feed outside gear.
`T1` brain, `T2` punch-in FX, `T3` external MIDI, `T4` external CV, `T5` external audio, `T6` tape, `T7` FX I, `T8` FX II.
The selected aux track lights its key red; instrument tracks light white.
External audio, tape and the FX tracks put main controls on `M1`, routing on `M2`, a filter on `M3` and an LFO on `M4`; the brain has `M1` and routing, external MIDI puts CCs on `M2` and `M3`.
Aux tracks have their own patterns, notes, parameter locks and step components, like instrument tracks.
By default the aux tracks answer MIDI channels 9–16 in order, brain on 9 up to FX II on 16.
In mix mode, pressing `mix` again switches between instrument and aux tracks.

procedures.goal: Open an auxiliary track

units.body:
Instrument mode is for composing; auxiliary mode is for transposing, effects and reaching outside
the box. The eight roles never change, and because the tracks sequence like any other, transpositions,
effect moves and outside gear can all be programmed per step.

units.title: Brain
units.summary: The brain (`T1`) works out the key and scale of the tracks routed into it, and its keyboard transposes them in key — live, or sequenced as notes on the brain track.

facts.text: The brain detects the key and scale of the routed tracks and transposes them musically — the whole song or only some tracks.
On the brain track, the keyboard transposes every routed track.
Brain notes recorded into its sequence play back as transpositions, so a one-bar idea follows a chord progression.
The brain's manual mode lets you set the key yourself when detection gets it wrong.
Tracks left out of the routing on `M2` are neither transposed nor used for key detection.
In a new project tracks 3–8 are routed to the brain and drum tracks 1 and 2 are not.
The brain has seven scales, shown in this order as major, dorian, phrygian, lydian, mixo (mixolydian), minor and locrian.
Brain settings are stored per pattern.
The brain's routing is stored per pattern, not per scene.
Arpeggiator notes follow the brain; OS 1.1.17 fixed arpeggios ignoring it.

The brain's `M1` is headed with the current key, such as c major, and draws a mini keyboard marking the scale's notes. Manual mode shows a hand and the root and scale fields; auto mode shows a brain head instead.
Link reads a crossed box when off and a two-digit number otherwise; with CC15 at 32, 64, 96 and 127 it showed 02, 04, 06 and 08.
`M2` slides in from `M1` and shows an in bracket running from the brain to track boxes 1–8, each on or off.
The brain has no filter page; CC32 and CC35 on its channel change nothing.
Over MIDI, CC12–15 on the brain's channel (9) drive its four `M1` encoders; CC12 shows manual at 0 and auto at 127.

procedures.goal: Take a track into or out of the brain

steps.note: the track's encoder; an encoder click toggles the page, tracks 1–4 or 5–8

parameters.name: scale
parameters.range: major / dorian / phrygian / lydian / mixo / minor / locrian

parameters.name: link
parameters.note: links an instrument track, to riff over the song as it transposes

units.body:
A fast way to write: sequence a beat, a bassline and one chord, then play or sequence root changes
on the brain track. Take leads and drums out of the routing when they should stay put.

units.title: Punch-in FX
units.summary: The punch-in FX track (`T2`) turns the keyboard into 24 momentary effects — lower octave for percussion tracks, upper for melodic ones; `shift + key` fires them from any instrument track.

facts.text: On `T2` each of the 24 keys is a different effect that lasts while held; held keys combine.
The lower octave acts on the percussion tracks, the upper octave on the melodic tracks.
Some effects also respond to moving the unit (gyroscope) or to the pitchbend strip.
On an instrument track, `shift + key` plays punch-in FX; the lower octave affects only that track, the upper octave its whole group.
Shortcut effects played while recording are written to the punch-in FX track.
Percussive engines such as the drum sampler form the percussion group; synth engines and the synth sampler the melodic group.
When effects conflict, the mute effect takes priority.
OS 1.0.32 stopped `shift + key` from triggering punch-in FX while external MIDI is in use.
Over MIDI, notes 53–76 on channel 10 fire the 24 effects as if the keys were held, with the track showing each animation.

Both octaves hold the same twelve effects in the same order, F to E — mute, stutter, repeat two steps, pan, repeat three steps, octave, follow, fill or ramp up, short, hat fill or ramp down, soft attack, random. Each takes a shape suited to the group it acts on. TE has not named them; these names are descriptive.
F (either octave) silences its group for as long as it is held.

F♯ stutters in time with the project's sixteenths — melodic tracks jump back to the start of each sixteenth several times and drop out for its last part; drums let only the first few tens of milliseconds of each sixteenth through, in mono.
A replays three sixteenths over and over, and G (on melodic tracks) two; the pattern keeps running underneath and carries on in place on release.
G on the drums presumably loops two sixteenths as it does on melodic tracks; the recordings did not show it.
G♯ moves the sound across the stereo field — each drum hit lands left or right by its place in the bar, and melodic tracks swing to one side.
A♯ drops melodic tracks' sequenced notes an octave.
On the drums, A♯ presumably raises the sequenced hits an octave.
B makes the other tracks of the group play the sequenced notes too, each with its own sound.
On the drums, C adds a kick and snare fill and D a hi-hat groove (closed on every sixteenth, open on the off-beat eighths), both on top of the pattern.
On melodic tracks, C makes each step's notes climb higher, gliding between them.
On melodic tracks, D makes each step's notes fall lower, gliding between them.
C♯ cuts every note or hit to a blip of about 25 ms.
D♯ softens attacks — drum hits fade in and synth notes swell in.
E randomises — drum steps play random keys of the kit and melodic notes leap by random intervals.

On the drums, the repeats, octave, follow and random rework the sequencer's own pattern and leave hits arriving over MIDI untouched, while mute, stutter, pan, short and soft change every hit and the fills add hits of their own.
On `T2` each of the 24 keys plays its own animation on the screen — planets, a digit clock, noise, hands, waves, sweeping lines and bars, and more.
With no effect held, the page shows a single dot tracing a heartbeat line across the dot grid, about every three seconds; it starts again from the left edge each time an effect ends.

procedures.goal: Record punch-in FX from an instrument track

units.body:
Punch-in FX are for performing: hold a key for a moment of change, let go and the track snaps back.
Recorded passes live on their own track, so they can be edited without touching the parts below.

From F to E, each octave runs: mute, stutter, repeat two steps, pan, repeat three steps, octave,
follow, a fill (drums) or rising ramp (melodic), short, a hi-hat groove (drums) or falling ramp
(melodic), soft attack and random. The rhythmic ones follow the project tempo.

units.title: External MIDI track
units.summary: `T3` plays and sequences outside MIDI gear over USB-C or the multi-out, sending on the channel set on `M1` (with bank and program); `M2` and `M3` hold eight CC slots and `M4` an LFO.

facts.text: The external MIDI track (`T3`) sends its keyboard and sequencer notes to connected MIDI gear.
Gear connects through the USB-C port, or through the multi-out jack set to midi.
Notes and CC values leave on the channel set with `E1` on `M1`, so set it to the channel the outside synth listens on.
TE's MIDI how-to sets only this `M1` channel; the project's midi page plays no part in it.
`M2` and `M3` hold four CC slots each; turning sends a slot's value, `shift + turn E1…E4` switches a slot on and picks its CC number, and the values can be sequenced and recorded.
The external MIDI track's LFO (`M4`) modulates the track's own parameters, such as a CC slot.
Program changes can be parameter-locked; OS 1.1.15 fixed such locks not working.
Community charts put the slot values on CC20–23 and CC32–35 of channel 11 and the slot numbers on CC28–31 and CC36–39.
Received on channel 11, CC12–14 set the track's channel, bank and program and CC40–43 drive the `M4` LFO; CC15 does nothing.
The `M1` page is headed midi with a DIN socket icon; channel reads 01–16, and bank and program show a crossed box at 0, then 1–128.
`M2` and `M3` slide in sideways from `M1`; each CC slot is a crossed box while off, or a large value with cc and its number underneath.
The `M4` LFO offers the CC slots as its destinations; a slot without a CC shows no cc set as the parameter.

procedures.goal: Play an outside synth from the OP-XY
preconditions: the synth is connected over USB-C
or to the multi-out set to midi

steps.note: on `M1`, the channel the synth listens on

units.body:
`T3` is a track whose sound lives in another box: set its channel to the synth's, pick a sound with
bank and program, and map the CC slots to the controls you want to move. Channel 11 is only where
the OP-XY listens for the track's own controls; the notes go out on the `M1` channel. For more
devices at once, use instrument tracks with the midi engine (which OS 1.1.33's preset browser did
not list).

units.title: External CV track
units.summary: `T4` sends note pitch as control voltage and a gate from the multi-out jack, so the keyboard and sequencer can play modular and vintage synths.

facts.text: Modular and vintage synths take pitch as a control voltage (CV) and note on/off as a gate.
On the external CV track (`T4`) the keyboard and sequencer play the connected CV device.
The multi-out carries CV on its tip (left) and gate on its ring (right).
Use a splitter cable that separates left and right, not one that keeps stereo — tip to the CV input, ring to the gate input.
The CV track's page is a voltmeter labelled CV, reading from −5 to +5 V.
CC12–15 on its channel (12) move nothing on that page.

procedures.goal: Set the multi-out to CV and gate

units.body:
The simplest aux track: the guide gives it no page settings, only notes, and on the unit its page is
just a voltmeter. Set the multi-out to cv
before plugging in, patch pitch and gate into the synth, then play `T4` like any other track.

units.title: External audio track
units.summary: `T5` brings one of its own five inputs — mic, headset, line in, USB audio or the main output — into the mix, and routes instrument tracks out of the multi-out jack, for example through an outboard effect.

facts.text: The 3.5 mm audio input takes line sources or a microphone, for vocals, horns and the like.
On the external audio track's `M1`, `turn E1` picks one of five inputs — mic, headset, audio input (the 3.5 mm line in), USB audio or main output.
These five are the external audio track's inputs only; the sample page has its own source control, documented with just mic, line in and USB.
On `T5`, choose the input with `turn E1`, then `click E1` to switch it on.
Sending audio out needs the multi-out set to audio.
`M2` sends instrument tracks to the aux output on the multi-out; only routed tracks leave there, each at an amount independent of the main mix.
For an outboard effect, send tracks out of the multi-out, return the effect into the audio input, and balance the return with drive, level and mix.
Community charts give CC12 on channel 13 as the input select and suggest the level is the track level, CC7.
Over MIDI on channel 13, CC13 sets drive and CC15 mix, and CC32, CC35 and CC40–43 reach the filter and LFO pages; CC12, the input select, was left untried so the microphone could not open.
`M1` draws the signal path — a microphone box marked fdbk block (crossed out while it blocks feedback), a line labelled input, then boxes for drive, level and mix.
Drive reads 00–20 and mix 00–99; level showed 75 in a new project.
Its `M2` routing page shows track boxes 1–8 and an out box, and its `M4` LFO aims at syn, filter or amp, with parameters such as param1, hi pass, volume and pan.

parameters.name: input
parameters.range: mic / headset / audio input / USB audio / main output
parameters.note: this track's own list, not the sample page's sources

parameters.name: level
parameters.note: the input's volume in the main mix

parameters.name: mix
parameters.note: how much of the routed tracks returns to the main output

units.body:
Two jobs share this track: as an input it puts a mic, synth or computer audio into the mix; as an
output it sends chosen tracks out of the multi-out, so an outboard effect can process them and come
back through the input. Instrument tracks can also feed the aux output from their send page.

units.title: Tape track
units.summary: `T6` grabs and rearranges audio playing in the unit: its keyboard plays clips of the tracks routed into the tape, and pitch, speed, loop length and mix shape the result.

facts.text: Tape picks out and rearranges audio playing inside the OP-XY, which makes glitchy effects easy.
On the tape track (`T6`) the keyboard plays clips of whatever tracks are routed into the tape.
Only tracks routed on `M2` run through the tape, each at its own amount, independent of the main mix.
Community charts read tape pitch as a speed multiple, x1 by default.
The tape page shows a reel icon with the speed as a percentage, a tape strip carrying a mini keyboard and the loop length as a number, and a mix box.
Speed runs from 50 % to 200 %, length from 1 to 16 and mix from 00 to 99. Over MIDI, CC13 at 63 gives 99 % and at 64 gives 101 %, so exactly 100 % cannot be sent.
Tape settings can be parameter-locked; OS 1.1.15 fixed locks not showing on the tape screen.
Over MIDI on channel 14, CC13 moves speed, CC14 length and CC15 mix on the tape page, and CC12 changes it only slightly.

units.body:
Route a drum track into the tape, then play `T6`'s keyboard to fire back fragments of what just
played; shorten the loop for stutters, drop the pitch for slow-downs.

units.title: FX I and FX II send tracks
units.summary: `T7` and `T8` hold the two send effects: any sounding track can feed them, FX I can feed FX II (one way only), and `shift + T7` or `shift + T8` opens the effect list for a slot.

facts.text: FX I and FX II are the two send effects; every track that makes sound can send to both, and FX I can send on into FX II.
On an FX track the keyboard plays the last selected instrument track, so you hear the effect on that sound.
`shift + T7` or `shift + T8` opens the effect list for that slot: `turn E4` scrolls it, and `click E4` or `M1` loads the highlighted effect.
On an FX track, `M1` shows the loaded effect's parameters.
On FX I, `shift + turn E4` on the `M3` page sets the send into FX II.
The link between the slots runs one way, FX I into FX II; the guide describes no send from FX II back into FX I, so put the effect that should come first on FX I.
What FX II's own `M3` shift layer holds is not documented, and that page has not yet been looked at on a unit.
Instrument tracks send from their send page (`shift` held on `M3`, `E3` for FX I, `E4` for FX II).
In mix mode, `M1` sets each track's FX I send with `turn E1` and FX II send with `turn E2`.
The guide's FX routing card repeats a CV sentence and its filter card names the tape track — copy slips.
The FX I page is headed with a boxed FX I and the effect's name, then four columns with labels above and values below, each a bar split by a marker at the value's height.
On FX I, `shift + T7` lists the effects — chorus, delay, dist, lofi, phaser and reverb.
Over MIDI, CC12–15 on channel 15 move the four columns of FX I.

units.body:
One reverb on FX II can serve every track, each sending as much as it needs, and chaining FX I
into FX II lets a delay fade into reverb. The chain only runs that way round, so reverb into delay
means loading the reverb on FX I and the delay on FX II. The effects themselves are described in the
effects area.

units.title: Aux routing, filter and LFO pages
units.summary: Pages shared by several aux tracks — `M2` routes instrument tracks in, `M3` is a high-pass and low-pass filter with sends on its shift layer, and `M4` is an LFO aimed at one of the track's own parameters.

facts.text: The brain, external audio, tape and both FX tracks have a routing page on `M2`.
On a routing page, an encoder click toggles the page between tracks 1–4 and tracks 5–8; turning a track's encoder adds or removes it, and on tape and external audio sets how much goes in.
External audio, tape and both FX tracks have the filter on `M3`; those four plus external MIDI have the LFO on `M4`.
OS 1.1.32 fixed aux track LFOs failing to affect the page parameters.
Community charts put the aux sends on CC37–39 of the track's channel.
Over MIDI, CC32 and CC35 move the external audio track's high-pass and low-pass and CC40–43 its LFO; the external MIDI track's LFO answers CC40–43 too.
On external audio the `M3` filter starts switched off; its high-pass is drawn rising from the left and its low-pass falling from the right.

parameters.name: FX II send
parameters.note: external audio, tape, and FX I (into FX II); FX II itself has no documented send

units.body:
These pages behave alike on every aux track that has them. The filter trims the lows and highs of
what the track outputs, keeping a reverb return clean; the LFO moves one of the track's own settings.

units.title: Send effects
units.summary: Six built-in send effects — chorus, delay, distortion, lofi, phaser and reverb — can be loaded on the two FX tracks, FX I (`T7`) and FX II (`T8`); `M1` of an FX track shows the effect's four controls.

facts.text: The OP-XY has six built-in send effects — chorus, delay, distortion, lofi, phaser and reverb.
Two slots hold them, the FX tracks FX I and FX II, which are auxiliary tracks `T7` and `T8`; either slot can take any of the six.
The loaded effect's four parameters sit on the FX track's `M1` page.
No MIDI CC is known that changes the effect type; choose it on the unit.
The effect list on the unit spells them chorus, delay, dist, lofi, phaser and reverb.
A new project starts with a delay on FX I, set to a dotted eighth, and a reverb on FX II.

procedures.goal: Load a different effect on FX I or FX II

steps.note: select FX I or FX II
opens the list of effects for that slot

procedures.result: The slot now runs the chosen effect and `M1` shows its parameters.

units.body:
Send effects work like the return channels of a mixing desk: tracks send a share of their signal to
FX I or FX II, and the FX track plays the processed result back into the mix, so one reverb can serve
every track. Each slot runs one effect at a time, and FX I can also feed FX II, never the reverse as
far as TE documents. The FX tracks themselves — sends, routing, filter, LFO and defaults — are
covered with the auxiliary tracks; the units here list what each effect's `M1` encoders do.

units.title: Chorus effect
units.summary: A chorus for FX I or FX II that layers pitch-wobbled copies over the sound to widen it; `M1` sets rate, depth, feedback and stereo width.

facts.text: The chorus layers copies of the incoming sound whose pitch and timing drift a little against the original, which thickens and widens it; pushed far, the drift becomes an obvious effect.
High feedback settings turn the chorus into a short delay with wobbling pitch.
The chorus's columns read rate, depth, feedback and stereo, as the guide names them.

parameters.name: depth
parameters.note: how far the pitch is modulated

parameters.name: feedback
parameters.note: how much of the output returns into the chorus

units.body:
A chorus makes one voice sound like several by adding detuned, slightly late copies. Keep rate and
depth low for a subtle widening of pads and keys; raise them for seasick vibrato. Feedback adds
resonance and, at the top of its range, a pitch-wobbling echo. Stereo decides how far the copies
spread across the field.

units.title: Delay effect
units.summary: An echo for FX I or FX II; `M1` sets the repeat spacing as a note value, fine-tunes it, and sets the feedback and the amount of dry signal.

facts.text: The delay plays back what it receives as a series of echoes.
Size (`E1`) sets the spacing of the repeats and reads as a note value, such as 1/8 dotted.
The delay's columns read size, fine, feedback and dry — `E2` fine-tunes the spacing and `E3` sets the feedback.
Dry (`E4`) sets the untreated signal against the echoes; at 0 only the repeats are heard.
Since OS 1.1.25 the delay stays steady when the tempo of an external clock wobbles.

parameters.name: fine
parameters.note: fine-tunes the spacing; the guide calls it amount

parameters.name: feedback
parameters.note: how many repeats come back; the guide calls it fine

units.body:
Set the rough echo distance with size, then fine-tune it and choose how long the echoes keep coming
back. For a classic send, keep dry at 0 so the FX track returns only the echoes. TE's guide calls the
middle controls amount and fine and describes size as eight named steps from micro to insane; on
1.1.33 the screen reads fine and feedback, and size shows note values, so the spacing follows the
tempo.

units.title: Distortion effect
units.summary: A clipping distortion for FX I or FX II; `M1` sets the drive into it, the clipping amount and low and high cuts that shape what enters it.

facts.text: The distortion clips the signal it receives, adding grit and harmonics.
Low cut (`E3`) and high cut (`E4`) act on the input, trimming bass and treble before the clipping rather than after it.
The unit lists the effect as dist, and its columns read drive, clip, lo cut and hi cut — the guide's amount is labelled clip.

parameters.name: clip
parameters.note: how hard the signal is clipped; the guide calls it amount

parameters.name: low cut
parameters.note: how much bass reaches the distortion

parameters.name: high cut
parameters.note: how much treble reaches the distortion

units.body:
Drive sets how hot the signal hits the distortion, clip how hard it is clipped. Because the two
cuts sit in front of the clipping, trimming the lows keeps bass from turning to mud, and trimming
the highs gives a darker, smoother crunch. As a send, it lets you add dirt to a drum bus or a lead
by degrees while the dry track stays clean.

units.title: Lofi effect
units.summary: A bitcrusher for FX I or FX II; `M1` sets the sample rate, bit depth, a quality control and drift, which spreads the result in stereo.

facts.text: Lofi is a bitcrusher. It roughens a sound by lowering its sample rate and bit depth, for lo-fi styles or just extra grit.
The guide gives no detail about the quality control (`E3`) beyond its name.

units.body:
Lofi degrades audio the digital way: fewer samples per second and fewer bits per sample. Small
amounts add a dusty edge to drums and keys; extreme settings turn anything into crunchy, aliased
noise. Drift widens the crushed signal across the stereo field. Sent from a few tracks at once, it
gives a whole mix a shared worn-out character.

units.title: Phaser effect
units.summary: A 12-pole phaser for FX I or FX II; `M1` sets the centre frequency of the sweep, its depth, its rate and the feedback.

facts.text: The phaser blends filtered copies of the sound with the dry signal; where the two are out of phase they cancel, which carves moving notches into the spectrum.
The phaser is a 12-pole design with 12 notches.
More feedback (`E4`) sends more of the phaser's output back into it, making the sweep ring and sing.
The phaser's columns read frequency, depth, rate and feedback, as the guide names them.

parameters.name: frequency
parameters.note: centre frequency the sweep moves around

units.body:
A phaser gives a sound a slow, swirling motion. Frequency places the sweep, depth sets how far it
travels and rate how fast. With feedback low the effect is gentle; turned up it becomes a pronounced,
whistling resonance. It suits pads, chords and hi-hats.

units.title: Reverb effect
units.summary: A reverb for FX I or FX II, from a small room to a cathedral; `M1` sets size, modulation, a tone filter and the dry/wet balance.

facts.text: The reverb puts a sound in a space, anything from a small room to a cathedral. Use it to make a part stand out or to smooth the whole mix.
Modulation (`E2`) adds a slowly swelling, chorus-like movement to the reverb.
The reverb's columns read size, mod, tone and dry, so `E3` is the tone control and `E4` the dry level.
The dry/wet control (`E4`) moves smoothly between send-style use, where only the reverb returns, and insert-style use, where dry signal passes through as well.

parameters.name: size
parameters.note: room size, small room to cathedral

parameters.name: tone
parameters.note: darkens or brightens the reverb; the guide calls it rate

parameters.name: dry
parameters.note: dry signal against the reverb; the guide calls it feedback

units.body:
The reverb is the classic send: one instance on an FX track, with each track sending as much as it
needs. Size sets the space, modulation moves the tail and the tone control darkens or brightens it.
TE's guide names `E3` and `E4` rate and feedback; the screen calls them tone and dry, which matches
what they do.

units.title: Arrange mode
units.summary: Arrange mode manages each track's patterns and combines them into scenes and songs; `E4` moves between the selected track's patterns and a click on it mutes the track.

facts.text: Arrange mode handles each track's patterns — adding them and switching between them — and strings them into scenes and songs, for building a song as well as performing it.
Pressing `arrange` while already in arrange mode flips between the instrument tracks and the auxiliary tracks; both kinds have patterns.
A track key picks the track to work on; instrument tracks light white and auxiliary tracks red, as in the other modes.
The step keys show the selected track's sequence in its current pattern.
`turn E4` scrolls through the patterns of the selected track, drawn as a column of numbered blocks, so the current one sits on the colour band.
`click E4` mutes the selected track.
In arrange, `M1`…`M4` open no pages; the footer names them new, copy, paste and clear (delete once the track has more than one pattern), and with `shift` held they manage scenes.

The arrange page shows eight track columns crossed by a band of track colours; the selected track's segment is bright and dotted with its notes, its number above, and the current scene number sits boxed at the bottom. On the auxiliary side a small icon appears at the top left.

procedures.goal: Open arrange mode
Switch arrange between instrument and auxiliary tracks
Play another existing pattern on a track

units.body:
Arrange is the bird's-eye view of a project. Pick a track and `E4` walks through its patterns while
the step keys show what each one holds; press `arrange` again for the auxiliary tracks. Patterns are
grouped into scenes, and scenes chained into songs. Since every change happens while the sequencer
runs, the same view doubles as a performance surface.

units.title: New, copy, paste and remove patterns
units.summary: In arrange, `M1` adds a pattern to the selected track, `M2` copies the current pattern with its whole sound, `M3` pastes it and `M4` removes a pattern; a track holds up to 16.

facts.text: `M1` adds a new pattern to the selected track, the one whose key is lit.
OS 1.1.15 raised the limit from 9 to 16 patterns per track; older TE texts still give 9.
`M2` copies the selected pattern together with its engine and all other settings.
`M3` pastes the copy. Pasted onto another track, it brings the complete instrument, engine and parameters included.
`M4` removes a pattern from the selected track.

On the device the arrange footer reads new, copy, paste and then clear or delete from left to right, so `M1` adds a pattern as the guide says; TE's screen art, which shows the order reversed, is wrong.
`M4` is labelled clear while the track has only one pattern and delete once it has more.
Since OS 1.1.25, a newly added pattern takes over the player type currently in use.

procedures.result: The track gains one more pattern, up to 16.

preconditions: the pattern to copy is selected

procedures.goal: Remove a pattern from a track

units.body:
The four module keys are the pattern toolbox of arrange: new, copy, paste and remove, always acting on
the selected track. A copy carries the full sound, so paste within a track for variations, or onto
another track to change a part's instrument mid-song. Editing the notes inside a pattern is a
sequencer topic.

units.title: Sound link
units.summary: With sound link on, a track keeps one sound while you switch its patterns instead of loading each pattern's own; the sound comes from a source pattern you choose. New in OS 1.1.0.

facts.text: Sound link arrived in OS 1.1.0.
In arrange, `turn E3` or `click E3` switches sound link on or off for the selected track.
While sound link is on, changing pattern leaves the track's sound and preset as they are; the sounds stored with the individual patterns are overridden.
The linked sound comes from one source pattern. To choose it, select that pattern with `turn E4`, then use `shift + turn E3` (or `shift + click E3`).
OS 1.1.3 fixed a crash when deleting patterns on a track that used sound link.

procedures.goal: Switch sound link on or off
Choose which pattern's sound the link uses

steps.note: select the pattern whose sound you want

units.body:
Normally each pattern of a track carries its own sound, so switching patterns can switch presets —
handy for instrument changes, not when you only want new notes. Sound link fixes the track to the
sound of one source pattern. The guide (v1.1.15) does not say what happens to the patterns' own
sounds when the link goes off again.

units.title: Scenes
units.summary: A scene stores which pattern each track plays plus the mix; a project has 99. In arrange, shift and a black key select one, and `shift + M1…M4` clone, copy, paste or reset.

facts.text: A project has 99 scenes. Each one remembers which pattern every track plays, together with the mix settings.
A scene runs as long as its longest pattern.
Since OS 1.1.0 a project setting picks how scene length is worked out; project files know three modes: longest (the default), shortest and time signature.
Holding `shift` and pressing a black key selects scenes 1–9, each key standing for its printed digit.
Scenes 10–99 start with `shift + accidental 0` (the last black key), followed by the scene number typed on the black keys.
Selecting an empty scene fills it with a copy of the current one, so a song can grow scene by scene.
`shift + M1` clones the current scene; `shift + M4` resets it, putting every track back on pattern 1.
`shift + M2` copies a scene and `shift + M3` pastes it into another.
Over MIDI, on any channel, CC85 selects a scene at once and CC83 and CC84 step to the previous and the next scene.
CC85 counts from zero, so value 0 selects scene 1 and value 98 scene 99.

Selected while the song plays (`shift` and a black key, in arrange), a scene takes over at once, mid-bar, its patterns carrying on from the song's place in the bar; from then on the unit plays that scene over and over and the song stops moving on. This is how to loop one scene.

Picked while stopped (`shift` and its black key, in arrange), a scene is what play starts with instead of the song's first scene, and it repeats — twenty bars of scene 7 in a test on OS 1.1.33, where the song would have moved on to scene 6.
`shift` and the black keys pick scenes only in arrange mode.
With `shift` held in arrange, the footer names `M1`…`M4` clone, copy, paste and reset, the scene actions.

units.body:
A scene is a snapshot of the arrangement — one pattern choice per track plus the mix — so switching
scenes changes the whole project at once. Because an empty scene starts as a copy of the current one,
building a song is mostly "next scene, change a few patterns". Changes are immediate unless queued.

units.title: Queued scene switching
units.summary: Scene changes normally happen at once; holding shift and tapping play before choosing a scene queues the change instead. The feature and its MIDI command (CC82) arrived in OS 1.1.0.

facts.text: OS 1.1.0 introduced delayed scene switching, together with a MIDI command that sets a delayed scene.
Unless you queue it, a scene you select takes over immediately.
To queue a scene, hold `shift`, tap `play`, then choose the scene with a black key while `shift` stays down.
The guide does not say when a queued scene starts; community documentation has the MIDI version switch at the next bar.
CC82, on any channel, sets the scene to switch to after a delay, where CC85 switches at once.
CC82 values 0–98 stand for scenes 1–99.

procedures.goal: Queue the next scene instead of switching at once

procedures.result: The chosen scene waits its turn instead of starting immediately.

units.body:
Jumping straight to a scene can land off the beat on stage. Queueing avoids that: tap `play` with
`shift` held before choosing the scene, and the change waits its turn; CC82 does the same over MIDI.
TE does not document when the queued scene takes over, and the scene-length setting (1.1.0) may play
a part.

units.title: Song mode
units.summary: Song mode chains scenes into a song order of up to 96 slots — dialled in with shift and the black keys, edited with a cursor, and set to loop or not with `E1`.

facts.text: In arrange mode, `shift + arrange` opens song mode.
Holding `shift` and pressing black keys appends scenes to the song order one after another, much like keying in a phone number.
Since OS 1.1.0, adding scenes and switching songs in song mode need `shift`.
A song order holds up to 96 scenes.
`shift + M2` and `shift + M3` move a cursor back and forth through the song order, so scenes can be inserted between others or removed.
`shift + M4` takes the scene at the cursor out of the song; the scene itself stays in the project.
`shift + M1` empties the whole song order without deleting any scene.
OS 1.0.45 added the option of stopping playback when the song reaches its end.

Play runs the current song from its first scene even outside song mode, and after a stop play starts it from the first scene again, unless a scene was picked in arrange first, which then plays instead.

The song page is headed song 1 with a loop icon and shows a grid of 32 slots, eight across in four rows marked 1, 9, 17 and 25; scenes appear as numbered circles, a white line marks where the next scene goes, and a ring walks along the order during playback.
The box beside count at the top right shows how many scenes the song holds.
The white cursor line shows only while `shift` is held, together with the lit footer.
During playback the playing scene wears a white ring with a small notch that goes round once while the scene plays; after stop the ring stays on the scene that was playing.
Holding `shift` lights the footer with clear all, ←, → and delete over `M1`…`M4`, the song editing keys.

units.body:
Song mode turns scenes into a finished structure — intro, verse, chorus — each scene playing for its
own length before the next. A cursor edits the list, and removing a scene from the song never
deletes it. Whether loop off is the stop-at-end option of 1.0.45 is not confirmed on a unit, nor how
the 32-slot grid shows an order longer than 32.

units.title: Multiple songs and cueing
units.summary: A project holds up to 14 songs, one per white key. In song mode shift and a white key select a song, `M2` and `M3` copy and paste it, and shift with minus or plus cues other scenes during playback.

facts.text: A project can hold up to 14 songs, one for each white key.
In song mode, `shift + natural` switches to the song stored on that white key.
With `shift` and a song's white key held, `M2` copies that song and `M3` pastes the copied song onto it.
Since OS 1.0.32, leaving and re-entering song mode brings back the song you used last.
While a song plays, `shift + [-]` and `shift + [+]` cue a different scene of the song order, which lets you skip ahead.

units.body:
Each white key holds a song, so one project can carry several arrangements of the same material — a
short and an extended version, or a whole set. Copying a song is the quickest start for a variant.
The guide does not say whether a cued jump waits for the current scene to finish.

units.title: Mix mode
units.summary: Mix mode sets each track's level, pan and FX sends on `M1` and runs the master chain — EQ on `M2`, saturator on `M3`, group levels, compressor and output level on `M4`.

facts.text: Mix mode is where you balance the project — levels, pans and FX sends per track, plus EQ and compression on the master.
Pressing `mix` while already in mix mode flips between the instrument tracks and the auxiliary tracks; both can be mixed.
A track key selects the track to adjust; instrument tracks light white and auxiliary tracks red.
Each scene stores every track's level and mute, so changing scene can change the balance too.
After the mixer, the summed signal passes through the EQ, then the saturator, then the compressor and limiter, and on to the main output.
A voice reaches the mixer directly and through its sends to the aux out, tape, FX I and FX II tracks, which feed the mixer as well.
In TE's signal flow diagram each send track can also feed the next one down — aux out into tape, tape into FX I, FX I into FX II — and no arrow runs back up, so FX II returns only to the mixer.

procedures.goal: Open mix mode
Switch mix between instrument and auxiliary tracks

units.body:
Mix mode has four pages: `M1` is the channel strip of the selected track, and `M2`…`M4` work on the
master — EQ, saturator, then group levels, compressor and output. Tracks reach the mixer directly and
through their sends; the sum then runs through the master chain to the output. Scenes store track
levels and mutes, so a balance change can be part of the arrangement.

units.title: Levels, pans and sends
units.summary: On mix `M1` the four encoders set the selected track's FX I send, FX II send, pan and level; clicking `E3` centres the pan and clicking `E4` mutes the track.

facts.text: `M1` in mix mode is the page for levels, pans and sends; a track key chooses which track the encoders adjust.
Over MIDI, CC7 sets a track's level and CC10 its pan, each on the track's own channel (1–16).
On an instrument track's channel, CC38 and CC39 set its FX I and FX II sends — presumably the same values this page shows.

Instrument tracks repeat these sends on their `M3` shift layer, whose rows run aux out, tape, FX I, FX II from the top — FX I on `E3`, FX II on `E4`. TE's drawing of that page puts FX II above FX I; the device does not.
The page draws eight columns, one per track, each with its number, a level line and a pan dot along the bottom; CC7 and CC10 sent over MIDI move them as they arrive.
Turning `E1` or `E2` briefly swaps the selected track's column for two boxed labels, I and II, each with a dark bar rising to its send level; after about a second the column comes back.
Sending CC38 changes a track's FX I send without calling up that I and II display.

units.body:
The `M1` page is a channel strip for the selected track: two send amounts, pan and level. The sends
decide how much of the track reaches the two FX tracks, so one reverb can serve the whole project.

units.title: Mute and solo
units.summary: In mix mode, shift + a track key mutes or unmutes that track and holding track keys solos them; instrument or auxiliary + a track key is a quick mute, and CC9 mutes over MIDI.

facts.text: In mix mode, `shift + Tn` mutes that track, or unmutes it if it is muted.
While `shift` is held in mix mode, unmuted tracks light up (white for instrument, red for auxiliary) and muted tracks stay dark.
A mute acts on a track's notes, not on its audio; no new notes start, while sound that is already playing rings out.
On the mix `M1` page, `click E4` mutes the selected track.
Holding one track key, or several at once, in mix mode solos those tracks.
Holding `instrument` and pressing a track key mutes or unmutes that instrument track; `auxiliary` does the same for the auxiliary tracks.
Over MIDI, CC9 on a track's channel sets its mute as a level rather than a toggle — 0 unmutes, any value from 1 to 127 mutes.

procedures.goal: Mute a track with the mode-key shortcut
