units.body:
`shift` shows the mute state on the track keys and toggles it; holding track keys solos them; and
`instrument` or `auxiliary` double as mute modifiers for their own group. A click on `E4` mutes the
selected track in arrange mode too. Mutes stop notes rather than cutting audio, so tails finish
naturally.

units.title: Master EQ
units.summary: Mix `M2` is a three-band EQ on the master — low, mid, high — plus a blend that fades from flat to the set curve; clicking an encoder resets its band, and `E4`'s click resets the whole EQ.

facts.text: The EQ on mix `M2` shapes the whole mix, not individual tracks.
`E1`, `E2` and `E3` boost or cut the low, mid and high frequencies.
`E4` fades between a flat response and the band settings: low values leave the mix neutral, high values apply the boosts and cuts in full.
Clicking `E1`, `E2` or `E3` resets that band; clicking `E4` resets every EQ value.
Over MIDI, CC90 moves the EQ bands, the channel choosing which — 1 low, 2 mid, 3 high.
CC90 on channel 4 changed nothing visible on the EQ page, so no MIDI control for blend is confirmed.
The EQ page pictures the three bands as groups of panels standing on an isometric grid floor, next to a slider track with an N at one end.

Each band tilts its own group of panels, flat at the minimum and rising with the value to lean at about 60° at the maximum, never fully upright; in a new project all three bands sat at the middle value, 64.
Turning `E4` slides a knob along that track and reshapes the whole scene; as it travels, the low and high panels flatten and the mid panels stand up.

procedures.goal: Open the master EQ
Flatten the EQ

parameters.name: blend
parameters.note: flat at low values, full curve at high values

units.body:
The blend control is the trick: set low, mid and high to an extreme curve — lows cut away for a
breakdown, say — keep blend at zero, and bring it up when the moment comes. At low blend values the
EQ stays neutral whatever the bands say, which makes sweeps quick and repeatable on stage.

units.title: Master saturator
units.summary: Mix `M3` is a saturator on the master bus; gain drives it, clip shaves off loud peaks, tone filters highs or lows and mix sets how much of it you hear.

facts.text: The saturator on mix `M3` works on the master, so it colours the whole mix.
Clip (`E2`) flattens the loudest peaks, reining in the dynamics.
Mix (`E4`) sets how much of the saturated signal you hear in the master.
No MIDI CC is known for the master saturator.
The saturator page shows four vertical tick ladders — gain, clip, tone and mix from left to right — each topped by a cap in its encoder's style.

procedures.goal: Open the master saturator

parameters.name: mix
parameters.note: amount of saturation in the master

units.body:
The saturator adds density and warmth to the finished mix. Gain drives it, clip keeps peaks in check
and tone tilts the result darker or brighter; mix blends it with the clean signal, so heavy settings
work in small doses. It sits after the EQ and before the compressor.

units.title: Master groups, compressor and output
units.summary: Mix `M4` sets the levels of the percussion and melodic groups, how much the master bus is compressed and the master level that feeds the output limiter.

facts.text: Every engine is routed to one of two groups automatically — percussive engines such as the drum sampler to the percussion group, the synth engines and the sampler to the melodic group.
`E3` compresses the master bus. Light settings even out loud and quiet moments; heavy settings squash the mix into a denser, harder-hitting sound.
`E4` raises the master level on its way into the output limiter.
No MIDI CC is known for the group levels or the compressor.
The master page shows the percussion and melodic levels as large numbers, a tall bar in the middle that `E3` shortens, and a VU meter from −20 to +3 above the word master.

procedures.goal: Open the master page

units.body:
The master page is the last stop before the output. The two group levels balance drums against
everything else without touching single tracks; the compressor glues the mix or flattens it for a
heavier sound; and the master level pushes the result into the limiter that guards the output.

units.title: Project view — new, save, rename
units.summary: The project key opens the project view, where you create a new project (`hold M1`), save (`M2`), save as (`shift + M2`), rename (`M3`) and open the project settings (`M4`).

facts.text: `project` opens the project view of the project you are working on.
`hold M1` in the project view creates a new project, saving your work automatically when autosave is on.
The guide mentions no confirmation step for a new project, and it does not say what happens to unsaved changes when autosave is off; with autosave off, save with `M2` first.
A new project starts with drums on tracks 1 and 2, then bass, pluck, lead, soft pluck, strings and pad on tracks 3–8.
`M2` saves the project and stores a version of it.
`shift + M2` saves a copy under a new name you type in.
`M3` renames the project: `turn E1` picks the character position and `turn E2` changes the character.
In the naming screen, `M1` confirms, `M2` moves on to the next character, `M3` cancels and `M4` deletes.
`M4` opens the project settings, which are separate from the system settings.

procedures.goal: Start a new project
procedures.result: A new project opens with the default sounds.

procedures.goal: Save the project as a copy with a new name

units.body:
The project view is the home of the current project: its name, the save keys and the way into its
settings. Other projects are opened from the projects folder (`shift + project`), not from here.

units.title: Autosave, versions and history
units.summary: Projects save themselves by default, and every save or autosave is kept in the project's history, so you can go back and load an older state.

facts.text: Autosave is on by default; switching it off in the project or system settings leaves only manual saves.
Each manual save (`M2` in the project view) also adds a version to the project's history.
The history keeps every save and autosave, so older states can be loaded and heard; `M2` in the projects folder opens it for the selected project.
Versions and autosaves carry the date and time from the clock page of the system settings.
On a computer (over MTP), the history files sit in a backups folder beside your projects; to back up one project, copy its file together with its history folder.
Over MTP the unit also shows projects/workspace.xy; it holds the project that is open.

procedures.goal: Save the project and add a version
Go back to an older version of a project

steps.note: select the project in the projects folder
opens its history; pick a version and load it

units.body: The history is a safety net for experiments: if a drastic change fails, load the version from before.

units.title: Projects folder — load, duplicate, delete
units.summary: `shift + project` opens the projects folder — factory projects, your projects, templates and autosaves — to load, duplicate, delete or view the history of a project. TE disagrees with itself about which end key loads and which deletes, so read the screen labels first.

facts.text: `shift + project` opens the projects folder, which lists factory projects, your projects, the templates folder and autosaves.
TE's text gives load to `M1`, and the key picture beside that step shows key 1.
`M2` shows the history of the selected project.
Duplicate copies a whole project with its patterns, scenes and tracks.
TE's text gives duplicate `M2`, the key it also gives history — a slip, since the key picture beside it shows key 3 and the screen drawing puts duplicate third, so duplicate is almost certainly `M3`.
TE's text gives delete to `hold M4`, and the key picture beside that step shows key 4 held.

TE's drawing of the folder screen labels the soft keys delete, history, duplicate, load from left to right, which puts delete over `M1` and load over `M4` — the reverse of its own text and key pictures.
The key order has not been checked on the device yet; the replica follows TE's text, so what the replica shows does not settle it.
On the arrange page TE's art showed the same reversal and OS 1.1.33 followed the text, so load on `M1` and delete on `hold M4` is the likelier order here too.
Read the label above `M1` or `M4` on the screen before pressing it, and above all before holding it; the guide mentions no confirmation step after the delete hold, so do not count on one.
Subfolders made over MTP appear with their names in square brackets; clicking any encoder opens one.
Since OS 1.1.25 a duplicate includes changes that were not saved yet.
Over MTP your projects live in projects/user.

procedures.goal: Open another project

steps.note: load in TE's text; check that the label above it reads load

procedures.goal: Delete a project

steps.note: with the project selected, and only after checking that the label above it reads delete

units.body:
The projects folder is the unit's file browser for projects. History and duplicate sit on the middle
keys whichever way the labels run; only the end keys are in doubt, with TE's text putting load on
`M1` and delete on `M4` and its screen drawing the reverse. Look at the labels before you press, and
never hold a key whose label you have not read: TE describes no way to bring a deleted project back.

units.title: Project templates
units.summary: Templates are projects to start from, kept in the templates folder of the projects folder and managed from a computer over MTP; since OS 1.1.17 one can be made the default.

facts.text: The projects folder has a templates folder for projects meant as starting points.
Project templates arrived with OS 1.1.15.
Your own templates are created and loaded with a computer over MTP.
Over MTP the folder is projects/templates.
Copying a project file into that folder should make it a template; the guide implies this but it is not confirmed on a unit.
OS 1.1.17 added a make default option for templates.
Presumably new projects then start from the default template; the changelog gives no details.

procedures.goal: Start from a template

steps.note: the templates folder sits next to the factory and user projects
a folder opens with a click of any encoder

units.body:
A template saves setting up the same tracks, sounds and settings for every new idea. Save your work
under a new name, since neither TE source says how a template is protected from being overwritten.

units.title: System usage indicators (voices, CPU, sample memory)
units.summary: Three small icons warn when a project runs out of room — voice count, CPU load and sample memory — and turn red when the limit is hit.

facts.text: Heavy projects can bring up three icons on screen, for voice count, CPU and sample memory.
The voice icon shows how many of the 24 voices are busy and appears only from 17 voices up.
The guide says the voice icon flashes red when a voice is stolen.
OS 1.1.25 reworked the stealing indicator so it reports every audible voice steal.
The CPU icon appears above 70 % load and flashes red at 100 %.
Before OS 1.1.32 the CPU overload warning could miss some stalls.
The sample memory icon appears while samples load and when more than 70 % of sample memory is in use.

units.body:
When a voice icon turns red, notes are being cut to make room for new ones. Give important tracks
fixed voices in the project settings, shorten release times or thin out chords; for CPU and sample
memory, use fewer heavy tracks or shorter samples.

units.title: Project settings
units.summary: `M4` in the project view opens the project's own settings — general (transpose), tempo (time signature, groove type), voices and midi — edited with `E1` page, `E2` setting, `E3` value.

facts.text: `M4` in the project view opens the project settings, which belong to the project and are separate from the system settings.
`turn E1` picks the page (general, tempo, voices, midi), `turn E2` a setting on it and `turn E3` or `turn E4` its value; `M1` leaves.
The tempo page sets the time signature — 3/4, 4/4 or 5/4, or 6/8, 7/8 or 12/8 — and shows the groove type, which can be changed there too.
The voices page shares out the 24 voices; allocation is automatic by default, and giving a track its own voices gives it priority.
Since OS 1.1.0 a project setting chooses how scene length is calculated; the guide does not describe it.
One of its modes is called time signature; OS 1.1.3 repaired it.

procedures.goal: Change a project setting

units.body:
Anything stored here travels with the project, unlike the system settings in `com → M1`, which
apply to the whole unit. The general and midi pages have their own units.

units.title: Global (project) transpose
units.summary: The general page of the project settings transposes the whole project, for example to match other music. Whether drums follow is unclear, and OS 1.1.21 simplified the setting.

facts.text: The general page of the project settings shifts the pitch of every note in the project, useful for matching the key of other music.
Whether drums follow is unclear — the guide says they do, while the OS 1.0.9 notes say global transpose no longer applies to drums; not yet checked on a unit.
OS 1.1.21 simplified the global transpose without saying how.
OS 1.1.25 improved how multisampled sounds respond to global transpose.
To follow a key live, or transpose only chosen tracks, use the brain track in auxiliary mode instead.

procedures.goal: Transpose the whole project

units.body:
Global transpose is a set-and-forget offset for the whole project. Because TE changed it after the
guide was written, check the screen for the current options, and listen to the drums after
changing it.

units.title: Track MIDI channels (project)
units.summary: The midi page of the project settings gives each of the 16 tracks a MIDI channel. Community tools say it lets a track on one of the OP-XY's own engines send its sequenced notes out; the external MIDI track and midi-engine tracks send on the channel set on their own `M1` page.

facts.text: The midi page of the project settings assigns a MIDI channel to each of the 16 tracks, for example to sequence external MIDI gear.
In a fresh project every track's channel is off, according to decoded OS 1.1.4 project files.
The external MIDI track and instrument tracks on the midi engine send on the channel chosen with `E1` on their own `M1` page; TE's MIDI how-to sets only that channel and never visits this page.
Community tools say the external MIDI track and midi-engine tracks send their notes without a channel here; not yet checked on a unit.
Community tools report that a track on one of the OP-XY's own engines sends its sequenced notes over MIDI only once it has a channel here and notes output is allowed in the MIDI settings.
Community tools report that a track given a channel here keeps playing through its own engine while its notes also go out.
The guide does not say what happens when a midi-engine or external MIDI track also has a channel here — which channel wins, or whether its notes go out twice.
The guide speaks only of sequencing gear from this page; whether notes played live on the keyboard also go out on the channel is not documented.
Incoming notes and CCs on channel N reach track N by default, channels 9–16 being the auxiliary tracks.
Whether a channel set here also changes what the track receives is not known yet.

procedures.goal: Give a track a MIDI channel in the project

units.body:
Two kinds of channel can be in play. The external MIDI track (`T3` in auxiliary mode) and
midi-engine tracks carry their own channel on `M1`: that is the one the outside synth must listen
on, and TE's steps set nothing on this page. This page serves the other tracks: by community
accounts it makes a track on one of the OP-XY's own engines send its sequenced notes as well, while
it keeps sounding. These channels are per project; the unit-wide notes switch in `com → M1` must
also allow sending, which it does on a stock unit.

units.title: Tempo, tap tempo and metronome
units.summary: The tempo key opens the tempo screen from anywhere; tap it to set the tempo by ear. `E1` sets BPM, `E2` and `E3` the groove, `E4` the metronome level (click to switch the metronome on or off).

facts.text: `tempo` opens the tempo screen from any screen.
The tempo runs from 40 to 220 BPM, the ends of the metronome weight's travel and of the range CC80 is held to.
Tapping `tempo` repeatedly in time with the music sets the tempo.
`turn E4` sets the metronome volume and `click E4` switches the metronome on or off.
Over MIDI, CC80 on any channel sets the tempo; on OS 1.1.33 the result is twice the value in BPM, held within 40–220, so only even tempos can be sent.

The tempo is one value for the whole project; it sits on no module page, so no parameter lock or LFO reaches it, and a tempo change over a song (a ramp) is made by hand on the tempo page, over MIDI (CC80), or by following an external MIDI clock.
A new empty project runs at 120 BPM (OS 1.1.33).
A new project starts with the metronome on, at about two thirds of its volume (the project file stores the click volume, with 0 for off).
The tempo page has a light background, the BPM as a large number on the left and a metronome in the middle carrying the groove type's two-letter abbreviation.
The metronome's weight slides down its arm as the tempo rises, from the top at 40 BPM to the bottom at 220.
The speaker icon at the top right loses its sound waves as `E4` turns the metronome down.
While the sequencer plays, the pendulum swings from one end to the other on every beat, and the beat's dot below it lights; stopped, it rests at the left end with no dot lit.
The swinging pendulum looks smeared, as if it left trails; the copies come from the screen's slow response rather than being drawn.

procedures.goal: Set the tempo by tapping

steps.note: tap in time with the beat

procedures.goal: Switch the metronome on or off

parameters.name: groove amount
parameters.note: right of centre adds swing, left of centre adds shuffle

units.body:
Tempo and groove are saved with each project, so every project keeps its own speed and feel. The
groove settings on `E2` and `E3` are explained under grooves.

units.title: Grooves, swing and shuffle
units.summary: A groove shifts the timing and velocity of sequenced notes to change the feel. Pick one of eleven types with `E2` on the tempo screen and dial swing or shuffle with `E3`; the bar menu can override the amount per track.

facts.text: A groove changes the feel of the sequencer by moving the timing of notes and changing their velocity.
Grooves also vary timing and velocity slightly at random, so the swing sounds less mechanical.
On the tempo screen, `turn E3` clockwise past the centre for swing or anticlockwise for shuffle; the two push notes in opposite directions.

`turn E2` on the tempo screen picks the groove type, in this order: shuffle, half shuffle, danish, bombora, wobbly, gaussian, accents, island nod, disfunk, roll over and prophetic. The metronome shows each as two letters — SH, HS, DA, BO, WO, GA, AC, IN, DF, RO, PR.
Shuffle is the everyday swing and half shuffle a lighter version of it; accents emphasises the important beats.
Bombora breaks up the beats on 2 and 4, and wobbly deliberately loosens the timing for a funkier, messier feel.
TE describes gaussian and island nod only in jokes, so judge them by ear.

The online guide leaves out four types. Danish relaxes the beat, disfunk turns funky one way and groovy the other, and roll over gives a slow, lazy hip-hop feel. TE gives prophetic no description at all.
`bar + turn E3` sets a groove amount for the current track that replaces the tempo screen's swing value; the groove type still comes from the tempo screen.
Over MIDI, CC81 sets the groove amount, drawn as a slider under the metronome on the tempo page — far left at 0, centred at 64, far right at 127.
Community MIDI tables give 63 as the no-groove value, one below the slider's centre at 64; which of the two is exactly neutral is not confirmed.

procedures.goal: Add swing to the whole project

steps.note: clockwise past the centre for swing, anticlockwise for shuffle

units.body:
Start with shuffle and a little swing, then try the other types on the same pattern; give a single
track its own amount in the bar menu.

units.title: The com page
units.summary: `com` opens the connection hub. Its main page handles bluetooth MIDI and the multi-out jack; the four module keys lead to system settings, controller mode, connected devices and MTP file transfer.

facts.text: `com → M1` opens the system settings: screen, keyboard, MIDI, clock, pitchbend, battery and the MIDI monitor.
`com → M2` switches to MIDI controller mode, where keys and encoders send MIDI to a computer or other gear.
`com → M3` lists the MIDI devices connected right now, each with its own send and receive switches.
`com → M4` starts MTP mode, used to copy samples, presets and projects between the unit and a computer.
On the com page itself, `E1` makes the unit visible to bluetooth MIDI hosts and `E3` chooses what the multi-out jack carries.

procedures.goal: Go to one of the four com sections

steps.note: system settings, controller mode, devices or MTP

units.body:
Think of `com` as the OP-XY's patch bay and system menu in one. The main page itself only holds
bluetooth MIDI (`E1`) and the multi-out setting (`E3`); everything else is one module key away.

Two sections change how the unit behaves until you leave them: controller mode turns the panel into
a MIDI controller, and MTP mode takes the USB MIDI connection away while files move.

units.title: System settings
units.summary: Device-wide options behind `com → M1`, in sections: system (brightness, country, power-off), keyboard (velocity, detune), midi, clock, pitchbend calibration, battery and the MIDI monitor.

facts.text: In the system settings `E1` picks a section, `E2` a setting within it and `E3` (or `E4`) its value; `M1` goes back to the com page.
The system section holds screen brightness, LED brightness, country and whether switching off happens at once or after a delay, which guards against powering down by accident mid-performance.
The keyboard section sets how the built-in keys respond to velocity and can detune them, by notes and by cents, for microtonal scales.
The clock section holds the date and time that the unit stamps on snapshots, autosaves and project versions.
The pitchbend section calibrates the strip — `E2` sets the sensitivity of its left side, `E3` of its right side, and `M4` runs the calibration.
The battery section shows the charge level and the input current limit.
OS 1.1.17 added a system setting for sample preview, which the guide does not list.

procedures.goal: Calibrate the pitchbend strip

steps.note: starts the calibration; follow the screen

units.body:
Most options here are set once: brightness, country, the date used to stamp files and how the unit
powers off. Two sections matter for playing — keyboard, where velocity is switched on and keys can
be detuned, and pitchbend, where you recalibrate the strip when bends feel lopsided. The midi and
monitor sections have units of their own.

units.title: MIDI settings
units.summary: The midi section of the system settings sets, separately for clock, notes and everything else, whether the OP-XY listens, transmits or does both; it also picks the channel that always plays the selected track and switches echo on or off.

facts.text: The MIDI options are one section of the system settings, reached with `com → M1`.
The section has five settings: clock, notes, other (every remaining message type), active track channel and midi echo.
Notes arriving on the active track channel play whichever track is currently selected.
On a unit with stock settings (OS 1.1.33) the section reads: clock in, notes both, other both, active track channel 1, midi echo off.
Clock, notes and other each take a direction; in (receive only) and both (receive and send) are confirmed on OS 1.1.33.
Community tools also describe out (send only) and off for these three settings.
With clock set to in, pressing `play` or `stop` sends nothing — no start, no stop, no clock ticks.

With clock set to both, every press of `play` sends a MIDI start (FA) — a press during playback sends another start — and `stop` sends a MIDI stop (FC). No continue (FB) or song position (F2) messages were seen.
With clock set to both, clock ticks (F8, 24 per quarter note) stream all the time, even while stopped.
With clock set to both, a start (FA) or stop (FC) from a computer starts or stops playback, and the unit sends the message back out.
Software that follows the OP-XY's play state and tempo over USB, this app included, needs clock set to both.
Even with midi echo off, a universal identity request (SysEx) sent to the unit came back on its output; what forwards it is not known yet.
OS 1.0.15 fixed the echo setting being ignored for notes from linked tracks.
Start and stop received from one device are passed on to the other connected MIDI devices.
A monitor page in the same settings lists whatever MIDI arrives — channel, value, clock and SysEx — which tells a message that never arrived from one that arrived but was ignored.
Switches for what is sent to and received from each connected device live separately, under `com → M3` (devices).

procedures.goal: Leave the system settings
procedures.result: Back on the com page.

parameters.name: section
parameters.note: system, keyboard, midi, clock, pitchbend, battery, monitor

units.body:
The midi section is where the OP-XY decides how it talks to other gear. Clock, notes and "other"
(every remaining message type, such as control changes) each get a direction, so the unit can, say,
take notes from a keyboard while ignoring its clock. The active track channel is a shortcut for playing
the OP-XY from a controller: whatever arrives on that channel plays the track you have selected.

Out of the box the unit only listens for clock (clock in), so it sends no start, stop or clock of
its own. Switching clock to both makes it a sync source: `play` and `stop` send start and stop, and
the tick stream runs continuously. This app suggests clock both during setup so it can follow the
unit's transport and tempo.

When a connection misbehaves, open the monitor page first: it shows whether a message reached the
OP-XY at all. Per-device switches live separately in `com → M3`.

units.title: MIDI monitor
units.summary: A section of the system settings that lists incoming MIDI from any connected device — each message with its channel and value, plus clock and SysEx — so you can check that gear sends what you expect.

facts.text: The monitor shows MIDI as it arrives from any connected device, with the channel and value of each message.
Incoming clock and SysEx appear on the monitor as well.
The monitor is a troubleshooting aid — confirming that a keyboard, computer or sequencer really sends the messages you expect before you change any settings.
The monitor was added to the system settings in OS 1.1.15.

procedures.goal: Watch incoming MIDI
procedures.result: Messages from connected devices appear as they arrive.

units.body:
When a controller seems to do nothing, the monitor settles the first question: did anything arrive?
If messages show up here but the OP-XY ignores them, look at the midi section (is notes or other set
to receive?) and at the device's own switches under `com → M3`. If nothing shows up, suspect the
cable, the connection or the sending device first.

units.title: Connected MIDI devices
units.summary: `com → M3` lists the MIDI devices connected to the OP-XY; for each one you switch what it may send to the unit and receive from it, or forget it.

facts.text: The devices page lists the MIDI devices connected to the OP-XY and lets you enable or disable individual inputs and outputs for each of them.
Per device you can switch clock, notes, other messages (CCs and similar), timestamp and velocity.
Community tools also describe a second page with a transport receive switch that must be on for start and stop from that device.
USB MIDI gear plugged into the OP-XY's USB-C port shows up here, which is where you decide what data goes to and comes from it.
`M2` forgets the selected device and removes it from the list.
A computer running this app should keep clock, notes and other enabled in its entry, or the app cannot follow or play the unit.

procedures.goal: Change what one device may send or receive

steps.note: set the value (`turn E4` works too)

procedures.goal: Remove a device from the list

units.body:
The devices page refines the midi settings per connection: use it when one device should be treated
differently — say, taking notes from a keyboard while ignoring its clock. `M1` returns to com. If a
device misbehaves, the MIDI monitor shows whether its messages arrive at all.

units.title: USB connections
units.summary: The USB-C port works both ways. A computer sees a driverless audio and MIDI device; as a host the OP-XY accepts class-compliant MIDI gear and audio interfaces plugged into it.

facts.text: The USB-C port carries audio and MIDI as a USB device (to a computer) and as a USB host (for gear plugged into the OP-XY).
A computer sees the OP-XY as a class-compliant USB audio and MIDI device, so no driver is needed; its one MIDI input and one MIDI output are both named OP-XY.
The computer can record the OP-XY's output as a stereo USB audio input at 44.1 kHz and 16 bit.
The USB link also offers an audio stream from the computer into the OP-XY; that it arrives as the external audio track's usb audio input is likely but not confirmed.
USB MIDI keyboards, controllers and synths plug straight into the OP-XY through a USB-C cable or adapter, with no computer involved; a powered hub helps gear that needs more power.
Audio interfaces work when they are USB audio class 1 or 2 compliant; ones that need a driver may not.
OS 1.1.32 fixed the unit sometimes failing to start while connected to USB.
In MTP mode the computer sees a file-transfer device instead, so USB audio and MIDI are gone until MTP ends.

units.body:
With a computer, one cable carries MIDI and audio in both directions — this app uses it to play and
hear the OP-XY. With other gear, the OP-XY is the host.

units.title: MIDI controller mode
units.summary: `com → M2` turns the OP-XY into a generic MIDI controller; with `shift` held, `E1`–`E3` set its channel, knob behaviour and octave keys, and `shift + com` leaves.

facts.text: Controller mode makes the OP-XY a general-purpose MIDI controller for any device, a computer included.
The encoders send either absolute values (0–127) or relative ones (the change since the last position).
`shift + com` leaves controller mode and returns to the com page.
Community measurements put the encoders on CC1–CC4 when turned and CC15–CC18 when clicked; relative mode sends 1–63 clockwise and 65–127 counter-clockwise.
The keys send CCs as well — `record`, `play` and `stop` send CC55–CC57 (127 on press, 0 on release), the step keys CC61–CC76.
The keyboard sends notes 53–76 with velocity; the volume knob sends nothing.

procedures.goal: Use the OP-XY as a MIDI controller

steps.note: the channel your software listens on

procedures.goal: Leave controller mode

units.body:
Controller mode drives a DAW, a soft synth or another instrument from the OP-XY's panel. TE publishes
neither the CC numbers nor the default channel, so set the channel first and confirm the CCs with
your software's MIDI learn.

units.title: Multi-out jack modes
units.summary: The 3.5 mm multi-out sends MIDI, CV and gate, a sync pulse (sync8, sync16, sync24) or audio; the mode is chosen with `E3` on the com page while nothing is plugged in.

facts.text: The multi-out has six modes: midi, cv/gate, audio and three sync rates (sync8, sync16, sync24).
The mode is chosen on the com page by turning `E3`.
The mode cannot change while a cable is in the jack, so set it before connecting.
In midi mode the jack is a MIDI output; a type A TRS-to-DIN cable reaches synths with DIN MIDI sockets, played from the external MIDI track (`T3`) or a midi-engine track.
In cv/gate mode the tip carries pitch CV and the ring the gate, played from the external CV track (`T4`) for synths with CV and gate inputs.
The sync modes send a clock pulse while the OP-XY plays — sync8, an eighth-note pulse, suits pocket operators and sync24 suits DIN-sync drum machines.
In audio mode the jack is an auxiliary audio output, fed by the external audio track's routing and the tracks' aux sends.

procedures.goal: Choose what the multi-out sends
preconditions: no cable is plugged into the multi-out

parameters.name: multi-out mode
parameters.range: midi / cv/gate / sync8 / sync16 / sync24 / audio

units.body:
Pick the job first, then plug in. The jack only sends — MIDI comes in through the MIDI in jack, USB
or bluetooth. TE does not say which gear sync16 is meant for; the output levels are listed with the
specifications.

units.title: Bluetooth MIDI
units.summary: Turning or clicking `E1` on the com page advertises the OP-XY as a bluetooth LE MIDI device; a host such as a computer, tablet or phone then connects to it for notes and clock.

facts.text: On the com page, turning or clicking `E1` makes the OP-XY advertise itself over bluetooth MIDI.
The OP-XY joins as a device; the other side is the host and makes the connection from its own bluetooth MIDI settings.
The wireless link carries notes and clock, in both directions.
Clock over bluetooth, incoming and outgoing, arrived in OS 1.0.29.
OS 1.1.15 fixed advertising that sometimes failed to start.

procedures.goal: Pair the OP-XY with a bluetooth MIDI host

steps.note: turning `E1` works as well; the unit is now discoverable

procedures.result: Choose the OP-XY in the host's bluetooth MIDI list to finish the connection.

parameters.name: bluetooth midi
parameters.note: advertise the unit (clicking does the same)

units.body:
Bluetooth MIDI is the cable-free way to play or clock compatible gear and apps. The OP-XY does not
search for partners itself: it only announces that it is available, and the host (a computer, tablet
or phone app) picks it from its list. Audio still needs a cable: the wireless link carries MIDI only.

units.title: MTP mode (file transfer)
units.summary: `com → M4` lets a connected computer browse the OP-XY's storage and copy projects, samples and presets; `M4` ejects. Macs need TE's field kit app, and USB MIDI is off while MTP runs.

facts.text: `com → M4` switches on MTP, so a computer can read and write the projects, samples and presets on the unit.
MTP is only offered while a computer is connected by USB, so plug in first.
macOS cannot open MTP devices by itself, so Macs need TE's field kit app; Windows and Linux need nothing extra.
`M4` on the MTP screen ejects the OP-XY from the computer.
Instructions that say `T4` for MTP (TE's sound-pack page among them) follow the OP-1 field; on the OP-XY it is `M4`.
In MTP mode the OP-XY shows up as a different USB device and its MIDI port disappears, so MIDI apps, this one included, lose the connection.
When the computer closes its MTP session, the OP-XY leaves MTP mode by itself and its MIDI port returns.
On OS 1.1.33 the top level holds projects (user, templates and the open project as workspace.xy), samples (user), presets (snapshot and user sound packs) and how_to_import.txt.

Each kind of file goes only in its own top folder (presets, projects, samples), and new folders can be made only inside those three; a copy that fails usually has a name the unit refuses or sits in the wrong folder.

A copied drum or sampler preset is a folder whose name ends in .preset, its patch.json beside its samples; it can sit anywhere inside the presets folder, a folder of your own there included. A synth preset without samples can also be a single .json file.
What you copy, rename or delete shows on the unit once the disk is ejected (`M4`).
The unit's own import note allows letters, digits, spaces, hashes, hyphens and round brackets in file and folder names, plus the extension's dot; keep to those even though OS 1.1.15 took UTF-8.
A project file does not carry its samples, so a project moved to another OP-XY needs its samples copied too.
OS 1.0.29 could corrupt files over 64 KB copied off the unit by MTP; 1.0.32 fixed it, and backups made under 1.0.29 may be damaged.
MTP accepts UTF-8 file and folder names since OS 1.1.15.

procedures.goal: Put the OP-XY in MTP mode
preconditions: a computer is connected by USB-C
field kit runs on a Mac
procedures.result: The storage appears on the computer (inside field kit on a Mac).

procedures.goal: Eject the OP-XY from the computer

units.body:
MTP is a mode, not a background service: live MIDI and file transfer take turns. Eject with `M4`,
or let the computer close the session, before unplugging.

units.title: MIDI CC reference
units.summary: The CCs TE documents — track volume, mute and pan, tempo, groove, scenes, project and master EQ — plus what we measured on OS 1.1.33, including play, stop and track-select CCs that TE's table leaves out.

facts.text: Most controls answer MIDI CCs out of the box; TE's reference table lists only the main ones, every one taking values 0–127.
On channels 1–16, one per track: CC7 volume, CC9 mute, CC10 pan, and CC46, which TE labels only "track parameters".
On any channel: CC80 tempo, CC81 groove, CC82 scene (switching at a delay), CC83 previous scene, CC84 next scene, CC85 scene (switching at once) and CC86 project.
CC90 drives the master EQ on channels 1–4.
Community tests map CC90 channel 1 to the low band, 2 to mid and 3 to high; reports on channel 4 (blend) disagree.
The delayed scene switch (CC82) was added in OS 1.1.0.
CC80 sets the tempo to twice the value in BPM within 40–220 — 60 gives 120 BPM, values up to 20 give 40 and values from 110 give 220.
CC9 mutes the track at any value from 1 to 127 and unmutes it at 0; it sets a state and does not toggle.
Missing from TE's table but working, CC104 at 127 starts playback and CC105 at 127 stops it.
CC102 on channel 1 selects a track counting from zero, so value 2 selects track 3.
The remote key-press CCs (CC106/CC107) that community tools used on older firmware have no effect on OS 1.1.33.
By default channel N addresses track N — 1–8 the instrument tracks, 9–16 the auxiliary tracks from brain to FX II.
Outside controller mode, turning encoders sends no CCs, so other gear cannot read the OP-XY's knob positions.

units.body:
TE's table covers the mixer and song-level controls; the encoders of each track's pages follow the
pattern in the track CC unit. Most CCs change the open project, which the unit saves by itself.
Remote key presses do not work on current firmware, so screens cannot be navigated over MIDI.

units.title: Track parameter CCs
units.summary: Community charts and our lane model give each module page four consecutive CCs on the track's channel, one per encoder — `M1` on CC12–15 up to the LFO on CC40–43 — and put the 24 drum keys on notes 53–76.

facts.text: Each module page answers four consecutive CCs on the track's channel, in encoder order `E1`…`E4`.
The `M1` (engine) page uses CC12–15, whatever engine the track runs.
`M2` uses CC20–23 for the amp envelope (attack, decay, sustain, release), CC24–27 for the filter envelope and CC28–31 for its shift layer: play mode, portamento, bend range and preset volume.
`M3` uses CC32–35 for the filter (cutoff, resonance, envelope amount, key tracking) and CC36–39 for its shift layer, the sends to aux out, tape, FX I and FX II.
`M4` (the LFO) most likely uses CC40–43; community charts label these four CCs inconsistently.
The mixer controls sit outside the lanes, on CC7 (level), CC9 (mute) and CC10 (pan).
On drum tracks the 24 keys play MIDI notes 53–76 from left to right (F3–E5 when middle C is 60).
Which sound sits on which note depends on the loaded kit, so check the kit rather than assuming a General MIDI layout.

units.body:
The pattern — page by page, four CCs per page, left to right — comes from community charts and
stored project data, not from TE, so treat it as a strong prediction. Filter cutoff on track 3 is
CC32 on channel 3; CCs outside the listed ranges (such as CC16–19) are unconfirmed.

units.title: Get started — a first project
units.summary: TE's four-part first session in our words — create a project, then build a drum beat, record a bassline, add chords and perform with punch-in FX, using the sounds a new project already has.

facts.text: A song begins with a fresh project — `project` opens the project view, and holding `M1` there creates one.
A new project comes loaded: drum kits on `T1` and `T2`, a bass on `T3`, a pluck on `T4`, a lead on `T5`, a soft pluck on `T6`, strings on `T7` and a pad on `T8`.
The walkthrough uses those defaults in turn — drums on `T1`, bass on `T3`, chords on `T7` — and finishes on the punch-in FX track, `T2` in auxiliary mode.
The unit keeps your work as you go, so switching it off loses nothing.

procedures.goal: Create a new project
procedures.result: An empty project opens with the default sounds on all eight instrument tracks.

units.body:
The first session builds one idea in four passes, each on a different track and each teaching one
recording technique: placing steps, recording live, entering chords on steps and performing effects.
Every step works with the factory sounds, so nothing needs loading or configuring first. Follow the
recipes in order; each one assumes the tracks before it already play.

units.title: Recipe — program a first drum beat
units.summary: On drum track `T1`, place a kick on every beat, a snare on the backbeat and hi-hats in between, then turn one hi-hat step into a ratchet with the multiply step component.

facts.text: With `T1` selected in instrument mode, each of the 24 keys plays a different drum sound.
The OP-XY remembers the key you pressed last, and pressing step keys places that sound.
In the default kit the lowest F (`key F3`) is a kick, the G beside it a snare and a C# key a hi-hat.
Holding a drum key and tapping `record` shows only that sound's steps, so it can go on steps already used by another sound.
The multiply component on `natural 3` with value `accidental 3` splits a step into three quick hits; the screen confirms with “divide into 3 trigs”.

steps.keys: key F3 → step 1 → step 5 → step 9 → step 13
steps.note: select the kick, then place it on the four beats

procedures.goal: Add a backbeat snare

steps.note: keep the snare key held throughout; only its steps are shown

procedures.goal: Fill in hi-hats

steps.note: keep the key held and press every other step; TE only says “the C# key”

procedures.goal: Turn one hi-hat into a triple hit

steps.note: keep shift down; step 7 blinks, then multiply and its value are chosen

procedures.result: The seventh step plays three short hi-hat hits.

units.body:
Choose a sound on the keyboard, then press the steps where it should play. The single-sound view
keeps kick, snare and hats out of each other's way, and one step component adds variation.

units.title: Recipe — record a bassline live
units.summary: On bass track `T3`, arm recording with `record + play`, play the line in, lengthen the pattern with extra bars or a slower track scale, and record a knob move as automation.

facts.text: On a synth track such as `T3` the 24 keys play notes chromatically, and `[-]`/`[+]` move them an octave.
`record + play` arms the track; the first step key flashes red while it waits.
Recording begins with the first note you play, or right away if you press `play` instead; `stop` ends it.
A line longer than the pattern plays over itself; `bar + [+]` adds bars, up to four in all.
For still more length, `bar + accidental` raises the track scale, which stretches every step.
Holding `record` and `stop` until the step keys fill red empties the track so you can record again.
During playback, holding `record` while turning an encoder records the movement; `bar + turn E4` smooths its steps.

steps.note: armed — the first step flashes red
the first note starts the take

procedures.goal: Make room for a longer line

steps.note: one more bar, up to four
clears the track before recording the longer take

procedures.goal: Record a knob move into the bassline

units.body:
Practise over the running beat first; once armed, the take starts on your first note. Recorded knob
moves are stored per step, like parameter locks, so they sound stepped until smoothed.

units.title: Recipe — add chords on steps
units.summary: On `T7`, slow the track scale so each step lasts a beat, enter chords by holding their notes and pressing a step, and stretch each chord across the steps it should ring.

facts.text: `T7` holds strings in a new project, a good home for sustained chords.
Play along with the beat first and count on which beats the chords change and how long the part must be.
`bar + accidental 4` sets the track scale to 4, so each step lasts four times as long and four steps make a bar.
To enter a chord, hold its notes on the keyboard and press the step where it should start.
Holding a chord's step and pressing a later step keeps the chord sounding until that step.
If the progression needs more room, `bar + [+]` adds a bar.

procedures.goal: Sequence a chord progression

steps.note: steps now blink four times slower
hold the chord, press its first step
hold that step, press where the chord should end

procedures.result: The chord plays from its step until the chosen end, pattern after pattern.

units.body:
Chords are easier to place than to play in time. A track scale of 4 turns the sixteen steps into
four bars of quarter notes, so a whole progression fits on one page of step keys: hold the chord,
press its step, then stretch it to where the next chord begins. Repeat for each change.

units.title: Recipe — perform with punch-in FX
units.summary: Open the punch-in FX track (`T2` in auxiliary mode), start the song and hold keyboard keys — each key is a different momentary effect, and several can be held at once.

facts.text: In auxiliary mode `T2` is the punch-in FX track.
Each of the 24 keys applies its own effect for as long as you hold it.
Holding several keys stacks their effects.
The punch-in track records and sequences like any other track, so effect moves can become part of the pattern.

procedures.goal: Play effects over the running song

steps.note: one key per effect; hold several to combine them

procedures.goal: Record an effect performance into the pattern

units.body:
Punch-in effects are the performance end of the first session: nothing to set up, just keys to hold
while the song plays. Try single keys first to learn what each does, then combinations. When a move
works, record it like any other part so the pattern repeats it.

units.title: Recipe — make the keyboard velocity-sensitive
units.summary: In the keyboard section of the system settings, set velocity to soft or hard so the built-in keys respond to how hard you play.

facts.text: Velocity lets the built-in keyboard play louder or softer notes depending on how hard you strike the keys.
The velocity setting has three values — off, soft for a gentle touch and hard for a forceful one.
The setting sits in the keyboard section of the system settings.
How much a sound reacts to velocity is set per preset, with the velocity sensitivity in the preset settings.

procedures.goal: Turn on keyboard velocity

units.body:
Match the curve to your touch: soft for a light playing style, hard for a heavy one. The setting only
concerns the OP-XY's own keys — notes from a MIDI keyboard bring their own velocity.

units.title: Recipe — play an external synth over MIDI
units.summary: Set the multi-out to midi before plugging in a TRS-to-DIN cable (USB gear needs no setting), then play and sequence the synth from `T3` in auxiliary mode on the synth's channel, set on `M1`. TE's steps set no project MIDI channel; set clock to both only if the synth should follow the tempo.

facts.text: Synths with DIN MIDI sockets need the multi-out set to midi and a type A TRS-to-DIN cable, DIN end into the synth, jack into the multi-out.
The multi-out does one job at a time, so in midi mode it carries no CV, gate, sync pulse or audio.
Synths with USB MIDI plug into the OP-XY's USB-C port (through an adapter if needed), need no multi-out setting and appear under `com → M3`.
TE's how-tos point to the devices page (`com → M3`) only for USB gear; whether a synth on the multi-out appears there is not documented.
The external MIDI track is `T3` in auxiliary mode; its keyboard and sequencer play the connected synth.
On the track's `M1` page, `E1` sets the MIDI channel — match the channel the synth listens on — while `E2` and `E3` pick bank and program.
TE's steps set only that `M1` channel; the project's midi page (`project → M4`) is not part of them.
Community tools also report that the external MIDI track and midi-engine tracks send without a project MIDI channel; not yet checked on a unit.
On a unit with stock settings, notes in the midi section of the system settings (`com → M1`) is at both, which includes sending.

Clock is its own switch in the same section; at the stock setting (in) `play` and `stop` send no start, stop or clock ticks, and set to both they send start and stop with a constant tick stream (seen over USB).
Community tools report that clock, start and stop go out over TRS MIDI as well as USB under that switch; only USB has been checked on a unit.
`M2` and `M3` hold eight CC slots: `shift` plus an encoder switches a slot on and picks its CC number, turning the encoder sends values, and the moves can be sequenced and recorded.
To sequence several synths, instrument tracks can run the midi engine too; TE's guide still calls it "external", its name before OS 1.0.15.
On OS 1.1.33 the preset browser listed no midi engine, so `T3` is the route to use on that firmware.
To send the notes of a track on one of the OP-XY's own engines as well, community tools say to give it a channel on the project's midi page.

preconditions: nothing is plugged into the multi-out yet

procedures.goal: Control a synth parameter by CC

steps.note: switch the slot on, choose the CC number

procedures.goal: Let the synth follow the OP-XY's tempo and transport
procedures.result: `play` and `stop` send start and stop, and clock ticks run continuously (checked over USB).

units.body:
If nothing sounds, check the channel first, then the cable route (multi-out mode, adapter type)
and, for USB gear, the device's switches under `com → M3`. Leave the project's midi page alone
unless a track on an OP-XY engine should send its notes too. Notes need no clock: switch clock to
both only when the synth's tempo-synced parts should lock to the OP-XY. Bluetooth MIDI synths work
too once the OP-XY advertises itself from the com page.

units.title: Recipe — play an analog synth with CV and gate
units.summary: Set the multi-out to cv/gate, split its tip (pitch CV) and ring (gate) into the synth's CV and gate inputs, then play and sequence from the external CV track, `T4` in auxiliary mode.

facts.text: CV (control voltage) carries the pitch of a note to analog and Eurorack synths; the gate is high only while a note is held and fires the synth's envelopes.
In cv/gate mode the multi-out sends CV on the tip and the gate on the ring.
Use a splitter that breaks tip and ring out to two separate plugs (one that keeps the stereo pair together will not work), sized for the synth — 6.35 mm on many desktop synths, 3.5 mm on Eurorack.
The tip lead goes to the synth's CV (pitch) input and the ring lead to its gate input; on a modular these usually sit on the oscillator and the envelope.
The external CV track, `T4` in auxiliary mode, plays and sequences the connected synth from the keyboard and steps.
The CV output spans −5 V to +5 V and the gate is 5.2 V high; TE does not state the pitch standard (volts per octave), so check the tuning.

procedures.goal: Play an analog synth from the OP-XY
preconditions: the splitter is not yet plugged into the multi-out

steps.note: the synth follows; sequence it like any track

units.body:
One voltage says which note, the other says when. TE's how-to stops after the cabling; the playing
happens on the external CV track. Connect everything before sending notes.

units.title: Recipe — sync a vintage drum machine
units.summary: Set the multi-out to sync24 and run a 3.5 mm-to-DIN-sync cable into the drum machine's sync input; `play` then sends clock, start, stop and reset.

facts.text: Older drum machines usually take DIN sync on their sync socket rather than modern MIDI clock.
Set the multi-out to sync24 so it sends that kind of sync signal.
The connection needs a cable with a 3.5 mm plug for the multi-out and a DIN plug for the drum machine's sync input.
With `play`, clock, start, stop and reset all travel down the cable, so the drum machine follows the OP-XY.

procedures.goal: Clock a DIN-sync drum machine from the OP-XY
preconditions: the sync cable is not yet plugged into the multi-out

steps.note: after connecting the cable; the drum machine starts with the OP-XY

units.body:
The OP-XY is the master here: it sets the tempo and the drum machine follows, starting and stopping
with the OP-XY's transport. Set the jack's mode before plugging in, since it cannot change with a
cable in place.

units.title: Recipe — sync a pocket operator
units.summary: Set the multi-out to sync8, run a plain 3.5 mm cable into the pocket operator's input, set the pocket operator to sync mode SY2 and press `play`.

facts.text: Pocket operators follow a slower clock than most gear; sync8 makes the multi-out send one pulse per eighth note.
An ordinary 3.5 mm cable runs from the multi-out to the pocket operator's input jack.
On the pocket operator, hold its function key (below the rightmost knob) and press bpm until the screen reads SY2.
In SY2 the pocket operator takes sync on its input and plays stereo audio from its output.
`play` on the OP-XY starts the pulse, and both devices run in time.

procedures.goal: Clock a pocket operator from the OP-XY
preconditions: the cable is not yet plugged into the multi-out

steps.note: after connecting the cable and setting SY2 on the pocket operator

units.body:
Because SY2 keeps the pocket operator's output in stereo, you can run its audio into the OP-XY's
audio input or a mixer while it follows the OP-XY's tempo. The OP-XY sets the tempo; the pocket
operator only listens.

units.title: Recipe — loop an external effect pedal
units.summary: Send audio out of the multi-out (set to audio) into the effect, bring the effect back into the audio input, and use the external audio track (`T5` in auxiliary mode) to pick the tracks that go out and balance the return.

facts.text: With the multi-out set to audio, one cable runs from it to the effect's input (adapt 3.5 mm to 6.35 mm for pedals) and a second from the effect's output to the OP-XY's audio input.
On the external audio track's `M1` page, `turn E1` to the audio input (the jack icon) and `click E1` to switch it on.
The external audio track's `M2` page sends instrument tracks to the aux output — turn an encoder per track, click to swap between tracks 1–4 and 5–8.
A single track can also be sent from instrument mode with its aux send, `shift + turn E1` on its `M3` page.
Drive (`E2`), level (`E3`) and mix (`E4`) on the external audio track's `M1` balance the returning signal; drive only affects analog inputs.

procedures.goal: Route tracks through an external effect and back
preconditions: nothing is plugged into the multi-out yet

steps.note: send tracks to the aux output

units.body:
The multi-out is the send, the audio input the return, and the external audio track the control room
in between: its routing decides what goes out, independently of each track's level in the main mix.

units.title: Recipe — play the OP-XY from a MIDI keyboard
units.summary: Plug a USB MIDI keyboard or controller straight into the OP-XY, route its mod wheel, aftertouch, pitch bend and velocity in the preset settings, and filter what it sends under `com → M3`.

facts.text: A USB MIDI keyboard or controller connects to the OP-XY's USB-C port with a USB-C cable or a USB-A adapter and is ready within moments.
A keyboard that needs more power than the port gives can run through a powered USB hub.
Notes arriving on the active track channel play whichever track is selected.
The mod tab of the preset settings (`shift + instrument`) routes mod wheel, aftertouch, pitch bend and velocity to synth parameters.
Under `com → M3` you choose, for that keyboard, whether clock, notes, other messages, timestamp and velocity get through.
A sustain pedal holds notes until it is released, since OS 1.1.15.
Since OS 1.1.17 the sustain pedal leaves arpeggiated notes alone.

procedures.goal: Send the mod wheel to a synth parameter
Choose what the keyboard may send to the OP-XY

units.body:
The OP-XY hosts the keyboard itself, so no computer is involved. Mod routings are saved with each
preset. If the keyboard plays the wrong track, check the active track channel; map knobs with the
CC reference.

units.title: Recipe — use an audio interface with the OP-XY
units.summary: Plug a class-compliant USB audio interface into the OP-XY; the main output plays through it, inputs 1–2 are used by default, and the sample page or the external audio track takes it as the usb source.

facts.text: The interface connects to the OP-XY's USB-C port with a USB-C cable or a USB-A adapter; a powered hub helps if it needs more power.
Interfaces that are USB audio class 1 or class 2 compliant work; ones that need a driver may not.
The OP-XY's main output then plays through the interface; the internal speaker may still sound, so turn the volume knob down or monitor on headphones.
With a multichannel interface the OP-XY uses inputs 1 and 2 unless you choose others.
On the `sample` page, `E1` sets the source to usb and `shift + turn E1` picks the input channel.
TE's audio-interface how-to picks the channel with `turn E2` instead; which gesture OS 1.1.33 uses is not confirmed on a unit.
To hear the interface's inputs live, set the external audio track's input to usb audio with `E1` and `click E1` to activate it.
OS 1.1.25 fixed audio-only interfaces being reported as disconnected.

procedures.goal: Sample from other interface inputs
Monitor the interface's input through the OP-XY

units.body:
Here the OP-XY is the USB host, the reverse of connecting it to a computer. The interface adds
better outputs for studio or stage and more inputs for sampling and live processing.

units.title: Recipe — use the pitchbend strip as a modulator
units.summary: In a track's preset settings, point the pitchbend at a synth parameter and set its amount (negative inverts), then turn the track's bend range off so the strip no longer bends pitch.

facts.text: The pitchbend strip can modulate a synth parameter of your choice instead of, or as well as, the pitch.
The routing lives in the preset settings (`shift + instrument`), under mod — pitchbend target picks the parameter and pitchbend amount sets how far it moves.
A negative amount inverts the modulation.
To stop the strip bending pitch, set the bend range on the `M2` shift layer (`shift + turn E3`) fully counter-clockwise, to off.
The routing belongs to one instrument track, so each track can send the strip to a different parameter.
Saving the track as a preset stores the preset settings too, pitchbend routing included.

steps.note: pitchbend amount, then how much (below zero inverts)

procedures.goal: Stop the strip from bending pitch

steps.note: leaves the preset settings for the envelope page
bend range, fully counter-clockwise to off

procedures.result: The strip now moves only the chosen parameter.

units.body:
Routed to filter cutoff or an effect send, the strip becomes a pressure-sensitive performance
control. Switch the bend range off as well, or every push also bends the pitch.

units.title: Recipe — back up projects to a computer
units.summary: Connect a computer, enter MTP (`com → M4`, with field kit on a Mac) and copy the projects folder; a single project needs its file plus its folder in backups.

facts.text: Connect the OP-XY with its USB-C cable first; MTP is only offered while a computer is attached, and a Mac also needs field kit.
In MTP mode the OP-XY appears as a drive with presets, projects and samples folders; on a Mac, open it from field kit's menu-bar icon if it does not open by itself.
Your projects sit in projects → user, next to a backups folder with each project's history files.
A complete copy of one project takes both the project file and its matching folder inside backups.
To back up every project at once, copy the whole projects folder to a safe place.
From the computer you can also delete projects, rename them and sort them into subfolders; names may use any UTF-8 characters.
Projects can use your own samples and presets, so a full backup copies the samples and presets folders as well.
Backups made while the unit ran OS 1.0.29 may contain corrupted files; make fresh ones on current firmware.

procedures.goal: Copy all projects to a computer
preconditions: the OP-XY is connected by USB-C
field kit is running on a Mac

steps.note: MTP mode; copy the projects folder on the computer
eject when the copy has finished

units.body:
Back up before a firmware update or a factory reset. Copying the whole projects folder also takes
the templates folder and the open project's workspace file along.

units.title: Recipe — load samples from a computer
units.summary: In MTP mode, drag WAV or AIFF files into samples → user or into your own folders inside samples, keep file names simple, then eject with `M4`; the samples appear in the sample library.

facts.text: The internal 8 GB drive has room for thousands of samples.
Connect the unit to the computer, then `com → M4` opens MTP; a Mac needs field kit to see the drive.
samples → user is where the OP-XY saves the samples you record on it, and files dragged there show up in the library.
Folders you create inside samples appear on the unit with their names in square brackets.
The OP-XY reads WAV and AIFF files only.
Stick to letters, digits, spaces, hyphens and # in file names; rename anything else before copying.
When the copy is done, press `M4` to eject, then unplug the cable.
TE's downloadable sound packs go the same way — unzip the pack and drop its folder onto the samples folder.

procedures.goal: Copy samples onto the OP-XY
preconditions: the OP-XY is connected by USB-C
field kit is running on a Mac

steps.note: copy the files into samples on the computer

procedures.goal: Find the new samples on the unit

units.body:
Loading samples is plain file copying once the unit is in MTP mode: organise with folders, keep names
to the allowed characters and convert other formats to WAV or AIFF first. Your own recordings land in
the same user folder, so it is also where you copy them off the unit.

units.title: Recipe — sketch a song fast with the brain
aliases: keep a track out of the brain
units.summary: Build a tiny loop — drums, a one- or two-note bassline, one chord — then record a progression on the brain's keyboard (`T1` in auxiliary mode) and the routed tracks transpose along; take a lead out of the routing on `M2`, and set the key by hand when detection gets it wrong.

facts.text: Start in a new project with a drum beat, a bassline of one or two notes and one chord on a pad or pluck track, one or two bars long.
The brain is `T1` in auxiliary mode.
`bar + accidental 4` on the brain sets its track scale to 4, so its sequence runs four times slower and spans four bars.
The brain has already detected the key and scale of the recorded parts and shows them on screen.
Notes played on the brain's keyboard transpose the routed tracks, chords included, so the simple loop follows a progression.
Parts that must not transpose, such as a lead, come out of the brain's routing on `M2`: turn an encoder to add or remove its track, click to swap between tracks 1–4 and 5–8.
Only routed tracks feed the key detection.
In a new project the lead is `T5`, the dissolve preset lead/gaussian.
A new project routes tracks 3–8 to the brain, the lead among them, and leaves the drum tracks 1 and 2 out.
The routing page draws the tracks the brain hears as boxes 1–8; on the replica an encoder turned clockwise takes its track in and counter-clockwise takes it out, a direction the guide does not give.
The brain's manual mode sits at the counter-clockwise end of `E1` (CC12 at 0 showed manual), and in manual `E2` sets the root and `E3` the scale.

units.body:
The brain does the harmony work: write simple parts in one key, then let the brain move them as you
play. Take any part that should stay put, such as a lead, out of its routing, and give the brain a
key by hand when it guesses wrong on a sparse loop. The progression can also be written rather than
played: one note per chord change on the brain's own pattern, which at track scale 4 lasts four
times as long as the loop. Once it works, arrange it into a song with scenes.

units.title: Recipe — build a song from scenes
units.summary: In arrange, a scene is a snapshot of which pattern every track plays — copy scene 1 into scene 2 with `shift + accidental 2`, give a track a new pattern there with `M1`, then key the scenes into song mode (`shift + arrange`) in playing order and choose whether the song loops.

facts.text: A scene remembers the pattern every track plays and their mix; a project has 99.
Choosing an empty scene fills it with a copy of the one playing, so the next section starts as the last one did.
`shift` and a black key choose scenes 1–9; scenes 10–99 start with `shift + accidental 0` and two more black keys.
In arrange, `M1` adds a new pattern to the selected track; the replica plays it at once in the current scene, which then remembers it, while other scenes keep their own choice.
`shift + arrange` opens song mode, where `shift` and black keys add scenes to the song order one after another and `shift + M1` empties it.
`E1` in song mode turns looping on or off; with it on, the song starts over from its first scene after the last.
OS 1.0.45 added stopping playback at the song's end; the replica stops there with loop off, which is not yet confirmed on a unit.
Since OS 1.1.0 the black keys add scenes in song mode only with `shift` held.
A chorus often needs only one or two tracks to change, such as a busier drum pattern or a new bassline, while the rest carry on; each changed track gets its own pattern in the chorus scene.

units.body:
Scenes turn loops into sections and song mode strings the sections together. Start from a loop that
already works as the verse, copy it into the next scene and change as little as makes the chorus lift:
one new pattern is often enough. Keep adding scenes for a bridge or an ending, then key the song in
the order it should play. With the loop left on, the song starts over at the end, handy while
writing; switch it off for a finished take.

units.title: Recipe — loop one scene
units.summary: Play runs the song, scene after scene. To hear one scene over and over, pick it — in arrange, `shift` and its black key, before play or while playing — and it repeats; or empty the song order in song mode so play keeps to the current scene.

facts.text: Play runs the current song from its first scene even outside song mode, and after a stop it starts from the first scene again.
While the song plays, `shift` and a black key in arrange switch to that scene at once, mid-bar, and from then on the unit repeats it; the song stops moving on.

Picked while stopped (`shift` and its black key, in arrange), a scene is what play starts with instead of the song's first scene, and it repeats — twenty bars of scene 7 in a test on OS 1.1.33, where the song would have moved on to scene 6.
`shift` and the black keys choose scenes only in arrange mode.
`shift + M1` in song mode empties the song order without deleting any scene, taking every scene out of the song's playback.
With the song order empty, play has no song to run, so the scene on screen keeps playing.

units.body:
The OP-XY treats play as "play the song": a new project's song holds scene 1, and a project with a
longer song walks through it from the top on every play. Picking a scene while it plays is the quick
way to stay somewhere, handy while jamming on one section. Clearing the song order keeps play on one
scene for good, until scenes are keyed back into song mode.

units.title: Recipe — make a track pump with the kick (duck)
units.summary: On the track that should make room, such as a bass or a pad, pick the duck LFO on `M4`, set its source to the drum track and choose how deep and how long each dip is; the metronome as source pumps evenly with no drums at all.

facts.text: Duck lowers the level of the track it sits on whenever its source plays, so a bass or pad ducked by the drums dips on every hit and swells back between them.
Choosing duck works like choosing an engine — `shift + M4` opens the list of LFO types, `turn E1` highlights duck and `click E1` takes it.
In a new project the drum kit sits on track 1, so source 1 ducks on every hit of that track, hi-hats included; a kick alone on its own track gives the classic pump.
Turned past the tracks, the source becomes the metronome, and the track then dips on every beat whether or not anything plays.
When the hi-hats share the kick's track, a kick on every beat is better served by the metronome as source, which pumps on the beats only; the drum track itself would duck on every hat too.
Amount on `E2` sets how far the level drops; around 60–80 is a clear pump, lower values a gentle breathing.
Hold on `E3` keeps the level down for a moment and release on `E4` sets how it recovers; keep both short for a tight pump on a fast beat, and lengthen the release for slow swells.

takes it; press `M4` if the page changed

procedures.result: With the drums and the bass playing, the bass dips on every drum hit.

units.body:
Pumping makes room: the bass or pad steps out of the kick's way, so both stay loud without
clashing, and the loop starts to breathe with the beat. The OP-XY does it with an LFO type rather
than a compressor, so it costs no effect slot and works on any instrument track. Duck the parts that
share the kick's low end, usually the bass and long pads, and leave the drums and short plucks
alone.

units.title: Recipe — turn a sound into a pluck
units.summary: A pluck starts at once and dies away while the key is still down — on `M2` set attack 0, a short decay and no sustain, then let the filter envelope close the tone as the note fades.

facts.text: With sustain at 0 a note fades out over the decay time even while its key is held, so the decay sets the length of the pluck.
Decay on `E2` of `M2` grows longer as it is turned clockwise; around 15–30 gives a pluck, higher values a longer ring.
Release runs the other way on the OP-XY, clockwise being shorter, so a crisp pluck wants `E4` well clockwise; lower values let notes ring on after the key comes up.
Clicking any encoder on `M2` swaps between the amp and the filter envelope, so the same four encoders set both.
For a pluck that starts bright and darkens, lower the cutoff on `M3`, raise the envelope amount on `E3`, and give the filter envelope a short decay and no sustain as well.
A little resonance on `E2` of `M3` adds a squelch as the filter closes.

A new project's two plucks show the shape in numbers. Beach bum on `T4` (epiano) and dielectric on `T6` (hardsync) start at attack 0, decay by 20 and 30 and release at 69 and 60; dielectric closes its ladder filter with an envelope amount of 48 and a filter decay of 14.

units.body:
A pluck cuts through a mix because its energy sits at the start of the note. The amp envelope makes
the level drop away and the filter envelope makes the tone drop with it, which is what makes it
sound plucked rather than merely short. With sustain at 0 nothing lingers, so fast sequences and
arpeggios stay clean. Longer decays drift towards bells and keys; a touch of FX II on
`shift + M3` gives the tail back without blurring the attack.

units.title: Recipe — a pad that swells in and fades slowly
units.summary: For a pad, play in poly with a slow attack, a high sustain and a long release — on the OP-XY that is `E4` turned counter-clockwise — open the filter slowly with its envelope and send the track to the reverb on FX II.

facts.text: Chords need play mode poly, `shift + turn E1` on `M2`, so that every note of the chord sounds.
A slow attack on `E1` of `M2` makes each chord fade in rather than start at once; the higher the value, the slower the swell.
A high sustain keeps the chord at full level for as long as the keys are held.
For a long fade after the keys come up, turn release on `E4` counter-clockwise; on the OP-XY lower release values ring longer.
A slow filter attack with a positive envelope amount on `M3` opens the tone as the chord swells, so the pad brightens as it grows louder.
In a new project FX II holds a reverb, so the FX II send, `shift + turn E4` on `M3`, adds space to the pad.

A new project's strings and pad show the shape in numbers. Draemy on `T7` (axis) swells in at attack 50 and bandpasser on `T8` (multisampler) at 35; both hold a high sustain, 76 and 99, and release at 30 and 33. Draemy's filter envelope opens at attack 64 with an envelope amount of only 17, and the track sends 53 to FX II.
Any sound can become a pad; in a new project `T5`, the legato lead, shows every step at work, since the strings on `T7` already swell.

units.body:
A pad is a bed rather than a part: it should arrive softly, hold still and leave slowly, so
nothing about it grabs attention from the beat. The slow amp attack and long release do most of the
work; the slow filter opening adds movement inside each chord. Hold chords for a bar or more and let
them overlap, and duck the pad with the kick if it muddies the low end.

units.title: Recipe — a filter wobble in time with the beat
units.summary: Pick the value LFO on `M4`, aim it at the cutoff on the filter page and give it a tempo-synced speed; the amount sets how far the filter swings.

facts.text: The value LFO turns one encoder of the track's pages up and down by itself, like a hand moving the knob in a loop.
Destination on `E3` picks the page, filter for a wobble, and parameter on `E4` picks the encoder there; cutoff is the first of the filter page's four.
Over the anti-clockwise part of its range the speed follows the tempo, so the wobble stays locked to the beat.
On the plain filter destination the wobble restarts with every note, so each note wobbles the same way; its free twin keeps running across notes.
A moderate cutoff with some resonance on `M3` makes the sweep easy to hear; with the cutoff fully open there is little left to move.

units.body:
A wobble is a filter sweep that repeats in time, the sound of a hand rocking the cutoff knob back
and forth. Faster synced speeds make it busier, slower ones turn it into a long rise and fall over
the bar. Parameter locks on the LFO speed for single steps give the classic change of pace in the
middle of a phrase.

units.title: Recipe — a squelchy acid bass
units.summary: On the bass track pick the ladder filter, set a low cutoff, high resonance and a strong, short filter envelope, then play mode legato with a little portamento so that overlapping notes slide.

facts.text: Picking a filter type from `shift + M3` takes you back to `M1`, so press `M3` to go on with the filter.
A low cutoff, high resonance and a large envelope amount with a short filter decay make each note open and snap shut, the acid squelch.
In legato play mode one note sounds at a time, and portamento makes overlapping notes glide from one pitch to the next.
Parameter locks on the cutoff or the envelope amount for single steps give the line its accents.

units.body:
Acid lives in the filter: a bright snap at the start of each note that closes almost at once, with
resonance singing at the cutoff. Program the line with some notes overlapping so they slide (a note
slides into the next only when it lasts past the next one's start; written end to end they only
touch, and the next starts anew), and a few locked accents where the filter opens further. Riding the cutoff live while the pattern loops is
half the fun.

units.title: Recipe — sample a loop and play it in slices
aliases: record a loop onto a key
slice a sample into the keys
units.summary: On a drum track, record a loop onto its top key from the `sample` page, then hold that key and press `M1` to cut it into even slices that spread over the keyboard and choke each other, ready to replay in a new order.

facts.text: Slicing is the drum sampler's, and a new project has drum kits on `T1` and `T2`.
On a drum track the take goes to the key you press on the record page (it lights up), so open `sample` first and choose the key there.
On the record page `turn E1` picks the source (the built-in mic, line in or USB), `turn E3` the gain and `turn E4` the threshold.
Holding `M1` arms the recorder and the take begins once the input passes the threshold, so a low threshold catches the loop's first hit.
Holding a key and pressing `M1` opens the slicer on that key's sample.
Even mode splits the sample into equal parts and `turn E4` sets how many; sixteen suits a one-bar loop cut into sixteenths.
The slices spread over the keyboard and choke each other, so one slice sounds at a time, as in a chopped break.
The replica fills the keys from the lowest, F3, upward (the guide says only that the slices fill the keyboard), so a loop kept on the top key, E5, stays whole there for up to 23 slices.
The slicer offers cancel and done, which the guide does not place on keys; the replica puts done on `M4` and cancel on `M3`.
For a drum loop with clear hits, transient mode cuts at the loudest ones instead; a sample with fewer hits gives fewer slices than `E4` asks for.

units.body:
Slicing turns a recording into an instrument: once the loop is spread over the keys, step-enter the
slices in a new order, repeat the kick slice, or play the hits live against the original loop on
E5. Even slices keep the loop's timing grid, so a straight beat cut into sixteenths lines up with
the sequencer's steps; tap mode suits phrases that do not sit on a grid.
